> **Write permission follows the mode the user gave the agent (2026-11-18, R10, D-22, §4.13; A-285, Ada's decisions,
> revised the same day).** Bypass merges and lands at once; ask answers a typed approval request bound to the
> manifest, which the harness presents; a forbidding mode is refused. The launcher (kiln passes each agent's mode) or
> the harness sets the policy, the stricter of consumer and volume governs, unset merges at once and lands under
> approval, and an agent never raises
> its own. Signed work is provenance, not permission. This closes, once built, "No grant can be issued on Linux from
> the CLI" (A-201's entry): under bypass the daemon grants its own landing. The first reading (a human-only proof,
> fs-server's options A–E) is withdrawn by Ada; its piece 2 (the presentation nonce and the signed `Grant`,
> d1a46ae9) is reverted, and the SSH verifier (1c31d1c7) is kept for signed work. **Built (2026-11-18): a volume's
> policy and landing under it** — `WriteAct`, `WriteMode { Bypass, Ask, Forbid }`, `WritePolicy { merge, land }`,
> `PolicySubject`, the issuer-proven `SetPolicy` (refused `Forbidden` on a consumer-bound channel), `Policy`,
> `Refusal::PolicyForbids { act, by }`; bypass lands in the presenting request, ask answers the approval request,
> forbid refuses (`crates/server/tests/write_policy.rs`, 4 of 4 on macOS arm64; the bypass test red with bypass
> turned off). **To measure** (the supervisor's): a bypass landing plans twice, the presentation and the granted
> landing's own plan; its cost over a granted landing of the same volume (wall time and shard time, 1, 1,000 and
> 10,000 files) says whether the granted landing should reuse the presentation's plan. **Owed, in order** (types
> agreed with g262, slates-api's owner):
> - **built (2026-11-18):** `Present` (never writes, whatever the mode) and merges under the policy (forbid refused,
>   ask `MergeApprovalRequired` then `SubmitApproved` of exactly that increment, unset merges at once); 7 of 7 in
>   `write_policy.rs`, the presentation test red with present-only broken;
> - **built (2026-11-18):** launcher-class proofs (grant, policy, merge approval, enroll, revoke) verify under the
>   issuer secret or the launcher secret the anchor holds (g262's region, A-299), and a policy names the version it
>   replaces, so a captured proof sets nothing once the policy moved (`Refusal::PolicyChanged`);
>   `launcher_secret.rs` 1 of 1 (red with the launcher secret ignored), `write_policy.rs` 8 of 8 (the replay test red
>   with the version check removed);
> - **built (2026-11-18):** a consumer's own policy (its record, set on the channel and reaching every shard's bound
>   slots before the answer, as a revocation does), held on the agent's own shard before routing: forbid refused,
>   ask turns a landing into a presentation and a merge into a held submit (`SubmitHeld`, `EditSubmitHeld`), bypass
>   passes to the volume's mode, so the stricter governs; `write_policy.rs` 9 of 9, the consumer test red with the
>   gate removed;
> - **built (2026-11-18):** the MCP and SDK land verb follows the policy (it already sent `Land`; its promises now
>   say so); `assert_materialize_lands_under_a_bypass_policy` over MCP;
> - signed work: a merge or landing may carry an SSH signature, checked and recorded (verified with its signer,
>   unsigned, invalid with its reason), and a volume may require signed merges — **built for merges (2026-11-17) and
>   for landings (2026-11-18), A-321**;
> - the end-to-end proof on adacachy: a bypass agent's landing written at once, an ask agent's after approval, a
>   signed merge verified and an invalid signature reported. **The landing half ran on Linux (2026-11-18):**
>   `write_policy.rs` 9 of 9 on Linux x86_64 and arm64, a real daemon and client over a real target directory (GitHub
>   run 44240968028, main 821d12f7d); signed work stays owed;
> - **built (2026-11-18, found by the two-node filesystem-server flow):** an agent approves no landing of its own. A
>   landing's grant verified its proof and manifest but not its channel, so a consumer-bound channel holding a genuine
>   launcher-class proof was granted, where a policy setting and a merge's approval are refused `Forbidden` whatever
>   the proof. `grant_verb` now refuses it first (`grant_by_consumer`): `an_agent_cannot_approve_its_own_landing` (red
>   without the guard: granted) and `fs_server.rs`'s server-node agent
>   (`docs/bugs/2026-11-18-an-agents-own-channel-could-approve-its-own-landing.md`). **Built the same day, its
>   siblings:** `Enroll` and `Revoke` verified the proof alone, so a consumer-bound channel holding a genuine proof
>   could enroll a fresh consumer (binding a channel that escapes its own consumer policy) or revoke another agent's.
>   Both now refuse `Forbidden` before the proof (`enroll_by_consumer`, `revoke_by_consumer`):
>   `an_agent_cannot_enroll_or_revoke_a_consumer`, each guard red-checked alone (GitHub run 44274679371, Linux x86_64:
>   without the enroll guard the agent's channel was handed consumer 11; without the revoke guard its revocation
>   answered `Ok`; with both, `write_policy.rs` 11 of 11, `consumers.rs` 1 of 1, the server's unit tests 311 passed,
>   clippy clean). The sweep of every launcher-proof check (the six callers of `landing::proven_by_launcher`, and
>   consensus control) found no other: consensus control already refuses any principal but an OS account.

> **W1 would have let a work off its green's shard merge under one volume's write policy: fixed before W1 landed
> (2026-11-18, g231; A-307, §4.16).** A-285 judges a merge's policy from the work's and the green's records on one
> partition; W1 (A-247) asks the green's owner for the verdict of a work on another shard, where neither shard holds
> both records, and its gate parks a verb before the verb runs, so a `SubmitApproved` would have reached the owner
> before its proof was checked. The work's mode now travels with the ask, the owner judges the stricter of the two, and
> an approval leaves the work's shard only once it verifies. Test:
> `a_merge_off_its_greens_shard_follows_both_volumes_write_policy` (eight shards). A-285's own tests run one shard.

> **W1 would have let a merge record reach its holders before its route: fixed before W1 landed (2026-11-17, g231;
> A-298, §4.16).** A-255 holds a version's merge record, which carries its submit's completion, until the submitting
> work's catalog register is committed, checking it on the green's owner shard. W1 (A-247) puts most works on other
> shards, whose records the owner's partition does not hold, so the check passed for them unseen; merging the two also
> failed to compile where A-255's record named a `work_id` that W1's owner half does not have. A submit off its green's
> shard now asks for its verdict only once its work's register is committed, waiting on the work's own shard
> (`work_home::Need::Route`). Test: `a_submit_off_its_greens_shard_waits_for_its_works_catalog_record_before_its_verdict`
> (three nodes at `f = 1`, two shards each, the holders withholding work catalogs). A-255's own test runs one shard a
> node, so every work there shares its green's shard.

> **A rebased work was restated into other bytes: fixed (perf, 2026-11-09, §4.16 "Rebase, the only corrective path").**
> A rename over a file, rebased and submitted, left the destination with the moved bytes followed by its own: 20 bytes
> where 10 were renamed in. An edit that replaced bytes came back with the work's own byte kept and an inserted one
> deleted. `rebased_from` restated a rename as a whole-file insert, and restated net ops (one pass over the head) at
> their head offsets in a journal that is replayed one operation at a time. A rename is now restated as a `Rename`, and
> each op where the pass stands when it reaches it. The oracle `a_rebased_work_submits_as_it_would_have` holds a rebased
> work to the same answer and head as the same work submitted, after a generated work merged ahead of it: 400 cases,
> red-checked on each fix. `docs/bugs/2026-11-09-a-rebased-work-was-restated-into-other-bytes.md`.
>
> **A work based before its file was replaced was spliced into the replacement: fixed (2026-11-19, A-612, g267; found
> by A-596's oracle; §4.16 "The verdict": "delete against modify in either direction").** A work edited a file at its
> base; after that base the green unlinked the file and made it again, renamed another file onto it, or replaced it
> beneath a directory's rename. The verdict found the path's content present (`merge_content`), mapped the work's ops
> through the replacement's one-insert delta (`insert_whole`) and spliced them at the new file's end: accepted. A rename
> of the file, so based, moved the replacement (`merge_rename` checked only that the source named something). Now the
> green records the last version that removed the file at each path (`Green::file_removed`: an unlink, a rename away,
> a rename onto it; rebuilt by replay, never folded), and a work based before it is refused `DeleteModify`, a rename of
> it `RenameRename`, whatever stands at the path now. Tests (`crates/merge/src/engine/unseen_bytes_tests.rs`): the
> three replacements, each refused, the same edit at the head accepted; the rename of each refused. Red on the Mac
> Studio with the fix reversed (kiln r613: made again, accepted as version 3, for the edit and for the rename), green
> with it (`cargo test -p slates-merge --lib`, 43 of 43). A-596's oracle bases works before replacements again. Bug
> record: `docs/bugs/2026-11-19-a-work-based-before-its-file-was-replaced-is-spliced-into-the-replacement.md`.
> Siblings seen, not changed (reading only): a mode or attribute change to a file replaced after the work's base is
> judged by that dimension's own last change, so it may land on the replacement; a rename whose source is a symlink or
> a hard link replaced after the base moves the new one (`file_removed` records files).

> **A truncate based before an append removed the appended bytes: fixed (2026-11-19, A-612, g267; found by A-596's
> oracle; §4.16 "The verdict", "Splice"; `slates_vfs::algebra`).** A work removed a file's tail to its end, composed as a
> truncate; after its base another work appended at that end. The two meet only at the truncate's edge, so the verdict
> accepted, and the splice cut to the end of the head's file (`apply`, `OpKind::Truncate`), removing the append the
> work never saw: a lost update; the version's delta stated four bytes where eight left. A rebase restated it as a
> truncate to the new length, and a rename's edits (A-547) cut the same way. Now a truncate mapped to a head that grew
> past its span is the delete of that span (`at_head`, the interval algebra's hunk over base bytes, disjoint from an
> append at its end by the edge rule), in `merge_content` and `edits_after_rename`, so both changes are kept and the
> delta, the chain entry, the history and a rebase's journal state exactly what left. Tests
> (`crates/merge/src/engine/unseen_bytes_tests.rs`): the submit (comments followed through its delta, exact), the
> rebase (a delete in the journal), the rename's edits, and the sweep of truncates against changes at their cut in both
> directions (an overwrite ending at the cut, an insert at the cut and an append kept; an overwrite inside the span and
> a shorter truncate conflicts; the same truncate identical). Red on the Mac Studio with the fix reversed (kiln r613:
> the file `<1>\n` each time), green with it (43 of 43). A-596's oracle bases truncating works behind the head again.
> Bug record: `docs/bugs/2026-11-19-a-truncate-based-before-an-append-removes-the-appended-bytes.md`.

> **Two inserts at one point conflicted in one order only: fixed (2026-11-19, A-668, g306; found by A-659's
> restatement; §4.16 "Position mapping", "The verdict"; D-27).** Two works insert at one point, each based before the
> other, one of them also overwriting the bytes from that point or truncating from it. Landed first, that one made the
> plain insert accepted ahead of both its changes; landed second, the two conflicted as inserts at one point. The walk
> through a delta (`crate::map::map_through_one`) stopped at the first operation starting at or after a range's end,
> and a point's end is its start, so canonical order (overwrite and truncate before insert at one offset) hid the
> insert behind it. D-27 decides it: a conflict in both orders, since accepting one ahead of the other chooses an order.
> Now the walk stops at an operation starting after the range's end, or at its end for a range that is not a point
> (`crate::map::lies_past`), and A-659's restatement walks the same way. Tests: `crates/merge/src/map/tests.rs` (the
> point meets an insert behind an overwrite and behind a truncate at it; both orders conflict at the verdict); A-659's
> stack oracle generates the shape, and a work between that a replica refuses must still land alone over the stack's
> works below. Windows x86_64 on jupiter (the macOS run owed): red with the fix out, 3 of 4 failing (the map test, the
> verdict's both orders, and the stack oracle, which met the pair by itself); green `slates-merge --lib` 166 of 166, fmt
> clean. The merged tree (A-668 at 92038d5aa over main e3234e618, r81): 179 of 180 (main's 178 and A-668's 2, both
> passing), fmt clean; the one failure, A-626's copy oracle census meeting no nested copy whose inner copy replaced a
> tree (0 of 30 nested pairs), is not A-668's, since that oracle bases every work at the head and so never reaches the
> walk A-668 changed, and it passed alone again (r131, 3 of 37); its owner's, filed. Bug record:
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-19-two-inserts-at-one-point-conflicted-in-one-order-only.md`. That census failure is fixed
> (2026-11-19, A-672, g307): one fixed history, run first, meets every case the copy oracle's census counts, whatever
> the seed, and the generated histories add to the counts (macOS arm64, Mac Studio, kiln r4: `cargo test --locked -p
> slates-merge --lib copy` 34 passed, the fixed history meeting all eleven cases; the other platforms' runs owed).

> **A work naming more than 65,535 paths aliased them: fixed (2026-11-19, A-621, g267; found on the push path by g225,
> A-618; §4.16 "Data model").** An op named its path by a 16-bit index, and interning answered `u16::MAX` for every name
> past the 65,535th, so the 65,536th and every later name of one work aliased one path; the deriver's index lookup,
> the verdict's reading of a rename's source and an attribute's name, and the server's laying-in of an attribute's
> value (which skipped it) narrowed the same way, and interning scanned every name, O(n²). Now an index is 64 bits in
> memory and on the wire: the ops document's version 2, with u64 path and op counts and 34-byte op records, and the
> chain entry's version 5. Interning looks a name up in an ordered map, and decode refuses a table naming a path twice
> (`DuplicatePath`); versions 1 and 4 are refused `BadVersion`. A work names as many paths as its caller's admission
> allows: a kernel tree's first push (about 97,000 files) is one work, and g225's interim refusal of a work past
> 65,535 names (A-618, `TooManyNames`) can go. Tests (`crates/merge/src/ops_doc/tests.rs`, moved there from
> `tests/ops_doc.rs`; `chain_entry`'s): 65,537 distinct names each their own through canonicalization, encode and
> decode; the comparison counter (doubling the names less than triples the comparisons, where a scan quadruples them);
> the determinism gate at that size (built twice, names declared in opposite orders, same bytes); the golden vectors
> re-derived for version 2 (`11ede55e…d370763b`) by an independent encoder and BLAKE3 that reproduce version 1's; the
> chain entry keeping an op's index past 16 bits. Green on the Mac Studio (kiln r692: `slates-merge --lib` 60 of 60,
> `slates-server --lib` green and merge-origin tests 31 of 31, fmt clean). Red with the old scan and 16-bit index
> restored inside the new types (r705: all four failed; doubling the names took 2,149,245,934 comparisons against
> 537,633,163). Owed to main: the merge crate's integration tests updated by reading (`tests/increment.rs`,
> `tests/special.rs`, `tests/chain_replay.rs`) and the server's suites. Bug record:
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-19-a-work-naming-more-than-65535-paths-aliased-them.md`. Its format change made no anchor layout
> bump (filed below, "Formats the segment keeps changed without a layout bump"); since the layout 12 of A-626 part 3
> (2026-11-19), every segment a build before it wrote is refused at adoption.

> **Formats the segment keeps changed without a layout bump: found open (2026-11-19, g307 by reading, on main's ruling for
> A-626 part 3; `crates/anchor/src/layout.rs`, `crates/db/src/op.rs` `Op::GreenAdvanced`).** The partition's op log and
> snapshots live in the anchor segment and hold every green's chain entries (`Op::GreenAdvanced`, the chain entry's bytes
> with the increment's ops document inside) and checkpoints (`Op::GreenCheckpointed`). The ops document's version 2 and
> the chain entry's version 5 (A-621), and the ops document's version 3 (A-646 part 2b), changed those formats with the
> segment's `LAYOUT_VERSION` left at 11. A daemon of either change adopting a segment an older one wrote would meet each
> older entry as `BadVersion` mid-service, the green fenced, where a bump refuses the segment once, typed, at adoption,
> before anything is served. The layout 12 of A-626 part 3 covers both from now on: every segment written before it is
> refused at adoption. Owed: the guard, a structural test tying every format version the segment keeps (the ops
> document, the chain entry, the checkpoint, the origin, the work log, every record a partition persists) to
> `LAYOUT_VERSION`, so a format change without a bump fails the build.

> **The identity's recount is no oracle on a green folded past a copy: found open (2026-11-19, A-626 part 3, g307, by
> reading; `Green::head_identity_from_scratch`, `Green::copied_tree_entries`).** The recount takes out what each copy
> made after the green's restore brought, reading the copy's source at the version before it (since part 3, through
> the copy's fix). A green built from its origin counts every copy, so once its histories are folded past a copy
> (`fold_history_before`, which also lets the copy's kept fix go), the recount reads below the floor for it. Only the
> recount is affected: the running identity and every sum moved below the head read what a copy brought only for a copy
> above the floor. No test folds a green holding a copy and then recounts it. Owed: a recount for such a green that
> reads no history below the floor and costs no fold a walk of a copied tree (a restore's `copies_before` comes from the
> checkpoint's sum; a fold has no independent sum to take), and a test that folds past a copy and recounts.

>    removal recorded, unless the increment removes it itself, and the link stands alone at the path. Before, the green

> **A rebased work restates its links after its own renames and removals: fixed (2026-11-19, A-663, g307; found by
> A-646's sweep, g267, by reading; §4.16 "Rebase, the only corrective path"; `Green::rebased_from`).** A clean rebase
> restated the verdict's effects as the work's journal in the verdict's order: content first (renames, creates,
> unlinks), then the metadata dimensions, hard links among them. A volume has real inodes, so a link restated after a
> rename or removal of the node it names met the path afterwards:
> - `ln g l; mv f g` put `l` on `f`'s file, not `g`'s old one, and the journal composed again did too;
> - a link to a node the work renames was restated after the node left its path (A-646's made node resolved to the
>   rename's source), in either order (`mv f m; ln m l`, `ln f l; mv f m`);
> - a link to a node the work also removes met an empty path.
>
> Found with them: a link made where the head holds another (`rm h; ln f h`) was restated with no removal of the
> head's, so the rebased work's next submit was refused `LinkOverExisting`.
>
> Fixed: the effects are restated in the order a volume replays them (`in_replay_order`): each link just before the
> first effect that moves its node away from the name it names it by or removes it there, after the effect that made
> its node, and a link made over the head's after that link's removal. Tests: `crates/merge/src/engine/restate_tests.rs`,
> each case red first, and an oracle over generated works holding four readings equal (the work's own order over the
> head with real inodes, the green that accepts it, the restated journal replayed, and the green that accepts that
> journal composed again), with a census of every case. Evidence (Windows x86_64, jupiter, 2026-11-19, the Mac Studio
> offline; the macOS run owed): red over main's engine 6 of 6 failing (`cargo test --locked -p slates-merge --lib
> restate_tests` at 91d14b44d); green over main at 78a670256, `cargo test --locked -p slates-merge --lib` 147 of 147
> (main's 141 and the 6 new), the oracle's census over 256 works 153 agreed, 102 refused typed, 1 conflict, with every
> case met (a rename over the link's name 5, rename then link 30, link then rename 32, removal 13, made again 26, to a
> made file 8); `cargo fmt -p slates-merge -- --check` clean.

> **A name's node replaced by a new file is composed as an edit of that node in place: found open (2026-11-19, A-663's
> oracle, g307, by reading; §4.16 "Composition at seal"; A-646's decision; `crate::increment`).** `rm x; touch x`
> (unlinked then made again) and `touch n; mv n x` (a new file renamed over `x`, the write-and-rename pattern) both
> compose to a delete of `x`'s base bytes and the new bytes, with no create (`apply_create`'s in-place replacement,
> `apply_rename`'s re-rooting). A hard link naming `x`'s node, the base's or one the work made before, then reads the new
> bytes: the green keeps the link on `x`, whose content changed. POSIX gives the link the old file and `x` a new one
> (A-646: "a later file at a path the node left is another node"). A rename onto a name the work made a hard link at is
> refused instead, typed (`PathKindConflict` from `check_no_file_directory_collision`), a file and a link at one name
> being among the deriver's compositions owed. A-663's oracle generates neither. Since A-669 a work that wrote to the
> old node first is refused, typed (`Unsupported`), never composed with its write lost. Owed: the replacement composed
> as the node model says (a new node at the name, the link's node handed on as `Green::node_moves` hands one), a
> failing test first, and the oracle's works widened to it.

> **A write to a file a hard link also names was lost when the work then removed the file or renamed another over it:
> fixed (2026-11-19, A-669, g307; found by A-663's oracle on its first run, Windows x86_64 (jupiter); §4.16 "Composition
> at seal"; A-646's decision; `crate::increment`, `Green::merge_handed`).** With the base holding `g` and a hard link
> `h` to it, a work that appended to `g` and then removed it composed to `Unlink g` alone: the deriver dropped a removed
> file's content operations (`apply_unlink` cleared them), and the green handed `g`'s node to `h` with the head's bytes
> (`Green::hand_over`). POSIX keeps the write at `h`, as the work's own volume does; the green and the rebase did not.
> A rename over the file (`mv f g` after the write) lost it the same way, and so did a write handed on through a rename
> (`mv g f; echo w >> f; rm f`).
>
> Fixed by the rule A-646's decision now states: the link a removed or replaced home leaves its node to takes the node
> as the version leaves it. The deriver keeps a removed file's writes and declares them at the least base link that
> still names its node as the base did (`heirs_of_writes`, each link's node fixed when the journal makes it); the engine
> makes that link the node's home with the writes, its mode and its attributes (`Green::merge_handed`); a rebase
> restates the work's own form, the writes on the home and then its removal (`Green::handed_in`). Refused, typed
> (`Unsupported`) rather than lost: a write whose node only links the work made still name, and a write to a file the
> work then made again at its name (the entry above). Tests: five cases in `crates/merge/src/engine/restate_tests.rs`,
> each red first, and A-663's oracle, whose works no longer leave the case out, with it in the census. Evidence (Windows
> x86_64, jupiter, 2026-11-19; the macOS run owed): red over main's engine, the five cases and the oracle failing
> (`cargo test --locked -p slates-merge --lib restate_tests` at 59ee404f5, 6 of 11, A-663's five passing); the first
> green run's oracle found a link resolved through the links standing at the seal (`ln h l; rm h`), fixed in the same
> change; green 152 of 152 over main at 0e755c9b1 (`cargo test --locked -p slates-merge --lib` at 72177dcd7, and at
> 5f6cc2d3a with the census showing the case rather than requiring it), fmt clean; merged with main at f6ec36df2
> (A-659's stacks), 169 of 169 at 85b5b7eee, fmt clean. Bug record:
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-19-a-write-to-a-file-a-hard-link-names-was-lost-with-the-file.md`.

> **A write to a file a later version linked was lost when the work removed the file: fixed (2026-11-19, A-670, g307;
> found by A-669's sweep, by reading; §4.16 "The verdict"; A-646's decision; `Green::leaves_to_an_unseen_link`).** A
> work based before a version that links `a` to `g` writes to `g` and removes it, or renames another file over it. Its
> deriver saw no link, so the writes went with the node in its own volume; the verdict accepted the removal, since a
> link made to a file records no change of the file, and the commit handed `g`'s node to `a` with the head's bytes.
> The same in a stack (A-659): an upper's base, its lower's post-state, never holds a link another work made while the
> stack was in flight, and the restated upper is judged as based on a version after that link.
>
> Fixed: the verdict refuses removing a file, or renaming another over it, when a link naming it now was made after
> the work's base and no link the base had to it outlives the work, unless the increment hands the node on itself
> (A-669): delete against modify, or rename against rename. The increment cannot say whether the work wrote, so a
> removal without a write is refused alike; the rebased work removes the file again, the link keeping the node. A
> stack's upper is refused alike for a link another version made under the stack (`upper_unseen_links`). A-643's
> whole-state model states the rule; A-663's oracle heads may link a file late. Tests: four verdict cases and a stack
> case, red first; a base link outliving the work keeps the removal accepted; A-659's stacks carry an upper's write
> handed on to a link (the question A-669 left, answered by test, nothing to fix). Evidence (Windows x86_64, jupiter,
> 2026-11-19; the macOS run owed): red over main's engine at cac45de71, 6 failing (the four cases, the stack case and
> the oracle's fixed history), 14 passing; green 178 of 178 over main at 6e42e7a2c (e8c10097e), fmt clean. Bug record:
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-19-a-write-to-a-file-a-later-version-linked-was-lost-with-the-file.md`.

> §4.16 "Rebase, the only corrective path"; `Green::rebased_from`).**
> 1. *A symbolic link made where the head holds another* (`rm s; ln -s t2 s`) is restated as the `Symlink` alone, as the

> **A chain entry's encoding scanned every op of the increment for each splice: fixed (2026-11-19, A-632, g267; found
> by A-621's reading; §4.16 "Commit", `crates/merge/src/chain_entry.rs`).** `put_applied` and `take_applied` found a
> splice's declared ops (`declared_ops`), and a copy's source version (`declared_copy`, A-586), by scanning every op of
> the increment for each effect: O(effects × ops), about 5 × 10⁹ visits for 50,000 splices of a 100,000-op increment,
> on the owner's commit and every holder's replay. An index built once per entry encoded or decoded (`Declared`)
> replaces both, so each op is visited once; the entry's bytes are unchanged. Test: a counter of the ops visited, a
> thousand splices visiting a thousand ops on encode and a thousand on decode. Red with the index rebuilt for every
> effect: a million each way (kiln r786); green on r786 (`slates-merge --lib` 79 of 79) and merged with main on r810
> (92 of 92). Bug record:
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-19-a-chain-entry-scanned-its-increment-for-every-splice.md`.

> **An edit after a rename was accepted and lost: fixed (2026-11-19, A-547, g225; found by perf, 2026-11-09, §4.16
> "Composition at seal").** The verdict now maps the destination's ops through what changed the source since the work's
> base and splices them into the bytes the rename moves (`Green::edits_after_rename`; an edit meeting such a change is
> an overlap conflict, never dropped); the chain entry's `Copied` carries them (tag `COPIED_SPLICED`, a rename alone
> encoding as before), replay applies them, and the rebase restates them after the `Rename`
> (`an_edit_after_a_rename_over_a_file_is_merged_with_the_renamed_bytes`, `crates/merge/src/engine.rs`; the parked
> server test is no longer ignored). Owed: the rebase oracle's generator still stays out of this case. What was there:
> A work renames `a` over `b`, writes at the end of `b`, and submits. It is accepted, and `b` holds `a`'s head
> bytes alone. This is on main with no rebase involved. The verdict skips a renamed-into path's content ops
> (`decide_content`) and copies the source's head bytes (`merge_rename`). The chain entry's `Applied::Copied { dst, from }`
> has no ops to replay, and replay maps an entry's effects before committing any, so a second `Spliced` effect cannot
> carry them. Owed: `Copied` carries the destination's ops, mapped through the source's deltas (a chain-entry format
> change), and the rebase restates them after the `Rename`. Red test, parked: `an_edit_after_a_rename_over_a_file_is_merged_with_it`
> (`crates/server/tests/green_post_state.rs`). The rebase oracle's generator stays out of this case until then.

> **The live record period visited every live volume of a shard in one turn: sliced (2026-11-17, A-200, CLAUDE.md
> "Bounded work everywhere"; g230).** `live_ship::period` ran each live volume's period work (`follow_candidates`,
> `resolve`, the whole record or image it owed, `pending_sends`) for all of the shard's volumes inside one
> `call_within` turn, a cost that grew with the volumes the shard owns while its clients waited. It now runs in slices
> of about the shard's step quantum (`period_slice`, counted `fleet.live.period_slices` against `fleet.live.periods`),
> each resuming after the last volume visited. Test: `a_shards_live_volumes_are_visited_by_the_period_in_slices_and_none_is_starved`
> (the quantum injected to one volume a slice, `Daemon::inject_live_period_quantum`). **Owed (measurement, the
> supervisor's):** the owner shard's longest step and its clients' p99 with thousands of live volumes, before and after.

> **A burst on a live volume shipped the whole volume: fixed (2026-11-17, AC-8.9, A-200 amended; g230).** The owner's
> credit was a fixed two entries (`live_ship::CREDIT`, R3 debt, with `RETAIN = 4`), and a publication it turned away
> left the volume owing a whole record: its next entry carried every byte of the volume to every holder. Every barrier
> publishes, so many writers on one volume put several publications inside one round trip, and the third shipped the
> volume (sixteen writers of half a page each, both holders held off their shards for a quarter of a liveness window:
> `a_burst_of_writes_to_a_live_volume_ships_its_changes_not_the_volume`, `crates/server/tests/fleet.rs`: on the fixed
> credit 13 of the 16 publications were turned away and the log took two more whole copies of the half-MiB volume; with
> the change none, no whole record, 16 entries and 16 in flight at once; this Mac, debug, 2026-11-17). Now the entries
> not yet durable and the retained tail are held to the wire bytes of the whole state an install would send
> (`slates_db::live::Bounds::of_whole`), so the volume ships whole only where that is the cheaper catch-up; the model
> and unit tests run in bytes (`crates/db/tests/live.rs`, three new). Bug record
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-17-a-burst-on-a-live-volume-shipped-the-whole-volume.md`.
> - **Owed (measurement, the supervisor's):** many writers on one large live volume, before and after: whole records,
>   bytes shipped, and the write's p50/p99/p999 (`fleet.live.whole`, `fleet.live.refused.no_credit`).
> - **Fixed the same day:** a lane shipped a holder's entries one exchange at a time (`live_ship::ship_lane`), so a burst
>   of `n` entries reached a holder in `n` round trips; the entries a holder lacks now go as one batch a congestion
>   window (`take_batch`, `serve_entries`, request kind 26; A-200's second amendment of 2026-11-17; 25 collided with
>   A-288's work route on merge, caught and fixed the same day, every fleet request kind now held distinct by a test). Owed (measurement):
>   a stalled holder's catch-up time and a burst's last-write latency, before and after, on a WAN-shaped path.

> **git's history, Mercurial and Subversion join the workload roster (2026-11-17, Part 6 "Real workloads"; A-289;
> Ada's goal of 2026-11-18).** Until now one 15-line git script was all the version control any route ran: no clone,
> merge, rebase, gc or repack, no mapped packs, no worktree, and no Mercurial or Subversion at all. The roster now runs
> `git-history` (a hard-linked local clone, branch, merge, rebase, stash, a worktree, tag, push, pull, gc, a full
> repack, verify-pack, fsck), `mercurial` (a named branch and merge, tag, bookmark, a hard-linked clone and its first
> commit, rebase, push, a shared store, verify) and `subversion` (an FSFS repository and SQLite working copies:
> checkout, commit, branch, switch, update back and forward, merge, tag, cleanup, verify, dump) on every leg that runs
> the roster: macOS's NFS loopback mount, the Linux lane's NFSv3 adapter and NFSv4.2, Linux FUSE inside containers
> (`oci-linux`) and the live virtio-fs guest. Each clone prints how many of its files have two names, so a mount that
> cannot link or reports a wrong link count differs. All legs share one environment
> (`slates_conformance::workload::ENVIRONMENT`), and the host determinism gate
> (`the_version_control_workloads_run_byte_identically_twice_on_the_host`) runs each twice in two directories a second
> apart and holds them identical: its first run (2026-11-17, macOS 26, git 2.50.1, Mercurial 7.2) found Mercurial's
> `fncache` written in a different order by each process (a Python set; now one hash seed), and a clone's reflog and
> `undo.desc` naming its source by absolute path (now excluded with the reason). **Closed in the same change:** a

> **Windows symbolic links through the WinFsp drive: built (2026-11-09, §4.6; A-275; landed 2026-11-17).** Every
> `CreateSymbolicLinkW` on the drive answered `ERROR_INVALID_FUNCTION`, so git and npm could make no link there and a
> link made on Linux showed as a reparse point Windows could not follow. Now a volume symlink is the Windows symbolic
> link: WinFsp's resolver follows it, a relative target is stored with `/` and shown with `\`, a directory link keeps
> its type in the inode's Windows bits (image 26, delta 9, an older reader refusing them), and making one asks for
> `SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege` as NTFS does, unless Developer Mode is on (judged by the drive from the opener's
> token, since WinFsp's own check refuses Developer Mode; a `CreateSymbolicLinkW` caller gets NTFS's answer in all four
> cases measured, and only a program writing the reparse buffer itself without the unprivileged flag is allowed under
> Developer Mode, since that flag never reaches a file system). winfstest's `t/reparse/02.t`, `03.t` and
> `t/streams/04.t` run to their ends: 78 cases newly pass, and three script-level entries become 30 case-level ones,
> each with its reason (355 to 382 entries; finer grain, no case that passed before fails). Stated differences: a link
> holds no data stream; a link POSIX made is a file link; a link relative to the drive's root is kept relative to its
> directory, so moved, it reaches another object where NTFS keeps it on `\x\y`. **Still owed:** generic reparse data (39
> entries), its own amendment after named streams.

> **`slates land` keeps every `--include` and `--exclude` it is given (2026-11-17, §4.15 step 1).** The command line
> kept the last value of each flag, so `--exclude /.git --exclude /target` landed `/.git` without a word, while the
> wire's filter has always taken lists. Each flag now keeps every value in order (`--grant` and the other single-valued
> flags still keep the last). Found by kiln's bare-metal engine, whose landings leave out `/.git` and what git ignores;
> an embedding host passes them through `slates_api::Filter` (A-278). Test:
> `args::tests::a_landing_keeps_every_include_and_exclude_given`. Record:
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-17-land-kept-only-the-last-exclude.md`.

> **The fault probe can read a page fault as free under load (found 2026-11-09 by the A-223 plan; fixed 2026-11-11 by
> liveness, 15e27a90 on agents/liveness-fault-probe).** `slates_machine::probes::faults` takes `base_ns` as the median of map, touch every page and unmap,
> less the median of map and unmap alone, over 256 pages, with a saturating subtraction. The two medians are taken in
> separate measurements, so under load the second can come within 256 ns of the first or pass it, and the cost reads 0.
> - **Seen:** `profile::tests::a_profile_measures_within_its_budget_and_round_trips_through_json` asserts
>   `faults.base_ns > 0` and failed in 1 of 10 full `slates-machine` suite runs on main 39c1a9e4 on fedora-2 (32 CPUs,
>   load 21-34), and in 0 of 10 runs of the test alone. The A-223 branch read the same: 0 of 10 alone, 1 of 3 and 0 of 10
>   in the suite.
> - **Why it matters:** consumers take `faults.base_ns.max(1)` (`config.rs`, `region.rs`), so nothing divides by zero.
>   But a 1 ns fault then feeds derived bounds, among them the arena region (`pages = 100 × 2 × syscall / fault`) and the
>   pre-fault slice.
> - **Fixed:** `faults` returns a `Result` and refuses a non-positive per-page difference with
>   `MeasurementTimeout { probe: "faults" }`, so `MachineProfile::measure_patiently` measures again within the probe's
>   wall ceiling. A populated or huge-page region measured at nothing reads `None`. Tests (red on main, `Ok(0)` and
>   `Some(0)`): `a_touched_region_no_slower_than_the_untouched_one_is_refused_never_a_zero_fault` and
>   `a_populated_region_no_slower_than_the_untouched_one_is_unmeasured` (ef529d8a). Record:
>   `docs/bugs/2026-11-11-the-fault-probe-reported-a-zero-fault-on-a-loaded-machine.md`.

> **The Windows wake estimate (A-223, found 2026-11-05 on jupiter, fixed 2026-11-06; the idle window's rule decided 2026-11-11, extended for closed loops 2026-11-18 by A-326, on main 2026-11-18 with the merge of liveness's branch; Windows' own window closed 2026-11-18 by A-361; a hold kept only while a shard's idle turns poll faster than it wakes, 2026-11-18 by A-387).**
> The boot probe let a Windows waiter's announcement stand in for its sleep, and the shards' online estimate learned
> kicks that met a thread not yet blocked. Both measured a handoff, 0.14–0.85 µs, so the idle window (100 times it) was
> 14–80 µs and owner shards parked between a single client's creates. Now the probe kicks only once the waiter's cycle
> count stands still, and it drops a wake its waiter's own switch count shows it never slept through. The shards judge
> their parks by that switch count too (`slates_machine::switches`; the bug record of 2026-11-06).
> - **Measured on CI at two shards** (`diag-liveness-2`, three quiet runs a runner): owner parks per 1,000
>   single-client creates fell from 30–88 to 0–1 per shard on x86_64 and from 2–7 to 0–1 on arm64. The single-client
>   p99 went from 45.5–49.3 to 33.3–37.7 µs (x86_64) and from 32.8–35.0 to 28.9–31.4 µs (arm64). The 8-client p99 stayed
>   within 7 % (495–503 against 511–519 µs; 474–494 against 499–531 µs). The probe reads 7.1–9.1 µs, confirmed.
> - **The idle window's rule: decided and built (2026-11-11, the supervisor's decision A).** The ratio of 100 had
>   come to multiply a real wake, 0.71–0.91 ms of window at boot, and the shard's live estimate, which counts the
>   run-queue wait its own spinning causes, lengthened it to hundreds of milliseconds under load. Now the window is
>   `max(F, the shard's wake estimate × the platform's multiple)` (`config::idle_window_ns` until A-361, §4.3, §4.7). F is R9's
>   50 µs provisioning floor (`config::PROVISION_FLOOR`), which `provision_bench` gates on too. The multiple
>   (`config::NO_ESTIMATE_MULTIPLE` since A-361) is 0 on every platform, so no estimate prices the window and a shard's
>   own spinning cannot lengthen it (`crates/server/tests/idle_window.rs`, on Windows too since A-361); until A-361 it
>   was 100 on Windows.
>   - Measured at two shards on CI (diag-liveness-35, BENCHMARKS "The idle window's rule"): a 1 ms-paced client's CPU
>     fell from main's 1,451–2,023 to 155–224 thousandths of a core on Linux, the loaded single-client p99 halved
>     (8.0 → 4.0 ms on x86_64, 9.8 → 4.0 ms on arm64), and the quiet p99 stayed within main's spread. As built
>     (diag-liveness-37): 188–219 quiet and 293–365 loaded on Linux.
>   - The paced client's quiet cost is judged by the supervisor's criteria, not a fixed bar: well below main's on
>     Linux (188–219 against 1,451–2,023 thousandths of a core), and on Windows A-223-alone's level, kept by decision A
>     (131–341). The plan's step 6 confirms it on the finished code against main.
>   - Measured and rejected: the floor of confirmed wakes (it queued too, 0.33–33.8 ms), the floor less Linux's
>     run-queue time (0 to 1.75 µs, the shards parked through a client's requests), the live floor × 100 capped at 4F
>     (twice the paced CPU), and the boot probe's smallest wake as a second input to `max` (6.8–346 µs on a loaded
>     boot, past F in 5 of 9 boots on each Linux runner).
>   - **Closed (C), A-361 (2026-11-18, goal g234): Windows' own window.** A Windows shard parked beside two spinners a CPU
>     waited 14–42 ms to run again because a thread dequeued from an I/O completion port gets none of the priority boost
>     Windows gives a thread woken from an event, a semaphore or an address, so the kicked shard queued at its own level
>     until a spinner's 31.6 ms turn ended (`diag-g234-wake-1`: completion port 29 and 14 ms at the median on
>     windows-latest and windows-11-arm, an event 15 and 6–7 µs, an event with its boost disabled 29 and 14 ms). Now a
>     blocked wait sits one level up and the window is R9's floor on Windows too. The multiple it replaces had made
>     windows of seconds from those waits, which spun past the watchdog's window after a WinFsp request: the anchor killed
>     a live daemon in 3 of 3 runs of g258's now-x86 lane. At two shards the paced client's CPU fell from 94 and 199
>     thousandths of a core quiet and 756 and 787 loaded to 7, 25 and 20, and the loaded single-client p99 from 157 µs
>     with 4 of 9 runs at 56–83 ms (x86_64) and 108 µs with one at 31.9 ms (arm64) to 130 and 148 µs (BENCHMARKS,
>     "Windows' own window"). Every idle spin now also ends by a ceiling a beat under the watchdog's least window
>     (`config::IDLE_SPIN_CEILING`, A-361), so no window, estimate or hold can bring a spinning verdict on a live shard.
>   - **Fixed (A-326, 2026-11-18, goal g234): a closed loop's other shards parked at R9's floor alone.** The plan's
>     step 6 (2026-11-12, diag-liveness-42 to -45 and adacachy2; every N in the A-223 plan's notes) found the rule
>     fails a quiet single client over three shards: p99 116.4 µs against main's 27.1 on ubuntu-24.04-arm, 144–331
>     parks per 1,000 creates, since a create goes to the partition its name hashes to and a loop returns to an owner
>     only after going round the others. A fixed `F × S` or `2F × S` window fixed it there (36.8 and 29.5 µs) but spun
>     for a paced client too (1,386–2,289 thousandths of a core at fifteen shards against main's 664). Now a forward
>     made for a request read within F of its shard's last client I/O holds its owner open for the loop's return at R9's
>     percentile, 2F × the least k with ((S − 1)/S)^k ≤ 1/100, never more cycles than the loop had run (§4.7, A-326;
>     `crates/server/tests/closed_loop.rs`). A paced client's requests hold nothing.
>   - **Fixed (A-387, 2026-11-18, goal g234): A-326's hold made a macOS single client slower at many shards.** The
>     measurer's quiet-gated Studio A/B (32 CPUs, 23 shards) found the spinning single client's p50 doubled once A-223's
>     rule and A-326 landed (48.5–86.9 to 97.6–105.8 µs) and its p99 up (200.3–251.3 to 262.1–298.1 µs). A held macOS
>     shard does not poll: its zero-timeout `kevent` sleeps 12–15 µs a turn with an involuntary switch (A-218). On a quiet

>     CPU the p99 1.34 against 1.87 ms; the quiet nine-shard p999 was 128.6 against 108.6 µs at the median, the spreads

>     3.4–5.8 cores). The first fix fixed the hold at none on macOS by `#[cfg]`; it is replaced by the shard's own
>     measurement: an owner keeps a hold only while the idle turn a request meets, learned from every turn of its idle
>     spins as E[T²]/E[T], is shorter than its wake estimate (`slates_rt::held_turn`), so a macOS shard declines, a Linux

>   - **Open: a macOS single client over many shards still misses R9's 50 µs** (2026-11-18, after A-387): p99 84.6–152.5
>     µs at nine shards on the quiet M4 Max and 147.6–249.3 µs at 23 on the shared 32-CPU Studio, unheld. Not yet

>     tails), an owner's park and kick (3.1–7.2 µs wakes here), and a cold first run (every p99 above 100 µs at nine
>     shards was a first run's).
>   - **Owed: the supervisor's measurement of A-223, its window rule and A-326 on main** (`provision_bench`, every N,
>     quiet and two spinners a logical CPU): on ubuntu-latest, ubuntu-24.04-arm, macos-latest, windows-latest and
>     windows-11-arm at 2 shards and the derived count, plus `PROVISION_BENCH_SHARDS=3` on Linux and a many-core Linux

> - **The client's Windows wake (sibling (d), fixed 2026-11-11).** The ipc client took any reply stamp inside its wait,
>   since the Event cannot say a sleeper was found, so a reply sent before it blocked was learned as a handoff. It now
>   judges its wait by its own switch count, as the shards do, and keeps its seed where the OS refuses the count. Of
>   16,384 racing parks a run on CI's Windows runners, main learned 11–48 of those that never switched out, the fix

>   after. Seen on the way: `presentation.rs` failed on Windows (`Unsupported { feature: "landing" }`, no Windows
>   landing writer, A-262), on main's code too, where CI never ran it; it built on Unix only, as the verb did, until the

>   lanes run it.

> **A parked Windows shard in a job that fixes its priority class still waits out its neighbours' turns (2026-11-18,
> A-361's open item; OPEN).** A-361 raises a shard one priority level while it is blocked in its completion port, since a
> completion port's waiter gets none of the wake boost an event's waiter gets. A job with
> `JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_PRIORITY_CLASS` keeps a thread's level where it was: on jupiter, under the job kiln's agent runs
> commands in (flags 0x2020, BelowNormal), `SetThreadPriority(ABOVE_NORMAL)` answered success and the level stayed
> normal, so beside 64 spinners a kicked shard still woke 30.75 ms late at the median against a parked thread's 12.5 µs
> (`wake_load` probe, 2026-11-18). The window stays R9's floor there, so the wait costs latency and never a spin or a
> kill; `a_parked_shard_wakes_beside_spinners_as_soon_as_a_parked_thread_does` skips loudly in such a job. A user
> APC as the kick carried no boost either (jupiter, loaded median 252 ms). **Owed:** a shard with no I/O outstanding
> parks where Windows boosts the wake (WaitOnAddress on its parking word), its kickers signalling the object its park
> names, with the parking protocol's loom model extended to the two objects.

> **The dirty-page test's precondition, proved each attempt (2026-11-09, A-248).**
> `a_dirty_shared_map_page_never_undoes_a_later_write_through_another_path` failed intermittently ("the sync says so:
> Ok(())", B10's gate, adacachy2, load about 66) when the kernel wrote the store's page back before the replacement. On
> kernel 7.3 a process spawn while the page is dirty does that: 6 attempts of 6 with a spawn in the window. That
> write-back is fresh and rightly applied, so the run tested nothing. The daemon now counts `fuse.writebacks_applied`.
> The test reads it around each store and retries an attempt whose precondition did not hold, up to 6, then fails
> naming the precondition. adacachy2: 10 of 10 before (load 66-68) and 10 of 10 after (load 66-77), no attempt missed. Record:
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-09-a-dirty-page-test-took-an-early-write-back-for-a-lost-refusal.md`.

> **A refused device node reached programs as "Unknown error 527": fixed (2026-11-08, §4.6, A-26; A-268; the refusal
> itself replaced by A-294 on 2026-11-17, which makes the node).** MKNOD of a
> block or character device, and NFSv4's CREATE of one, answered `BADTYPE`, which the Linux client turns into its
> internal `EBADTYPE` (errno 527): 331 cases of a full pjdfstest run over NFSv4, and the NFSv3 lane alike. Now a taken
> name is `EEXIST`, an unwritable directory `EACCES`, then `EPERM`, as a local file system without device nodes answers
> `mknod`. No list changes: no case expects `EPERM` from a device `mknod`.

> **The WinFsp drive keeps Windows' attribute bits, and a file's read-only state is its mode: built for the volume and
> the drive (2026-11-08, §4.6; A-262).** A-209 had left HIDDEN, SYSTEM, ARCHIVE and READONLY out ("the volume's
> permission is POSIX's mode"), so `SetFileAttributes` answered success and kept nothing and every file reported
> `NORMAL`. Now a file's READONLY is its mode's write bits (DrvFs's and Samba's mapping), and the other bits, with a
> directory's READONLY, are kept in the inode's two bytes of tail padding (168 B, unchanged; tree_heap 260, 275 and 293
> B per entry, unchanged). winfstest's 18 ATTRIBUTES cases come off its list (373 to 355). The Windows base plane reads
> them since stage 3's base half: a fingerprint carries the disk's bits apart from a DrvFs-mapped mode (until then the
> Windows base reported the attribute word itself as the mode, `0x20` as `0o040`). **Still owed under A-262:** a Windows
> landing applying them (the Windows writer exists since A-185, 2026-11-18: it sets a file's `READONLY` from its mode
> and keeps every other bit the file holds, applying none of the volume's; Linux and macOS carry them unapplied), and
> the merge's dimension, owed when works are mountable (no work can set the bits today, so no merge drops them).

> **A file removed while open over NFSv4 was reclaimed at once, and the client renamed it aside: fixed (2026-11-08,
> §4.6 NFSv4 state; A-260).** An NFSv4 open held nothing in the volume, so a REMOVE of an open file reclaimed it (its
> handle answered `NFS4ERR_STALE`), and the server never answered `OPEN4_RESULT_PRESERVE_UNLINKED`, so the Linux client
> renamed every such file to `.nfs*` until the close (pjdfstest `unlink/14.t:4`; git, editors and sqlite do it, and a
> landing would carry the name). Every open and delegation now holds its file, from its record's commit to its end's
> (a CLOSE, a return, a revocation, a client's purge), the hold taken again from the journal at a recovery and given
> back at its attachment's end. Red tests: a removed open file's GETATTR answered `NFS4ERR_STALE`; now it serves at nlink
> 0 with its bytes until its last close, also across a daemon restart, and its 64 KiB come back at the close or at its
> client's lease lapse. Still owed: NFSv3 has no open, so its clients' silly renames stay (NFS-OPEN on the NFSv3 lists).

> **A chained async call stalled after its first step: fixed (2026-11-09, found by CI's diag list-3).** The async
> driver reported a call ready once until it was finished, so a chained call (a listing's next page, a large edit's next
> put) was never reported again and both SDKs' async listings past one page failed `Stalled`. `Driver::continued`
> re-arms the call; both SDKs call it (`docs/bugs/2026-11-09-a-chained-async-call-stalled-after-its-first-step.md`).

> **A volume listing outgrew one reply: fixed (found by liveness, fixed 2026-11-08, A-263, §4.4 `list`, §4.3).** `slates volume
> list` was refused "reply too large for the bulk area" from 100 volumes on a two-shard daemon, so an operator could not
> list what a server holds. `List { after }` is now answered a page at a time, `Listed { volumes, next }`: volumes in id
> order, a reply chunk's worth, each shard sending at most a page. The client walks the pages, sync and as an async
> chain. A new volume's name is bounded so its summary fits one page and its status one reply (2,896 bytes since
> 2026-11-18, A-267; it was the page's 4,012, whose status was refused; `InvalidName` past it), and an unrecovered
> volume's cause is cut to fit beside it; recorded, the cause is bounded (a base at `create`: 1,023 bytes on macOS, 3,812
> on Linux and Windows; a reason at 256) so `status` names it whole. **Under load:** at load about 160 on this Mac (2026-11-09) creates
> past about 2,300 volumes on two shards were answered `Stalled` by the client's own reply deadline, and `volume_list.rs`
> counted each and asked again. Since A-232 a call waits while its daemon lives and `Stalled` is gone, so the re-land
> (2026-11-17, goal g247) creates plainly; how long a create takes past a few thousand volumes under that load is not
> yet measured. 3,000 volumes list on two shards, and a walk under churn lists each survivor once
> (`docs/bugs/2026-11-08-a-volume-listing-outgrew-one-reply.md`).
> - **`changed_since`, the same shape: fixed the same way (A-264, 2026-11-08, revised 2026-11-09).** Refused at 800
>   changed files; now paged from a change index (the paths each version changed, recorded as it commits) in version
>   order, each page ending at a full reply or its slice of the shard's step, so a page costs the changes it passes and
>   never the tree. It reports every dimension (`changed_between(v, head)`), where it read the content index alone. One
>   path always fits a page alone: a green's paths arrive in requests, whose framing is larger than a page's (the
>   longest an edit carries, 4,044 bytes, is answered). Merging a mounted work is owed and must bound its paths to one
>   page when it lands. `changed_between`, which `advance` invalidates by, reads the same index (one
>   computation in product code); the history walk is the tests' model (`test-model`), checked against at every
>   version, below the checkpoint, across folds and after a restore
>   (`docs/bugs/2026-11-08-a-greens-changed-since-outgrew-one-reply.md`).
> - **`audit`: numbered, bounded, one partition (A-265, 2026-11-08).** Refused between 50 and 100 records; paging it
>   found every record numbered 0, the audit unbounded in memory and snapshots, and each shard keeping its own, a client
>   reading its own shard's alone. Now numbered in `apply`, a derived window kept (`table_bytes / size_of::<AuditRecord>()`,
>   the oldest dropped and counted; the operator horizon waits for a measured landing rate), the unwritten audit ring
>   removed, every record held by the control shard's partition, and the read paged
>   (`docs/bugs/2026-11-08-the-audit-numbered-nothing-and-kept-everything.md`).
>   - **A record owed across shards survives a crash: fixed (2026-11-18, goal g247; AC-2.10).** A record made on
>     another shard reached the control partition after its own atom committed, so a crash between the two lost that
>     batch. It is now owed in its atom (the partition's outbox), sent from the oldest owed until the control shard's
>     acknowledgement is recorded, sent again by the reap tick when it was not, and appended once however often it is
>     sent (a per-partition mark the batch's own record moves). Anchor layout version 10. Tests:
>     `crates/db/tests/audit.rs`, `crates/server/tests/audit_crossing.rs`
>     (`docs/bugs/2026-11-18-an-audit-record-owed-across-shards-was-lost-to-a-crash.md`).
> - **`grants`: paged, and the table holds live grants (A-266, 2026-11-08).** Refused between 25 and 50 grants; paging
>   it found every grant kept for the daemon's life and none ended at its term. Now paged in grant-id order, a grant
>   leaves the table at its terminal step (its history is the audit), the reap ends grants past their term, and a
>   target past what a grant's summary holds on one page (3,995 bytes) is refused before presenting
>   (`docs/bugs/2026-11-08-a-principals-grants-outgrew-one-reply-and-were-kept-for-good.md`).
>   - **An expiry is audited, and a grant a landing found past its term ends too: fixed (2026-11-18, goal g247).** An
>     expiry wrote no audit record, so an expired grant's history was its `grant_issued` alone; each is now recorded
>     with a `grant_expired` record in one atom (`record_expiry`), sent to the control partition from another shard as
>     the sweep's one batch. And a landing's check marked a grant past its term expired in its shard's table alone,
>     which the sweep, taking issued grants, passed over: the grant was never recorded ended, stayed listed as issued
>     and stayed in the table until a restart. The check now only reads. Tests:
>     `every_grant_ended_at_its_term_leaves_its_expiry_in_the_audit` and
>     `a_grant_a_landing_found_past_its_term_still_ends_and_is_audited` (`crates/server/tests/grants_pages.rs`),
>     `a_grant_a_landing_found_past_its_term_is_still_due_for_the_sweep` (`crates/land/src/grant.rs`)
>     (`docs/bugs/2026-11-18-a-grant-a-landing-found-past-its-term-was-never-ended.md`).
>   - **A grant whose issue was refused covers nothing: fixed (sibling, 2026-11-18, goal g247).** `issue_grant` issues
>     in the shard's table before the durable `GrantIssued`, and nothing took the grant back when that record or its
>     atom's commit was refused: the approval was answered `Unpublished`, and a landing naming the id the refused issue
>     took ran under it. A refused record now ends the grant there, and a rolled-back atom's grants leave the shard's
>     table (`reconcile_unpublished_effects`, `Grants::retain`). Test: `a_grant_whose_issue_was_refused_covers_no_landing`
>     (`crates/server/tests/grants_pages.rs`).
> - **A status's drift: the first that fit, a count, and a paged read (A-267, 2026-11-08).** A status with 600 drifted
>   entries was refused; it now carries what fits beside its other fields and `drifted_elided`, `Drifted` reads them all a
>   page at a time, `slates status --drift` walks it, and both SDKs read it whole with `drifted(volume)`. Since
>   2026-11-17 (goal g247) a page re-checks only the witnessed entries it passes, in inode order under a slice of the
>   shard's step, where each page re-read the whole status
>   (`docs/bugs/2026-11-08-a-status-with-much-drift-outgrew-one-reply.md`).
> - **A list a verb's own reply carries: fixed (A-267, 2026-11-17, goal g247).** Reproduced at 400 entries, each refused
>   "reply too large for the bulk area": an advance and a rewitness after taking effect, a presentation after it was
>   recorded, and a granted landing's `LandingConflict`, replaced by `BadRequest`. Each now carries what one reply holds
>   and counts the rest (`invalidated_elided`, `paths_elided`, `conflicts_elided`, `entries_elided`), every reader
>   showing the count. A sibling fixed the same way: a finished landing's degraded cells (`degraded_elided`; one a
>   directory where the host refuses a directory's sync). A status's mount budget counted paths alone; that was an
>   accounting correction, never a refusal, since a partition's attachment table is bounded and the 400-mount test met
>   that bound first (corrected 2026-11-18)
>   (`docs/bugs/2026-11-17-lists-a-verbs-own-reply-carries-outgrew-one-reply.md`).
> - **A name a status could not hold: fixed (A-263, A-267, 2026-11-18, goal g247).** A volume created under the
>   listing's longest name (4,012 bytes) was listed and its status refused "reply too large". A name is now bounded by
>   the status at its widest on any host too, 2,896 bytes (2,931 before A-332), and a status's mounts take no more than the room the rest of
>   its report leaves (`docs/bugs/2026-11-18-a-volume-under-the-longest-name-could-not-be-statused.md`).
> - **Every reply list, swept (2026-11-18, goal g247).** Every list a reply carries is paged, carried with a count,
>   or bounded by a closed set (the transports, a landing's action counts) or a consensus group's voters; telemetry
>   drains in bounded batches, and the daemon's status pages by bytes. A volume's name is the one variable field found
>   that a reply could not hold, fixed above. Since signed work (A-321) joined main: a volume's trusted signers
>   (`Policy { signers }`) are bounded by the one `SetSigners` request that set them, whose chunk is a reply's and whose
>   fixed fields are wider than the reply's; and a presentation's reply carries the statement a signature signs, which
>   names the target, so a target too long to be answered beside its summary and verdict is refused
>   `Target { TooLong { longest } }` before the presentation is recorded (`presentation_overflow`; a grant's listing
>   alone took targets up to 3,995 bytes, and such a presentation's reply would have been refused after it was
>   recorded; test `a_presentation_too_long_for_one_reply_names_the_longest_that_fits`).
> - **A merge verdict's windows: fixed (A-267, 2026-11-17, goal g247).** `Submitted` and `Rebased` were refused at 400
>   windows. The work keeps its last conflicting verdict, the reply carries what fits with `conflicts_elided` and its
>   `verdict` id, `Conflicts` reads the rest, and the client hands back every window, sync and async; a replaced or
>   forgotten verdict is refused `VerdictReplaced`. Under A-247 the green's owner judges and answers every window, and
>   the work's shard, which serves the work's reads, keeps them (`kept_conflict`); a signed submit's verdict
>   (`SubmittedSigned`, A-321) is carried and kept the same way. **Open:** a verdict is kept in memory
>   alone, so a restart between a conflicting submit and its walk answers `VerdictReplaced`, and the caller submits
>   again; and the owner's completion record of a conflict off the work's shard holds every window (bounded, as the
>   verdict is, by the work's journal), the one durable record of a reply that is not cut to one reply.
> - **`read_base`: paged (A-267, 2026-11-17, goal g247).** It read the whole base file into the daemon's memory and
>   answered it in one reply, refused past about 4 KiB; now a page at a time with the file's size and its
>   fingerprint's stamp, the client refusing a file that changed between pages. The whole-file `Read` verb, a second
>   read path beside the paged `ReadRange`, is retired: refused `Unsupported`, naming `ReadRange`, and kept with
>   `ReadBytes` in its published place, so no wire tag after it moves (D-15, `crates/ipc/tests/wire_order.rs`).

> **A version appended before its owner restarted never committed: fixed (2026-11-07, §4.16 Commit, AUD-11;
> A-246).** A restarted owner rebuilt its greens from their chains, but not the merge records
> it still owed its holders (they lived in memory), so a version appended before the crash and not yet placed was never
> shipped again and its retried submit was refused `Overloaded` until the client gave up. Goal 4's primary-kill rung
> at 1,000 clients, `f = 1`: 1,770 oracle failures, versions 507 to 514 on the green with no client told. The restart
> now re-enqueues every replayed version's record. Red test: the version never committed in 60 s after the restart;
> now it commits, and the test ends in 3.3 s. Record:
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-07-a-version-appended-before-its-owner-restarted-never-committed.md`.

> **Open (perf, 2026-11-08): A-247's step two, works across nodes.** Step one spreads a green's works over the shards of
> its owner's node (`crates/server/src/work_home.rs`). A `CreateWork` forwarded from another node still places the work
> on the green's shard, so the three-node `f = 1` rungs are not yet helped (every verb still forwards to the owner's
> node). What it owes: a rule for the work's node (the creating client's, with its name reachable from any node), the
> owner's asks over the fleet exchange, and the lease gate on the owner's half of a remote verdict.
> Progress (A-697, 2026-11-20): part a1 built, the owner's admission of another node's work by a forwarded
> `AdmitWork` (rights from the green's record, the floor at the head, answered once); part a2 built behind a test hook
> (a holder makes the work on its client's partition, admitted over the fleet, its base read from its replica); part b
> built (the holder moves and drops the work's floor at the owner, `MoveWorkFloor`, monotone); part c built (a
> holder's submit committed by the verdict its replica computed, taken by position at the owner, `SubmitComputed`);
> part d built (the submit settles once the holder's replica holds the version); part e built (a holder's work comes
> back from its log over the holder's replica after a restart); a holder work's rebase and copies built over the
> replica; a creation a restart caught releases its floor at the owner (part e2); the increment carried by reference
> to placed content, one copy of each byte (main's ruling: the forward carries a 4 MiB increment, but at f = 1 a 4 MiB
> holder submit took 3.5-4.8 s and a local one 2.8-3.4 s in a debug build, with the inputs shipped back to the holder
> that composed them; release measurements owed before and after), and part f (takeover and the routing flip) are open.
> A forwarded write's deferred acceptance is answered by its commit since 2026-11-20 (it was polled a heartbeat at a
> time). A borrower waiting for a lent record session is woken by its return since 2026-11-20 (it slept a
> pace between looks). Owed from that sweep, each with its own wake: a broadcast's stragglers (`owner_location.rs`), a
> FUSE mount helper's exit (`fuse.rs`); the forward lane's throughput (about 200 MB/s on loopback); and the shared-green
> bench run's exit 4 at 64 MiB under memory pressure.

> **Open (perf, 2026-11-09): A-247 step one's verdict tail.** At 3,000 clients on one node the rung takes 4.3–4.6 s against
> main's 8.0, every edit, read and creation faster and no reply lost, but SubmitAccepted p99 is 56–72 ms against main's
> 42–62 (BENCHMARKS). The owner is the bottleneck, and rebases cost it more than verdicts (`map_rebase` 333 samples
> against `judge_submission` 226 of 1,121). Owed: the owner's cost per verdict and per rebase.
>
> **Open (perf, 2026-11-09): main drops acknowledgement parts at 3,000 clients.** `xshard.reply_dropped` counts 4,074 to
> 4,474 a run (main 80be552a and db9c514e): results carried home past a full channel for one coordinator period. A
> diagnostic build of db9c514e counted every one as an acknowledgement scatter's part (4,364 of 4,364 and 4,418 of 4,418);
> no verb's reply was among them and no client waited out a reply deadline (this entry said so until the diagnostic). A
> lost part leaves its shard's release unsettled, so the client is refused `AcknowledgementOwed` until a later
> acknowledgement settles it, 25,868 to 28,995 times a run, each a pause and a resend. Fixed on agents/perf-replies
> (every result waits for room while its shard lives). BENCHMARKS, "Why main's two figures differ".

> **Fixed (2026-11-18, A-491): the give-back's slice was learned from wall time.** `learn_give_back_rate` divided by
> the shard's clock, so on a loaded host a preempted step taught a small slice and a give-back took thousands of steps
> (2,572 to 3,042 at load about 100, on a Mac whose whole give-back is 18 to 21 ms of CPU) rather than hundreds, and
> the recovery test's give-back case failed once under load on adacachy (main's r271). A step is now timed by its shard
> thread's own CPU clock, steps a coarse clock (Windows) shows no CPU for folded into the next it shows
> (`daemon::GiveBackRate`; `a_give_back_step_learns_its_slice_from_its_own_cpu_not_the_wall_clock`). **Owed (main's):**
> `a_boot_give_back_holds_its_shard_a_slice_of_cpu_a_step` under load, and the give-back's step count at load against
> the 2,572 to 3,042 above.

> **A submit resent after its owner's restart was applied a second time: fixed (2026-11-08, §4.16 "Commit", §4.9; A-252).**
> The waiting submit lived in memory, so after a restart its resend under the same id found no completion and ran
> again as a new version: 4,261 oracle failures on fixtures' 1,000-client primary kill, 83 versions no client was told.
> The accept now records, in the same transaction as the version's append, a typed `Seen::Awaiting` (`Op::CompletionAwaiting`,
> carried through snapshots), so a resend joins the wait or is answered its version, never run again. The rung after it:
> oracle 0 on every run that finished (five of them 13.1 to 13.9 s), and 7 of 18 runs stalled on a fence that is W3's and
> independent of this fix (`BaseUnavailable` at recovery; open, A-257, liveness).
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-08-a-submit-resent-after-its-owner-restarted-was-applied-twice.md`.
>
> **Another principal's use renewed a CLI attachment's term: fixed (2026-11-09, §4.7, A-230; fixtures' sweep after
> A-255).** Each verb that names an attachment renewed a termed one before checking that the caller was its principal,
> so any channel that knew the id could keep another account's write attachment, and its write lease, alive past its
> term. Now only the attachment's principal's use renews or ends it. Red-checked:
> `a_cli_attachment_is_renewed_by_its_own_principals_use_alone` fails with the check out, the owner's late write
> succeeding. The sweep's other identities were already checked against the session; the bug record lists where.
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-09-another-principals-use-renewed-a-cli-attachments-term.md`.

> **A submit resent after its green's takeover is answered its version: fixed (2026-11-09, §4.16, §4.8 Lookup; A-255).**
> Before, the resend was refused `OwnerUnreachable` without end: its work, by whose id it routes, dies with its owner, and
> the completion window with it. Now the completion rides the green's chain entries and merge records, which the
> successor adopts. The work's catalog record names its green and is the resend's route: held, or learned from a
> location round. A version's record ships only once its work's catalog is committed. The resend is answered
> `Submitted { version }`, and a copied key reaches nothing (A-SEAT's door). A submit made right after its work's
> creation costs about 0.35 ms more, for the catalog's own commit: median 1.59–1.64 ms against 1.25–1.29 ms on an idle
> Mac Studio, and 109 ms while the catalog waited for the period. Still open:
> - losing the green's owner twice needs the ledger-prefix transfer (GAP-A9-7);
> - the cross-region case is not yet tested;
> - the 0.35 ms could be overlapped by a pipelined dispatch;
> - ~~the route has no end for a work whose owner died, a store with no bound (CLAUDE.md §2 item 8)~~: **ended
>   (2026-11-17, A-288).** Nothing retired a work's catalog record: only a volume's owner writes its tombstone, and a
>   work never comes back, so every work alive at an owner's death was held, by its adopter and every holder, for as
>   long as the fleet ran. Now the route is kept only while the green's owner holds a completion of the work's submits
>   that the route can reach, one a client on another node than the work's owner made and has not acknowledged. A
>   client of the owner's own node resends to that node, never through the route. The merge record (format 2) and
>   chain entry (version 3) name such a submit's work, and the successor records the completion under it
>   (`CompletionRecord::work`, `Partition::completions_routed_by`). The route's adopter asks the green's owner each
>   period (`crate::work_route`, fleet stream 25), and a route answered "none" closes through the destroy's two
>   tombstone stages. The owner also drops its own takeover copies when a tombstone retires, which a destroyed
>   taken-over volume had kept too. Red first: on main 7c6faee27 the route was still held by both survivors after the
>   acknowledgement (`retired false, counted 0`, 429 s on a loaded Mac).
>   `a_works_route_ends_once_the_greens_owner_holds_none_of_its_completions` now also holds a work its own owner's
>   client submitted from, retired with nothing acknowledged. That form is red on main dbf53afa2 too (`its route
>   retired false; ... retired false, counted 0; held at the end [Ok(true), Ok(true)]`, 860 s at load 57 to 91), and
>   green with the fix on the same Mac (macOS arm64, debug): 6.91 s at load 11 to 37 on 7c6faee27, and 8.56 s at load
>   108 merged with main b7c294959. Both routes retired on both survivors, counted twice. Still held, A-288's open list:
>   - a route to a green destroyed (a given-up one too, which is then neither served nor `unrecovered`), or lost to a
>     second takeover it cannot survive (GAP-A9-7), while the route is kept: the green has no owner to answer;
>   - ~~a route to a green its successor gave up on~~ (the give-up after the failover SLO's attempts, d3f4ddbe2):
>     **ended the same day.** The green was never served, so its shard answered no question and the route stayed, though
>     nothing it led to could answer. Now the green's shard answers for a green it holds `unrecovered` too, from its
>     partition's count, which is final there; a green whose takeover is still pending is refused as before. Red first,
>     on a lone node with a planted green given up naming its chain: the route kept, all 111 questions refused, 14.4 s
>     at load 33 to 37. Green: refused at all 10 questions while the green was pending and kept at every read, then
>     retired at the first question after the give-up, its tombstone recorded and retired, 5.7 s at load 48 to 52
>     (`a_route_to_a_green_its_successor_gave_up_on_is_retired`);
>   - a route whose completion its client never acknowledges (a client of another node that died, or one that never
>     writes to the green again), as the completion record itself is: only an acknowledgement or a client lease ends
>     either, and RIFL's client leases are not built;
>   - a route kept by an adopter that restarts warm. Its holder copies come back with it, but the routes it kept
>     (`pending_catalogs`) do not, so it neither re-places nor retires them. This is A-255's own gap, found by reading
>     on 2026-11-17; no test shows it yet.
>
>   `docs/bugs/2026-11-17-a-works-route-was-never-retired.md`.
>

> **A version commits in one exchange, and retention no longer decodes the whole ledger per put: fixed (2026-11-07, §4.16
> Commit, §4.10 retention; A-244).** A-235 left five hops a version (the inputs' offer
> and transfer, then the record, each behind a wake), and a holder's retention decoded every merge record for every held
> manifest per put, quadratic in a green's history. Now a record carries its inputs in one shipment, and retention reads
> the one ledger position a held input can be named by. 500 sequential submits at `f = 1`, release, load about 10: p50
> 265 µs, p99 731 µs, max 1.13 ms (was p50 6.7 ms, p99 34.7 ms, max 62.4 ms). Still owed: a smaller per-version cost

> **A snapshot's release decoded the log it covered (found and fixed 2026-11-08, §4.3, §4.8).** One commit's poll walked and
> decoded every record since the last snapshot only to reach the tail: 654 ms over 1,000,000 records in release and 14.9 s in
