>
> - **On a busy machine the anchor kills a live daemon, and then its successor, and the clients give up** (open; the
>   anchor's half is the top entry's, unassigned). Mac, single-node anchored daemon, load 60 to 89, 300 to 1,000
>   clients:
>   - The anchor killed a live daemon whose heartbeat lapsed. The successor "never beat inside the recovery budget",
>     recovering 300 to 1,000 works and their green's versions, and was killed again: twice, and four times in another
>     run.
>   - The clients' reconnect budget ran out first (0 reconnects, 172 and 439 clients gave up), and the restart reset
>     the works (A-207's port is reverted on main).
>   - The harness's oracle then failed 30 checks: versions it never saw accepted, and heads it could not replay. Those
>     are submits whose outcome their clients never learned, and the oracle treats them as never accepted. It owes a
>     sound treatment: read which versions the green took and fit the unknown submits to them.
>
> - **Memory per client, attributed** (2026-11-06). Mac, in-process daemon over `kernel/`, 300 clients at 32 a
>   connection, works kept (`--keep-works`). Memory is not load-sensitive.
>   - **Per same-machine connection, about 8.4 MB of daemon RSS.** At 1,000 clients, 1,000 connections peaked at
>     12.5 GB and 32 at 4.4 GB. Multiplexing 32 a connection makes it about 0.26 MB a logical client, and over the
>     network the server pays none of it.
>   - **Per accepted version, about 0.16 MB of live heap**, but RSS grew about 3.4 MB a version (one round, 300
>     versions: 1.15 GB; three, 900 versions: 3.20 GB). `vmmap` puts the difference in freed large blocks still
>     resident ("MALLOC_LARGE (empty)", 597 MB to 2.5 GB). A counting allocator found 464 allocations of 1 MiB or more,
>     9.4 GB in one level, from `Partition::to_snapshot` ← `Db::snapshot` ← `Db::commit`, with buffers growing to
>     134 MB.
>   - **The cause.** The partition keeps every accepted increment in `green_chains` (bounded, refused
>     `Capacity { table: "green_chains" }` at the cap) "until checkpointing folds old chain entries (owed)". So each
>     version costs its increment for good, and each snapshot taken when the log fills re-encodes the whole chain.
>   - **What it means at 100k** (extrapolation): 3 rounds × 100k clients is 300k increments, about 48 GB of chain,
>     each snapshot re-encoding it, and the cap refusing submits well before.
>   - **Closed for the owner's partition (A-238, 2026-11-06,
>     `docs/bugs/2026-11-06-a-greens-chain-kept-every-version-it-ever-took.md`).** A green's chain is checkpointed at
>     its reachable floor once the increments to fold reach the checkpoint's size. Recovery restores from the
>     checkpoint and replays only the tail. The settle before a submit folds until its claim fits.
>     - **Its recovery fenced the green until 2026-11-08 (A-257).** A checkpoint at the floor passed the base of an
>       entry left above it, and recovery re-judged that entry at a base the restored green no longer held:
>       `BaseUnavailable`, the green fenced, every acknowledged version unreadable (5 of 5 restarts in every
>       recovery-slicing run, 7 of 18 primary-kill rungs). A chain entry now records what its verdict resolved and
>       recovery applies it; holders still judge the increment. Entries 789 bytes against 611, the accept's p50 +4-5 µs.
>       At f = 0 the entries after the last checkpoint are checked by digest alone. A green fenced before stays fenced
>       (`docs/bugs/2026-11-08-a-checkpoint-passed-a-retained-entrys-base-and-recovery-fenced-the-green.md`).
>     - Under a 256 KiB cap, 200 versions of 8 KiB from a work that keeps up are all accepted. Before, the chain cap
>       refused at version 31, and then the retention fold at version 34.
>     - The partition's snapshot grows by at most 39,168 bytes from version 40 to 200; before, it grew 1,329,920
>       (`crates/server/tests/green_checkpoint.rs`).
>   - **Still owed:**
>     - At `f > 0` the holders' replicas and holder records still grow a version at a time.
>     - ~~A takeover adopts the whole chain into the successor's partition.~~ Since A-333 (2026-11-18) the successor
>       records the green by its adoption of its own holder ledger: nothing of the chain up to the adopted version.
>     - A checkpoint keeps 40 bytes for every accepted identity.
>     - The checkpoint walk is not sliced.
>
> - **The quiet arm's first rungs: correct, and far from 1 ms** (Mac Studio, load 5 to 9, one node; BENCHMARKS, "The
>   load test's quiet arm"). At 1,000 clients p50 is 35 to 73 ms and p99 158 to 227 ms; at 3,000, p50 197 to 219 ms. The
>   oracle had 0 failures. Before A-247 every operation of a green's works was served on the green's one shard (about
>   112 µs an operation, 8,960 a second), so a closed-loop client's latency was clients × service time. At 3,000 clients
>   the green's retention cap refused 2,405 submits `BudgetExceeded`: a version keeps the whole previous bytes of every
>   file it overwrote, and the history folds only down to the oldest base a live work holds. Walls owed for the 10k–100k
>   rungs (the green chain's checkpointing above is closed on the owner):
>   - ~~a green's works served off its owner's shard~~ **step one on main (A-247, landed 2026-11-17 by g231)**: on
>     the owner's node a work lives on the shard its name hashes to. Its creation, its first read of each base file,
>     its verdict and its rebase ask the owner; every other verb runs on the work's shard. Across nodes (step two) is
>     open (above). The asks still queue on the owner, so its CPU a verdict and a rebase is the next wall (perf);
>   - ~~history that keeps what a version overwrote, not whole files~~ **closed (A-242, 2026-11-07)**: the
>     history is copy-on-write (`crates/merge/src/history.rs`). A version costs the bytes it wrote and its piece
>     lists. Behind a held floor, 64 versions of 64-byte overwrites of a 1 MiB file under a 16 MiB cap: 16 of 64
>     accepted before, 64 after (`green_retention.rs`, CI runs 42358895080 and 42367326179);
>   - a stated offered load per client for the 1 ms bound. At zero think time, 100k clients at 1 ms is 10⁸
>     operations a second. **The harness's half is built (2026-11-17, g231):**
>     - `--think-us` is the mean of an exponential pause drawn after every reply and before each client's first
>       request. Many independent clients' requests together approach a Poisson stream whatever each one's own pauses
>       (the Palm–Khintchine theorem). The fixed pause it replaces sent every client's first request at the same
>       instant and kept the clients bunched after, which no fleet of independent agents does.
>     - Every level prints an `offered` row: replies, verdicts and rebases a second, and the time-averaged number of
>       clients in flight, thinking, pausing after a refusal for now, and held, and their sum. A held client is due to
>       send and not sent, by the harness's sweep or its connection's ring or in-flight bound; its wait is summed at
>       its send and is in no latency row, since a latency is stamped at the send.
>     - Unit tests in the example (`cargo test -p slates-client --example load_bench`): the draws' mean and their
>       shares past one and two means against the exponential's, within five standard errors of 200,000 draws; two
>       workers' draws apart (fewer than 1% equal); the row's account of each state of the clients and their sum; a
>       level of no wall time reporting zeroes.
>
>     **Why think time 0 cannot meet the bound, on any build.** Each round of a client holds a verdict, the green's one
>     serialized step. In the closed loop at think time 0 the owner finishes at most one round per verdict's cost of its
>     CPU, so a round takes at least the clients × that cost (Little's law). The owner's CPU a verdict was 21.0–26.9 µs
>     on W1 and 37.6–50.9 µs on main db9c514e (BENCHMARKS, A-247's owner-CPU tables, 2026-11-09). So at 1,000 clients a
>     round takes at least 21 ms on W1 and 38 ms on main. A round is six requests (four edits, the append and the
>     submit), and holding each under 1 ms at think time 0 would need a verdict of at most 6 µs at 1,000 clients and
>     60 ns at 100,000. A conflict adds verdicts and rebases to the round, and lowers both bounds further.
>
>     **The statement (Ada's decision, 2026-11-18, the option g231 proposed).** "1,000 clients under 1 ms" is measured
>     at up to 1,000 merges a second, §1.4's offered increment rate per green: tens of increments a second for a few
>     agents, thousands for a fleet session (hecate MERGE.md §7). The bound holds when every kind's p99 stays under
>     1 ms at 10³ or more verdicts a second with 1,000 clients and no oracle failures. The green rate is the same at
>     every rung, so a client's share falls as the clients grow. At 100,000 clients a thousand increments a second is
>     one submit a client every 100 s, about an agent's pace; at 1,000 clients it is one a second each.
>     - Each rung sweeps its think mean so the verdicts a second (the `offered` row) span the fleet row, 10³ to 10⁴.
>     - Each rung reports the highest rate at which every kind's p99 stays under 1 ms: the rung's capacity at the
>       bound, which ratchets upward only.
>     - The bound holds where that capacity covers 10³, the fleet row's floor.
>     - The closed loop at think time 0 is the rung's capacity, reported in verdicts a second and never against the
>       bound.
>
>     **The judgment is the harness's (2026-11-18, g231).** Every level prints a `bound` row after its oracle: the
>     bound (1 ms) and the rate it is stated at (10³ verdicts a second); the level's verdicts a second; the worst p99 of
>     every kind, each attempt's and each operation's, with its row and kind; the clients held, given up or starved;
>     the oracle's failures; and `met` yes or no. A level meets the bound only at the stated rate or above, with every
>     p99 under it, no failure, and no client given up or starved. `Cycle` and `Round` now leave out their client's own
>     think pauses: left in, a cycle at about 200 ms a pause holds five of them, and no paced level could meet the
>     bound. A cycle also starts at its first edit's first send, so a refusal for now of that edit and its pause are in
>     it. Unit tests in the example: a round's cycle and round are its requests' time and none of its pauses, through
>     a conflict's resolution too; a cycle starts at the first send; the row meets the bound with every kind under it at
>     the rate, names the kind over it (a p99 of exactly 1 ms is not under), and fails below the rate, with an oracle
>     failure, with a client given up or starved, and with nothing timed.
>
>     **The harness's instants are sound, and it says what it may have added (2026-11-18, g083).** The measurer's
>     1,000-client runs on main `7d760c4ea` (BENCHMARKS, "The 1,000-client bound on main") had three oracle failures,
>     each at a point whose harness was starved of its CPU, and one recorded a submit's round trip of 5 µs where the
>     run's submits took 374 to 399 µs. The cause was the harness's: it stamped a send after `Client::begin` had handed
>     the request to its ring, and a reply before `take_ready` read the ring, so a worker the host preempted in either
>     gap recorded a send after the verdict that reflected it, or a reply before it came, and the oracle's bounds
>     (`support/load_oracle.rs`) were unsound. Now a send is read before its handing over and again after it, and a
>     reply after its ring was read, on the host's monotonic clock (the daemon's spans' clock). Each attempt also has a
>     `floor` row: its reply was not there when the connection's previous drain began, so the daemon and the ring took
>     at least that long, whatever the harness's sweep did; `max_drain_gap_ns` is now the longest window a reply's
>     arrival could not be placed in (it counted a connection's idle time before). Tests, failing first: a worker kept
>     off its CPU right after handing a request over, while the daemon's one shard answers, still stamps its send before
>     the daemon's reply was written; and one kept off right after its drain's clock read still stamps the reply it
>     takes after the daemon read the request (`a_send_is_stamped_before_the_daemon_can_have_answered_it`,
>     `a_reply_is_stamped_after_the_ring_it_was_taken_from_was_read`).
>
>     **The harness splits each latency by the producers' stamps, measures its own noise, and charges the server only
>     for its own part (2026-11-19, g083, A-559).** Main's reading of r100: the rounds with a bad p99 were the rounds
>     where `load_bench` itself stalled (accepted submits' p99 29.2 and 22.9 ms beside sweeps of 33.8 and 37.5 ms and
>     unseen windows of 44.0 and 37.6 ms; 2.7 and 0.42 ms beside 11.0 and 5.1 ms). Every slot now carries its
>     producer's stamp in the four bytes that were padding (`slates_ipc::slot`, "The stamp": the low 32 bits of the
>     host's monotonic clock as the slot was written, the lowest bit set so zero is unstamped), so the client knows when
>     its request landed and the daemon's reply landed, not only when the sweep took it. An attempt's harness part is
>     the time before its request landed and after its reply did (`slates_machine::attribution::harness_part`); a
>     latency's sums its attempts' and its client's held sends; the server part is the rest. The `floor` rows are
>     replaced by `latency_server`, `latency_harness`, `operation_server` and `operation_harness`; an attempt with a stamp
>     missing or out of order is the server's whole (`unsplit`). Before each level, as many threads as it has workers
>     watch the clock for 100 ms (`slates_machine::bench::longest_gap_ns`, `destroy_rows`' probe), and the longest gap
>     is the level's noise floor (the `noise` row). The `bound` row judges each kind by its server part
>     (`slates_machine::attribution::judge`): `met\tharness` when every server part is under the bound and some latency
>     is not, never charged to the server, `met\tno` when a server part is at or over it. Tests, failing first:
>     `slates-machine`'s attribution rule (a reply a stalled sweep left in the ring is the harness's time; an unstamped
>     or disordered exchange keeps its whole latency the server's; a quantile charged only for its server part), the
>     slot's stamp (widened back to its landing within a wrap; zero and a pre-clock landing are none; carried through a
>     write and a read), and the bench's own (`a_level_past_the_bound_only_by_the_harnesss_part_is_harness_bound`).
>     **Owed (main's):** the bench and the suites compiled and run (the example is no `--lib` target), and the A/B again
>     on a quiet machine with the split rows.
>
>     **Where a slow request's time goes (2026-11-18, g083's trace diagnostic, never on main).** Each attempt the
>     harness timed was joined with every span the daemon's shards held for its request (each shard's sink sized to
>     hold the run; the owner's answer to each ask and each resumed verb spanned too), on the Mac Studio at 1,000
>     clients over 23 shards, main `f6d37937b`'s code with the diagnostic, in-process, load 14 to 17. At a think mean of 50 ms (1,121
>     verdicts a second) an edit's p50 was 141 µs and its p99 2.2 ms; of it the verb itself took 12 µs at the median
>     and the owner's answer 13 µs at the p99, and the rest was waiting for a thread: the request in the client's ring
>     until its shard read it (p99 634 µs), the hop to the work's shard (267 µs), the ask out to the owner, batch and
>     queue (397 µs), the answer back (127 µs), the reply home (238 µs), and the harness taking it (25 µs at the p99,
>     2.7 ms at the p999). In the slowest 1% the means were 1.8, 0.9, 2.1, 0.4, 0.7 and 3.6 ms; at 20 ms (2,682
>     verdicts a second) 2.2, 1.6, 4.5, 0.5, 1.2 and 8.5 ms. Each `floor` p99 (the product's alone) was 1.6 to 2.7 ms at
>     50 ms and 2.2 to 4.6 ms at 20 ms. Every shard parked and woke about 7,500 times a second: the doorbell's herd
>     (A-381, closed below). The owner ran at 33% and 51% of a core; every other shard at 13 to 28%.
>     - **Closed: the doorbell's herd (A-381, 2026-11-18).** On macOS and Windows each client's ring kicked every shard;
>       now it marks the shard its region names and the doorbell thread kicks only the shards marked. Each shard's
>       parks fell 59% and the shards' CPU 20 to 34% at 1,000 clients; the latencies moved with the box's load (14 to 52)
>       more than with the change, so no latency is claimed for it (BENCHMARKS, 2026-11-18).
>     - **Closed: an ask waiting out the batch before it (A-388, 2026-11-18).** One batch of asks was out to an owner at
>       a time, and the wait for it was about half of an ask's way to the owner (p99 1.6 to 2.1 ms for submits and
>       rebases at 50 ms); a shard now keeps two out.
>     - **Closed: a work's hop from its client's shard (A-400, 2026-11-18).** A work lived on the shard its name hashes
>       to, so every verb of it crossed from its client's shard and back; it now lives on its client's shard, its name
>       held by an alias where the name hashes. Priced first by naming works onto their clients' shards: an edit's p99
>       about halved and its p50 40% lower at 1,000 clients.
>     - **Open, the owner's one thread:** a first touch of a base file, a verdict, a rebase and a read of the green each
>       still cross to the green's owner and queue there. A-273's replicas, which took the reads and rebases off it,
>       were measured and rejected (A-528, 2026-11-19): what keeps the p99 above 1 ms under contention is next.
>
>     **The rung's starved clients were the harness's hot set, and the round is reported, not judged (2026-11-18, g083,
>     A-416).** Every 1,000-client run had 16 to 29 clients starved, and the bound requires none: the harness drew its
>     `--hot-files 800` with replacement over `kernel/`'s 700-odd eligible files, so every file was hot and some three
>     to five times hotter than the rest. The hot set is now that many distinct files and at most half the files long
>     enough to edit, refused (`refused`, exit 1) otherwise, so the rung's 800 need a larger tree (`fs/`, 2,365 files).
>     And the bound judges every request kind and the cycle, a whole edit and merge, as §1.4's status names them; a
>     round, as many edits and merges as its conflicts make, stays in the `latency` row (191 ms at its p99 with every
>     request at 0.47 to 1.33 ms, the Mac Studio, 50 ms think mean). **Owed, measurement (the supervisor's):** the
>     rung under the set rule (`--tree <linux-v7.4-rc1>/fs`) at think means of 200, 100, 50 and 20 ms.
>
>     **The harness's workers parking between replies: measured and rejected (2026-11-18, g083, A-421).** Each worker
>     spins for its whole level, a core each taken from the daemon it measures. A-421 had a worker park on its
>     connections' completions between replies and sends; the supervisor's A/B (run r155, the Mac Studio, `fs/`, 1,000
>     clients, load 6 to 27) found the longest sweep shorter in 1 pair of 6, no client held either way, and the p99 worse
>     once the box was loaded (an edit's 26.9 ms against 8.6 ms at load 25 to 28), so the parking was taken back out the
>     same day and its lint fixes kept (BENCHMARKS, "A load-test worker that parks between replies"). The same runs
>     show the goals' remaining gap: every edit and submit p99 under 1 ms at the lightest load but one run, 3 to 35 ms
>     from load 11 to 28.
>
>     **Owed, measurement (the supervisor's):** the 1,000-client rung on main with W1 (A-247 step one, landed
>     2026-11-17) against main before it (02c6469e5). Each think mean runs as its own invocation with a fresh daemon,
>     interleaved across builds: every kind's p50, p99, p999 and max, the `offered` row and the `bound` row. A think
>     mean of about 200 ms gives about 10³ verdicts a second at 1,000 clients (a round of about six requests a client),
>     and about 20 ms gives about 10⁴. The run's own verdicts a second are the figure. The goal is met when a level at
>     1,000 clients reads `met yes` at 10³ verdicts a second or more.
>
>   The 10,000-client rung (same Studio, load 9.8 to 10.9, 313 connections) did not finish within its 30-minute bound.
>   After 1,775 s about 2,170 of 10,000 clients were done and about 11,600 submits counted, with daemon RSS 17.6 GB.
>   At the 1,000-client rate the rung's roughly 950k operations take under two minutes, so a submit costs far more at
>   this scale; the green's history and the rebases are the suspects, not yet measured. Its percentiles are lost: the
>   harness prints them at the level's end, and the bound killed it. The Studio's runner then went offline.
>
>   **Rerun on A-238 (2026-11-07, same Studio, load 1.5 to 7.5): it is a stall, not throughput.**
>   - It did not finish in 1,800 s. The daemon used 5 min 22 s of CPU in the 30 minutes, and its RSS sat flat at
>     19.7 GB from the first minutes.
>   - 535 requests sent in the run's first second were still unanswered at 1,795 s (Edit, ReadHead, Rebase). The
>     harness's workers froze (worker 0 at 1,130 of 1,264 clients done from 1,600 s on).
>   - The daemon logged "the control shard's beat task ran 918331 ms after its last turn … in the gap the shard ran 2
>     steps and 1 polls": a shard asleep for 15 minutes with requests waiting, a lost wakeup by the look of it. A-228's
>     watchdog does not flag a parked shard.
>   - At 3,000 clients, W3 and main measure the same (three runs each, wall 72 to 105 s, `SubmitAccepted` p50 0.58
>     to 0.92 s). The 2,410 to 2,456 `BudgetExceeded` per run were W2's.
>   - Owed: the stall's diagnosis (which shard, which ring, which wake), raised to the supervisor.
>
> **The oracle at 100,000 clients (2026-11-17, g232).** The harness's oracle counted both of a conflict's bounds by
> scanning every accepted submit, for every conflict: at the 10,000-client rung's 111,708 conflicts and 26,598 accepts
> that is 5.9 × 10⁹ comparisons, and at 100,000 clients about 6 × 10¹¹ (an extrapolation at ten times of each), hours
> of the harness's own CPU after its clients are done. It also tried every head between the bounds, and held three
> whole copies of every touched file (before the level, the head and the replay: about 5 GB over the whole kernel's
> 1.67 GB). The oracle is now its own file (`crates/client/examples/support/load_oracle.rs`): the bounds are two binary
> searches over the accepted instants sorted once, a slot's writes are found by binary search, only the heads where one
> of the submit's slots was written are tried (the expected set cannot change between them), the replay runs in place
> over the bytes before the level, and each head file is read, compared and dropped in turn. Its test
> (`crates/client/tests/load_oracle.rs`) keeps the serial oracle it replaced as the reference: over 512 generated levels
> a serial green judged (some submits made wrong after), the two name the same failures in the same words and order;
> handwritten cases hold each failure kind and a conflict that fits only past its lowest head. Red-checked: trying only
> the lowest head failed both that case and the property; counting a reply at the send's own instant as before it
> failed the property. The harness prints the oracle's own time (`oracle_ns\t<n>\tsubmits\t…\theads\t…`). Owed: the
> time measured at a 10,000-client rung before and after.
>
> **Version 0 over the kernel at `f = 1` (2026-11-17, g232, A-286): built, measurement owed.** The topology the goal
> names (one primary and two replicas) could not set up a green over the whole kernel. At `f > 0` version 0's inputs,
> the encoded origin, were made in one poll (walk, encode, archive) at the green's creation and again on every pass of
> the record plane until version 0 placed, shipped whole in one message, and restored, decoded and seeded on each holder
> in one poll. Over 1.67 GB each of those is seconds of one shard's poll, past A-232's watchdog. No fleet test had a
> green over a base, so the path had never run. Now:
> - the owner makes the inputs once, a share at a time (`crates/server/src/merge_origin.rs`, `OriginInputsJob`);
> - shipments carry at most one slice's verification of what each target lacks, and the target answers with what it
>   holds (`merge_service::ship_version`, `record_inputs_answers`; `Committed::answers` in `slates-cluster`);
> - holders seed their replica a share at a time (`ReplicaSeed`), the first slice as the record arrives;
> - inputs archives are chunked at 1 MiB, so the kernel's origin is about 1,600 extents, not 100,000 to 400,000.
>
> Test: `a_green_over_a_base_places_its_origin_at_f1_a_slice_at_a_time` (`crates/server/tests/fleet.rs`: three nodes at
> `f = 1`, a 256-file base on node a; version 0 placed, both holders at version 0, a submit after it accepted as version
> 1 on both, the counters `merge.origin_inputs.made`/`.slices`, `merge.inputs.partial`, `merge.replica.seeded` and
> `.seed_slices`, and no node keeping a probe for half the placement). Unit: the streamed archive equals the whole one
> in every cut; a shipment's bound; the owner's reading of answers; the seed against the whole seeding's identity, a
> wrong identity and unheld inputs; a seed whose green is forgotten meanwhile (a tombstone, a takeover's reclaim)
> installing nothing, red without the install's hold check; `Committed::answers`; `ContentHold::held_manifest`/
> `held_chunk`.
>
> Measured by the fleet test (debug build, a loaded Mac at load 41, 2026-11-17): version 0 placed at `f + 1` in 951 ms
> while 3,321 status probes were answered, the longest 22 ms. The owner made the inputs over 475 slices and shipped
> them in 4 partial shipments; each holder seeded over 359 slices. Main without the change, same base and runner:
> placed in 1.66 s, the longest probe 298 ms, from a 4 MiB origin. A poll's cost there grows with the origin, so
> over 1.67 GB it is the seconds the watchdog ends. Owed:
> - the measurement over the whole kernel on the launcher (`crates/cli/tests/load_scale.rs`): the owner's and the
>   holders' longest polls while version 0 places, and the time to place it;
> - a restarted owner remakes version 0's inputs before it re-ships the record (A-246);
> - ~~a takeover successor gathers version 0 from its hold in one call (`recover_green_inputs`);~~ closed by A-333
>   (2026-11-18): the successor adopts the replica it built from version 0 when it was placed;
> - a large increment's archive is remade from its chain entry on each pass that ships it;
> - version 0's archive is kept while any candidate lacks version 0, which is for good if a candidate never answers and
>   membership does not remove it;
> - a holder's seed gathers the size its held manifest declares, at most a chunk's bytes an extent, uncharged, as the
>   one-call restore before it was: an owner's manifest naming one chunk many times makes a holder gather that many
>   copies. The seed's transient bytes (gathered, decoded, seeded) want charging to the shard's budget;
> - ~~sibling, found reading `held_inputs` (not changed here): its restore cap is the archive's distinct chunks' bytes and
>   one more chunk, on the rule that an inputs archive names each chunk once. A fixed-size cut names a chunk again
>   wherever the inputs repeat a chunk's bytes at a chunk boundary (two identical runs of a chunk or more), and such
>   inputs are refused `merge.inputs_undecodable` for good. A failing test is owed before any change.~~ Closed by A-383
>   (2026-11-18): such inputs were refused `merge.inputs_unheld` (not `undecodable`) at every shipment; a holder now
>   gathers them extent by extent, charged to its shard's budget while it recomputes.
>
> **Fixed 2026-11-18 (g232, A-313): a restarted holder refused every later version of its greens.** A warm restart keeps
> a holder's accepted records and held inputs, but its replica of each green lived in memory alone, so it answered every
> later record `merge.out_of_order`, for good, while the owner shipped it again every pass. With one primary and two
> replicas at `f = 1`, one replica's restart left every version one holder's answer from stalling, and a second stalled
> the green. Now the holder rebuilds the replica from its records and held inputs a slice at a time before it judges the
> record (`merge_origin::rebuild_replica`). Test: `a_holder_restarted_over_its_segment_recomputes_the_greens_next_version`
> (`crates/server/tests/fleet.rs`): red, the restarted holder answered version 2's record out of order 4,586 times and
> version 2 never placed within the test's 60 s; green, placed in 2.56 s with one rebuild counted (kiln r1017,
> 2026-11-18; `docs/bugs/2026-11-18-a-restarted-holder-refused-every-later-version-of-its-greens.md`). Still open,
> found beside it:
> - a restarted holder's `merge.refused` (a green refused for good after a mismatch) is in memory too, so the restarted
>   holder rebuilds such a green and refuses it again only at the version that mismatched;
> - a rebuild over a long chain recomputes every version the holder accepted (300,000 at the 100,000-client rung's three
>   rounds), since the holder keeps no checkpoint of its replica; the holder's growth per version is A-238's owed item.
>
> **Step one 2026-11-18 (g232, A-404): a replica keeps a durable checkpoint at its owner's committed floor.** Each
> merge record names the newest version its owner knew committed (record format 4); a holder keeps its replica's
> checkpoint there as a held piece, and a rebuild starts from it and recomputes only the versions after it
> (`a_rebuilt_replica_starts_from_the_checkpoint_its_holder_keeps`: versions 1 and 2's increments not held, the replica
> rebuilt to 3). Step two, the same day: the holder's ledger drops its positions after version 0 and below the
> checkpoint's own, and its retention releases the inputs they named
> (`a_holder_lets_go_of_the_records_and_inputs_its_checkpoint_stands_for`), so a replica's records and inputs are bounded
> by the versions its owner has not yet committed. A-238's owed "the holders' replicas and records grow per version" is
> closed by A-385 and A-404.
>
> **Fixed 2026-11-18 (g083, A-476): a takeover successor's chain lacked the versions its checkpoint stood for.** A
> successor that had let go of its ledger's positions below its held checkpoint (A-404) named its adopted versions by
> the ledger alone, so its chain began after them (`a_successor_two_versions_behind_adopts_the_versions_between_and_serves_the_green`,
> 2 of 4 runs on Linux, at and before A-273). The versions through its adoption are now named by the ledger where it
> holds the position and by the checkpoint's record of what it accepted where it let go of it
> (`merge_origin::ledger_identities`; test `a_successors_chain_names_the_versions_its_checkpoint_stands_for`). Its
> engine, its rebuild and its durable state were right throughout. Record:
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-18-a-successors-chain-lacked-the-versions-its-checkpoint-stood-for.md`.
>
> **Fixed 2026-11-18 (g232, A-385): a holder's replica of a green kept every version's values.** An owner folds its
> green's histories to its per-green budget, never past a live reader's version; a holder's replica, the engine it
> recomputes every version on and a takeover adopts, folded nothing. Now each merge record names where the owner's engine
> had folded (record format 3) and the holder folds its replica there once it holds the version, as a rebuild does at
> each version. Test: `a_holders_replica_keeps_no_more_history_than_its_owner` (`crates/server/tests/fleet.rs`): 130
> versions of 4,043 bytes under a 256 KiB chain cap, both replicas folded below 66 holding 260,288 bytes of history, the
> owner's to the byte; with the fold a no-op they held 524,643 bytes, folded below 0 (kiln r133, Mac Studio). Still
> open, A-238's owed: a holder's ledger records and held inputs grow per version until a durable checkpoint of the
> replica on the holder lets them go below the floor.
>
> **Fixed 2026-11-18 (g232, A-383): a version whose inputs repeat a chunk was refused by every holder, for good.** A
> holder restored a version's inputs within the archive's distinct chunks' bytes and one chunk more; inputs cut at fixed
> offsets name a chunk at several extents wherever they repeat a chunk's bytes at the cut (a run of one byte three chunks
> long is enough), so every holder refused the version `merge.inputs_unheld` at every shipment and, at `f = 1`, it never
> placed. Now a holder gathers the inputs extent by extent and charges what the recomputation holds (twice their declared
> size) to its shard's budget first, refusing `merge.inputs_over_budget` past what it can admit. Test:
> `a_version_whose_inputs_repeat_a_chunk_is_recomputed_by_every_holder` (`crates/server/tests/fleet.rs`): passed in
> 4.15 s; red on main's holder code, the submit `DeadlineExceeded` after 60 s and each holder 4,583 refusals (kiln r49,
> Mac Studio; `docs/bugs/2026-11-18-inputs-repeating-a-chunk-were-refused-by-every-holder-for-good.md`). Still open:
> the recomputation of one version, gather included, is one call, costing what the increment's size costs.

> **Fixed 2026-11-18 (g232): the late-submit test judged a green's history by factors no measurement gave.**
> `a_submit_late_in_a_greens_history_is_answered_as_fast_as_an_early_one` (`crates/server/tests/fleet.rs`) held the median
> of the last 50 of 300 submits to four times the first 50's plus 2 ms (R3), from windows minutes apart, so a load that
> changed between them read as a cost of history. Its macOS failure on CI (run 44298844583, main 1e82ebda1) was not that
> bound: the owner ran one poll of 3,417 ms after about 69 submits, its holders declared it dead, and the 70th submit
> waited out the client's 120 s. That is the signature of the record plane's spin main fixed after that run (340d4f6fb,
> g251: a nudge after every ship ran back-to-back passes in one poll), and 14 runs on the Mac Studio, quiet and under 48
> spinners, never repeated it. Now, after 300 versions of one green, 50 pairs alternate a submit on it with one on a
> fresh green, the order in each pair alternating, and the Wilcoxon signed-rank statistic W+ of the old-minus-fresh
> differences must stay within n(n+1)/4 + z·√(n(n+1)(2n+1)/24), z = 4.7534 the normal quantile of a spurious failure in a
> million runs (NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook §1.3.6.7.1): 1,129.9 at 50 pairs. Kiln r3592, the Mac Studio, debug build: W+
> 420 to 801 in 5 quiet runs and 331 to 772 in 3 under 48 spinners, both greens' medians 3.7 to 4.4 ms; with 20 µs a
> version of the green's history injected into the submit path, W+ 1,225 and the test failed.

> **Fixed 2026-11-18 (g232, A-376): every version re-published the whole content hold.** The content hold's image was
> one piece (A-270), every chunk, manifest and stage a holder keeps, recomputed at every publication and re-put whenever
> it changed, which at `f > 0` is every version of a green: after A-372 about a tenth of a holder's time at 1,000
> versions (`sample`, Mac Studio, debug), and deltas big enough that the journal checkpointed about as often as it
> logged. Now the hold is a piece per chunk, per held manifest and per stage, it notes each piece it changes, and a delta
> carries those (image version 30). Test: `a_holders_publication_carries_the_content_it_puts_not_the_whole_hold`
> (`daemon.rs`): on main's code a put's delta grew 158 bytes a put, now one size. With A-367, A-372 and this, the
> late-submit test's late median at 300 versions is 2.28 to 2.37 ms against early 2.31 to 2.49, and at 1,000 versions
> 3.76 against 6.00 (kiln r3543, Mac Studio, debug): no growth with a green's history left at `f = 1` on the commit path.
>
> **Fixed 2026-11-18 (g232, A-372): every version re-judged every version's inputs its holders kept.** A holder runs the
> retention rule after every record it accepts and every put it holds, and the rule judged every manifest held for the
> object, each by decoding the ledger position at its placed sequence (`content_retention::retain_object`), so a green's
> every version decoded every version's record before it: on the Mac Studio, a debug build, `sample` of the late-submit
> test at 1,000 versions found a fifth of each holder's time in that rule (1,364 to 1,413 samples of about 6,570), the
> late median at 18.2 ms against the early 2.16. A ledger never rewrites an accepted position, so its inputs placed below
> its newest accepted version were judged when their records came; now the rule judges those placed at or past it
> (`ContentHold::retain_placed_from`, over the hold's manifests indexed by placed sequence, charged with them), and the
> newest placement is one read. Test: `a_greens_retention_judges_only_the_inputs_its_newest_version_can_change`
> (`content_retention.rs`): the last of 64 versions judges one manifest, every input still held (red with the rule
> judging a ledger whole). Kiln r3491, the Mac Studio, debug: the late-submit test's late median at 300 versions 2.92 to
> 3.28 ms against early 1.87 to 1.96 (it was 4.4 to 6.4 against 2.0 to 2.4), and at 1,000 versions 8.49 against 2.28
> (18.2 against 2.16). What remains is the content hold's image, one piece re-encoded and re-put at each publication,
> about a tenth of a holder's time at 1,000 versions, which also brings the checkpoints a delta's size triggers.
>
> **Fixed 2026-11-18 (g232, A-367): every version re-published every version its holders kept.** A held register was
> one piece holding every position its acceptor kept (A-270), and a green's register on its holders is a ledger, never
> compacted; a holder publishes before it acknowledges each version, so each version's publication re-encoded and
> re-wrote the holder's whole ledger, and a commit at `f > 0` grew by a position a version (Mac Studio, debug build:
> `a_submit_late_in_a_greens_history_is_answered_as_fast_as_an_early_one`'s late medians 4.3 to 7.1 ms against early
> 1.9 to 3.6 ms over 300 versions; at the goal's 300,000 versions about 60 MB a version on each replica). Now a register
> is a head piece and a piece per accepted position, and a delta carries the positions a holder's acceptor accepted or

> `a_holders_publication_carries_the_position_it_acknowledges_not_the_whole_ledger` (`crates/server/tests/recovery.rs`):

> **Fixed 2026-11-18 (g232, A-333): losing the primary of a kernel-sized green lost the green.** The takeover successor
> rebuilt the green beside the ledger it holds as one of the green's holders: version 0's inputs and every increment's
> restored whole and every accepted record decoded in one poll, then the origin's bytes and every increment recorded
> again in its partition and the green replayed twice in another. The partition's merge budget (a quarter of a shard's
> metadata reserve, about 333 MB a shard on a 64 GB machine of 16 shards) refused the kernel's 1.67 GB origin at its
> first record, and the takeover was given up at the failover bound (`NotRecovered { TakeoverIncomplete { refused } }`).
> Now the successor records the green by its adoption of its own holder ledger (`Op::GreenAdopted`) and serves it with
> the replica it already had, brought to the adopted version a slice at a time; a restarted successor re-adopts it at
> boot before admitting clients (`crates/server/src/green_adopt.rs`). Test:
> `a_successor_adopts_a_greens_ledger_past_its_merge_budget_and_keeps_it_across_its_restart`
> (`crates/server/tests/fleet.rs`: three nodes at `f = 1`, each partition's merge budget a quarter of the 4 MiB base the
> green's origin is walked from; owner a stopped for good, then the successor restarted warm): green in 4.92 s on the Mac
> Studio (kiln r2370, debug build), five versions committed across the takeover and the restart, the replica rebuilt
> through version 2 in 325 slices at the restart's re-adoption; red on main's code, the takeover refused 100 times and
> given up (`NotRecovered { TakeoverIncomplete { waited_on: "refused" } }`). Found and fixed beside it:
> - a restarted successor of any taken-over green wrote its merge and catalog records at its own host's epoch, below the
>   fence its takeover raised at every holder, since only `placed_heads` named the promotion epoch and a restart forgets
>   it: the green never advanced again. The green's record now keeps its takeover (`VolumeRecord::taken_over`) and
>   `merge_service::record_epoch` falls back to it (red without it: version 3 never placed again, version 4 unanswered at
>   60 s; `docs/bugs/2026-11-18-a-restarted-greens-successor-wrote-below-its-takeovers-fence.md`);
> - a destroyed green's tombstone was one past its chain's length, short after a checkpoint (A-238), so it could be older
>   than versions its holders had accepted (`a_destroyed_greens_tombstone_is_past_its_head_whatever_its_chain_holds`,
>   `crates/db/tests/model.rs`: 3 and 2 before, 6 and 5 now).
>
> Still open:
> - a successor whose ledger ends two or more versions below the adopted one (the ledger-prefix transfer of records,
>   GAP-A9-7), and a new candidate that holds nothing of the green (AUD-14's transfer to a new candidate set);
> - the adoption records the gathered completions in one call on the owner shard, up to each client's bound per client:
>   at 100,000 clients that is up to some hundreds of thousands of records in one poll;
> - a successor with no replica whose ledger lacks inputs below the adopted version rebuilds from version 0 at each
>   attempt (bounded by the failover SLO's attempts), where keeping the partial replica would resume it;
> - a green taken over past its tolerance is not marked so in its record (A-332 marks a volume's: the takeover round keeps
>   the shortfall of a volume's head register only, `takeover::record_adoption`), so a green's loss report cannot say a
>   version acknowledged only to the lost hosts may be gone;
> - flagged for removal: `GreenOriginated` (a green's origin as bytes in its partition) has no producer since A-333, so
>   its replay (`GreenReplay`'s decode, `OriginInputsJob`'s recorded stage, a checkout's hash of the bytes) runs only in
>   the tests that record one; the operation's tag stays, since every operation after it is numbered by its place.
>
> The topology launcher is `crates/cli/tests/load_scale.rs`. It runs one primary and two replica server nodes in
> region 0 at `f = 1`, and client nodes in region 1, so the client nodes are never the green's holders. One harness
> drives every client node (`--instance a,b,…`), so one oracle judges every submit. It is portable (`ps`, `pgrep`),
> so it runs on macOS. Not yet through a rung: with a debug daemon on the loaded Mac, `base pin` of `kernel/`
> outlasts the CLI's 1 s reply deadline, and the green is then refused `ConsistentBaseUnavailable`. In release the
> pin takes 278 to 637 ms for 754 files. That is the open "pinning a tree of many files" item (loadtest's, above),
> and it is the wall for the whole kernel as the workload.
>
> Sanity rungs, Mac, in-process daemon, loaded arm (load 46 to 62 on 18 CPUs, the fleet suite running): 10 and 100
> clients over `kernel/`, at one and ten logical clients a connection, oracle and own files 0 failures, no
> backpressure, no starved clients. The latencies measure the box, not slates: the worker threads were descheduled
> for up to 147 ms between drains of one ring (`max_drain_gap_ns`), so the quiet arm is on the Studio. A
> `rebase_conflicts` of exactly 100 at 100 clients, in both forms, was coincidence: a third run counted 99. Every named
> window is one of the client's own hot slots, rewritten by another client between its resolution read and its
> rebase, so the head really moved (the harness names the first five a worker meets).

> **One refused receive ended a fleet node's transport (found 2026-11-06 as the UDP reset's sibling, fixed
> 2026-11-07).** `Demux::run` read every refused receive as the socket's end, so an earlier send's report stopped a
> node's serve socket for the daemon's life. Now every receive loop in `rt`, `transport` and `server` ends only on the
> socket gone (`RtError::receive_refusal`), and counts the rest by kind in status. Tests on the simulated fabric hold
> the demultiplexer, an endpoint's handshake and a DNS lookup each failing before its change; see the bug record of
> 2026-11-07. Owed: the membership plane's change has no test of its own.

> **A submit at `f = 1` waited for the coordinator's period: fixed (2026-11-06, §4.16 Commit;
> A-235).** The merge record plane ran once per 100 ms coordinator period, putting a version's inputs at one
> period and shipping its record at the next. One submit at a time on an idle three-node fleet took 208 to 647 ms, and at
> 1,000 clients on Linux every accepted submit was answered `Overloaded`. Now an enqueued version, or a newly
> acknowledged input or record, wakes the coordinator, which runs the merge plane at once (`nudge_record_plane`,
> `pace_running_merges`). A version's inputs go only to the holders whose next record it is, since a lagging holder let
> go of the inputs it needed next (`merge.inputs_unheld` 53 and 71 in two runs). Median now 2.7 to 4.4 ms (debug build,
> 5 of 5). Still owed: more than one version a holder per pass, so a hot green's versions still commit one round trip
> apart. Record: `docs/bugs/2026-11-06-a-submit-at-f1-waited-for-the-coordinators-period.md`.

> **A submit in a three-process fleet at `f = 1` was never answered: fixed (2026-11-06, §4.8 joint writes, §4.16
> Commit; A-234, `Quorum::committed_within` reviewed by raft-chaos).** A green made on the bootstrapper while its council formed had
> its merge records enqueued under the bootstrap's one-candidate placement, and pending records were never
> re-placed; once they were, the joint placement joined the bootstrap's one-member settled cohort, which can never
> give `f + 1`. Pending merge records now follow the current configuration each period, as heads do
> (`PendingGreen::retarget`), and a joint cohort smaller than the quorum needs every member
> (`Quorum::committed_within`). In-process red test: 0 of 8 answered before, 5 of 5 after (1.2 s); three-process CLI
> test: 0 of 5 before, 3 of 3 after (2.3 to 3.0 s). Record:
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-06-a-submit-in-a-three-process-fleet-is-never-answered.md`.

> **The anchor kills live daemons on a busy machine (found 2026-11-06, audit step 7; fixed by A-228, Windows CI owed).** Under the
> A/B bar's load, two spinners a logical CPU (8 on CI's 4-CPU Windows runners), the anchor killed daemons that were
> alive and serving because their heartbeat lapsed its 1,000 ms liveness budget. A busy machine is the normal case
> (Ada's rule), so a starved but live daemon must not be killed.
> - **Seen:**
>   - Diagnostics run 42161838327 (`diag-winfsp-overlap-28`, four daemons beside the spinners), x86_64 run 1: the
>     anchor killed sep1 (main `28359a75`, unchanged receiver) and comb1, logging `the daemon's heartbeat lapsed;
>     killing it`. That run's late heartbeats (gaps of half the budget or more): sep1 16, comb2 13, comb1 11. The DLL
>     build (`71cf09ac`) does not log them.
>   - Run 42130583401 (`diag-winfsp-overlap-20`, two daemons) lost x86_64 run 3 the same way, to the DLL arm's daemon.
>   - Run 42080252187 (winfsp-bench, `eb0983ec`'s entry) lost one run likewise, the DLL arm's on x86_64.
>   - A killed daemon's drive dies, and `mount_bench` fails that run's whole loaded phase for every arm.
> - **The budget is a fixed number, not derived:** `slates_server::daemon::LIVENESS_BUDGET_NS = 1_000_000_000`, a
>   `Shape:` constant documented as "a second; the supervisor's input until the CLI takes the operator's value". The beat
>   cadence is a tenth of it (`HEARTBEAT_NS`, 100 ms), so nine beats fit in it. Nothing in it is measured from the
>   machine or its load.
> - **What misses is the shard, not a heartbeat thread.** The heartbeat is a task, `heartbeat_loop`, on the control
>   shard's own executor (`crates/server/src/daemon.rs`), so a beat misses whenever that shard's thread does not run.
>   `log_late_beat` shows what it did in each gap. In the run 1 above the shard ran 2-4 steps in 974-1,036 ms. Its
>   longest poll was 503-576 ms, with all 3-5 of the gap's polls unattributed (none counted as a task's own CPU,
>   blocked in the kernel, or preempted by the host), and its timer overrun was 42-92 ms. That reads as the thread kept
>   off the CPU. That Windows reports that preemption as unattributed is a hypothesis, not checked.
> - **What was tried:** winfsp-bench's `eb0983ec` measured every shard thread at `THREAD_PRIORITY_ABOVE_NORMAL` (run
>   42080252187). Neither that arm nor the normal one lapsed there, each alone beside the spinners. It was not adopted
>   because it cost x86_64's loaded p50s. **The heartbeat alone at a raised priority was never tried, and cannot be as
>   built:** it is a task on a shard, not a thread of its own.
> - **Fixed by A-228** (2026-11-06): the beat is written by an owned watchdog thread pinned to no core, which judges
>   each shard in its own CPU time (A-65's rule): stuck once a window passes with no step and no CPU progress, or with a
>   window's CPU run; starved otherwise, and alive. (2026-11-08: a shard the scheduler has waiting for a CPU is starved
>   too, however long its clock stands still; see "A starved shard was judged wedged".) The anchor holds the beat to the window plus its own measured
>   lateness p99. Tests, each failing first where it can: `crates/server/tests/liveness.rs` — a starved control-shard
>   poll gapped the beat 1.53 s on main and 0.26 s with A-228 (macOS arm64, load 54–70); a wedged non-control shard
>   and a spinning one never stopped main's beat, and with A-228 stop it (1.007 s after the wedge; after 1,063 ms of the
>   spinner's CPU, 2.98 s of wall at load 56). A half-window block and two spinners a core beside the daemon keep the
>   beat under the window on both. The real-process frozen-daemon test still kills at the lapse (1,045 ms old against a
>   1,044 ms bound: the window plus a 44 ms lateness p99). Owed: the Windows runners under the bar's load (diag branch),
>   then macOS and Linux beside them. Record: `docs/bugs/2026-11-06-the-anchor-killed-live-daemons-on-a-busy-machine.md`.
>
> **A principal is compared across hosts with no host (security, fixed 2026-11-07 by A-237; owner: clients).** Fixed:
> every principal carries its host's certificate anchor, a forwarded principal is rescoped by its session's anchor, and
> a refused forward is `NotShared` naming the share that would let it in (record:
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-07-a-principal-was-compared-across-hosts-with-no-host.md`). Found with it, and fixed in its own change first: a
> taken-over green kept no shares, since a green shipped no catalog register
> (`docs/bugs/2026-11-07-a-taken-over-green-lost-its-access-list.md`). What it was: A
> verb forwarded to a volume's owner on another node carries the requester's principal "as the origin node authenticated
> it" (`crates/server/src/verbs.rs` `ForwardedRequest`). The owner dispatches a read under it, and runs a write under
> it, as is (`serve_forward`); the origin's host keys only the completion record. `rights_of` then grants a principal
> equal to a volume's owner or access entry, and a host account carries no host (`slates_db::catalog::Principal::Uid {
> uid }`). Three collisions follow:
> - every Windows channel is `Uid { uid: 0 }` (the bootstrap object's mode is the authentication: only the daemon's
>   user opens it, and `slates_ipc::rendezvous`'s `current_uid` is 0 on Windows), so any two Windows users on different
>   nodes are one principal across a forward;
> - a Windows user is Unix root's principal: a forward from any Windows node meets a root-run daemon's volumes as their
>   owner, and the other way round;
> - one uid on two Unix hosts, usually two people, is one principal across a forward.
>
> What does not cross hosts: grants and landings (issued on the local control channel), remote attachments
> (`Consumer::Remote { host, client }`) and enrolled consumers (found by id on their record's partition). Decided
> (supervisor, 2026-11-07): every principal that crosses hosts is scoped by its origin host's authenticated identity,
> owner and access entries record (host, account), and `rights_of` compares the scoped principal (A-237). A fleet account
> mapping, one person's accounts on several hosts as one principal, is a separate open design item for Ada; until it
> exists, cross-host access needs an access entry naming (host, account). Found while checking a wrong premise: a
> Windows consumer does attest (`crates/server/tests/consumers.rs`, green on main on ubuntu x86_64 and arm64, Windows
> x86_64 and arm64 and macOS, diag `consumers-1`). What remains of that is naming: on Windows the host account is
> recorded as uid 0, Unix root's number, and §4.13 says the rendezvous authenticates "uid/SID" while the code
> authenticates by the object's ACL and never reads a SID (held; the supervisor decides after A-237).
>
> **A fleet account mapping (open design item for Ada, 2026-11-07).** After A-237 a local account means something only
> on its host, so one person's accounts on several hosts are several principals: a volume shared across the fleet needs
> an access entry for each (host, account). Whether the fleet should map accounts to one fleet principal, and who may
> assert such a mapping (it is an authority over every node's volumes), is undecided.

> **Starved is not stuck: the r3k clean rung at `CPUWeight=1` did not exercise the rule (2026-11-08, adacachy).** One
> 3,000-client clean rung on `47de249b` (fixtures' arguments, `capped3.sh` unit, 100 ms sampler; run by the A-228 step 5
> agent because fixtures was paused on its weekly limit) logged 0 wedged, 0 starved, 0 spinning and 0 lapsed lines. No
> Starved line appeared and no shard thread sat 800 ms with flat CPU, so the run says nothing either way about the rule;
> the replays and the real-thread tests carry it. It ran at load 17–22, beside loadtest-scale's `CPUWeight=1` build.
> Baselines, on older trees: `rungs8/r3k-clean2` (3,000 clients, load 22–60) logged 8 wedged and 2 lapsed;
> `rungs9/ab-clean-2` (10,000 clients) logged 2 wedged, 4 spinning and 1 lapsed, both wedged shards state R throughout
> their flat windows on its samples.
>
> | Rung | Reconnects | Resends | Longest outage | SubmitAccepted p99 |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | `rungs8/r3k-clean2` | 86 | 420 | 1.78 s | 31.5 s |
