  directory: `state done`, 4,173 entries written, **`diff -r` silent every run**, 503 barriers.
  - **Timing is load-dominated, not an A-132 regression.** Three runs at load 21–40 took 4.7–7.5 s; one run at load 13
    took **1.8 s**, in line with the 1.54 s median recorded before A-132 (which was at load 12–16).
  - **Measured-and-rejected: a persistent per-landing barrier worker.** The hypothesis was that A-132's one thread a
    barrier (503 for this tree) cost the landing. Instrumented on HEAD during the real landing: thread spawn was
    **8.7 ms total over 503 barriers (17 µs each)**, against the barriers' own `fdatasync`/`F_BARRIERFSYNC` work of
    369 ms and a whole-await overhead (spawn + park + unpark + lease) of 46 ms (2.5% of the 1.8 s). Reusing one worker
    thread would save ~8 ms on a 1.8 s landing. Not built; recorded so it is not re-proposed. The barrier's **I/O** is
    the cost, and it already runs off the shard.

### 2026-10-10 (late): CONFIRMED — a landing's finish advances every entry in one unsliced step (R4, condition 12)

The last unbounded step on the shard during a landing, after A-132 moved the barriers off it. **Measured**, not estimated:
the engine's in-memory advance (`land_advance`, `crates/vfs/src/base.rs`: forget each landed overlay entry or rebase it
from the snapshot, then invalidate listings) timed over the simulated host (`land_bench finscan`, scratch, 2 runs):

| entries | advance | per entry |
|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 0.95–0.99 ms | 0.95 µs |
| 10,000 | 10.0–11.0 ms | 1.05 µs |
| 25,000 | 25.2–29.1 ms | 1.08 µs |
| 50,000 | 52.3–53.2 ms | 1.05 µs |

- **Linear at ~1.0 µs/entry** (≈1.68 µs/entry on a real volume, from the 600-entry server measurement). So **~105 ms at
  100k files, ~1 s at 1M** — one step, on the shard, holding every other client for its whole duration. Real OCI images
  and monorepos reach those counts (condition 2). This breaks R4's bounded-work rule and condition 12's p99 at scale;
  the common case (≤16k files, ≤17 ms) does not feel it.
- **Not a correctness bug:** the landing lands correctly; it is a scalability/latency bound. Not a regression (it
  predates A-132). A-132's `finish_granted` runs it inside one synchronous `with_state`, so today it is atomic — no
  concurrent verb sees a partial advance.
- **The fix — slice the advance** (the next piece, for its own run): a resumable cursor over `landed`, stepped under
  the shard's per-iteration budget, driven by the server's `drive_granted_landing` between yields like the write and
  sync phases, with the completion's DB record still committed as one atom at the true end (A-127). Crash mid-advance
  is safe by construction — the in-memory advance is not durable until that commit, so a restart rebuilds the
  un-advanced overlay from the log and the resume re-lands.
- **The open question to resolve first (why it is not a rushed fix):** slicing makes the overlay→base read flip
  non-atomic. Reads stay consistent (a forgotten entry reads the base, which now holds the identical landed content),
  but a concurrent **drift** query (§4.5/§4.6) could, for the window between an entry's placement and its witness update,
  see a landed entry whose witness is still the old base — a transient false drift. Needs the drift path read to confirm
  whether it ignores overlay-shadowed entries (likely safe) or must be fenced during the advance. Confirm scope with Ada
  per the debugging protocol before building.

### 2026-10-11: the landing's finish is sliced (A-133) — the confirmed O(entries) advance, closed

Closes the confirmed finding of 2026-10-10 (the finish advanced every entry in one unsliced step, ~1 µs/entry,
~105 ms at 100k — an R4 bound at OCI/monorepo scale).

- **Built.** The advance runs one entry a unit under the shard's step budget, driven by the server between yields; the
  report's counts, the held count and the all-advanced flag are accumulated over the loop, so the former `advanced`
  (a manifest-keyed `BTreeMap` + `Vec`) and the six terminal count passes are folded in and nothing O(entries) runs in
  one unit. `land_advance` split into begin/one/end; `Phase::Advance`; `finish_step`; `step_finish`/`complete_finish`.
- **Bounded, measured** (in-memory host, 125 µs budget, p50/p99 flat 1k→100k): steps of p50 126 µs, p99 130–752 µs at
  every size, against the one unsliced ~105 ms step. The max is a rare tail outlier on the shared VM (6.4 ms at 100k over
  793 steps), not an algorithmic step — per-unit instrumentation found no O(n) unit (one 556 µs outlier across 100k).
- **The drift question, resolved.** The earlier "no false drift" note was wrong for a *modified* base file: it is copied
  up yet keeps its base witness, so from the write-phase placement until its advance a `status` query sees it as transient
  self-drift. This is **pre-existing** (the write phase is already sliced) and the advance's `base_forget` clears both the
  witness and the recorded drift, so the drift set only shrinks during the advance. The real guarantee, tested
  (`a_sliced_advance_reads_consistently_and_leaves_the_base_clean`): reads return the landed content at every slice, the
  drift set never grows, and the base is clean once the advance is done.
- **Equivalent and durable.** The sliced-vs-one-call oracle holds (62 land tests); the completion's records commit as one
  atom (A-127), the advance being in-memory so a crash before the commit rebuilds the un-advanced overlay and the resume
  re-lands. Server landing suites (29) and vfs (256) green; workspace clippy and `xtask check` clean.
- **Owed (smaller, noted):** `begin`'s `close_dirs` and `end`'s listing invalidation are O(open dirs)/O(dirs), one unit
  each, bounded by the delta's directories as the sweep and sync phases are — not O(entries).
- **Still open from A-132:** a thread kept for the landing's barriers (persistent worker measured-and-rejected
  2026-10-10, spawn 8.7 ms/503 barriers), the directory syncs and media barrier still on the shard, the metadata calls,
  and the base plane's cold reads.

### 2026-10-11: condition 5 re-validated at HEAD; base reads are at the NFS floor, not a shard hold (A-132 read-path owed, answered)

`docs/wip/bench/overlay/overlay_diff.sh /usr/lib 3` on the Linux NFSv4.2 client at `864ec139` (release build, Docker VM,
load 11; tree copied to tmpfs so readers start from RAM):
- **No regression from A-130/132/133.** slates cold read 1.58–1.78 s, warm 621–985 ms for 5,863 files / 540 MB —
  faster than the kernel's own NFS server (cold 1.77–2.03 s, warm 1.20–1.29 s), at the client's floor; the land plan is
  exact (`create=5 delete=3 replace=10`) in 2–3 ms against `diff -rq` 406–461 ms.
- **Adversarial (condition 4/5):** an outsider edit of an untouched base file was seen through the mount in 1 ms and the
  next `slates land` planned it as a `ModifyModify` conflict, never silently merged.
- **Answers A-132's owed "base cold reads on the shard are unmeasured" for the read path.** The cold read is ~270 µs a
  file and is NFS client per-call overhead, not the base `pread`: on fast storage (page cache / tmpfs) the host read is
  sub-µs, so it is not a shard hold. Moving base reads off the shard is therefore **lower value than feared** — it would
  matter only for a slow or contended *base* disk, a narrower case. Deprioritized by measurement before building; revisit
  only with a measured slow-disk signal.

### 2026-11-01: every platform's mount, like for like, quiet and under load (T-4.8, condition 12)

Step 2 of the VFS and DAX plan measured slates' host mount beside each platform's own file system on all five platform
cells (`docs/wip/bench/fsbench/`, `crates/cli/examples/mount_bench.rs`; BENCHMARKS, "Every platform's mount, like for
like"). T-4.8 is recorded on every cell; Windows has no RAM VHD of its own, so its baseline is NTFS on the runner's disk.
The x86_64 overlayfs leg the 2026-10-19 condition-12 entry left owed is done.

Each platform's largest lever, named from its own numbers (BENCHMARKS has the tables):
- **Linux x86_64 and arm64: the daemon's turn on a busy CPU.** With every core loaded, every call the daemon serves
  reaches whole milliseconds at p99 (a create 3.7–6.0 ms on x86_64 and 1.1–5.3 ms on arm64, against overlayfs's
  17–47 µs), in steps of a millisecond, while a read the page cache answers stays at 2.5–3.3 µs. Quiet, the next lever
  is each mutating call's recovery publication before its reply (D-18), about 30 µs above an 11–15 µs round trip.
- **macOS arm64: the calls Apple's NFS client makes for each change.** About 24 NFS calls a file cycle, 13 of them
  LOOKUPs (the daemon's own count), make a create, rename or unlink 8–25× APFS on a RAM disk at the median and 4–9× at
  p99 under load (5.2–6.4 ms for a rename). The 2026-10-06 diagnosis found these calls to be the client's, beyond a v3
  server's reach; the owed transport with caching or delegation the macOS client keeps (2026-10-07) is this lever.
- **Windows x86_64: the daemon's turn on a busy CPU, with a stall near 36 ms.** With every core loaded a create's p99
  is 74–131 ms, against NTFS's 0.36–0.39 ms. Quiet, every run had a stall near 36 ms in a call's path through WinFsp
  to the daemon, while the machine's own wake never took more than 2.3 ms.
- **Windows arm64: a 4–5 ms wait on every open and close of a file the run had written** (an open 3,980–4,188 µs
  against NTFS's 9 µs, in every run; 0.18–0.22 ms on x86_64). Under load those medians reach 4.5–15.8 ms.

Owed from this measurement:
- **The daemon's turn on a busy machine, every platform:** an unprivileged scheduling hint per OS, each verified
  against R10 and then measured under load before any lands. Linux's EEVDF scheduler takes a requested slice through
  `sched_setattr` (docs.kernel.org, "sched-eevdf"); macOS's QoS class was tried on 2026-10-07 and was inconclusive;
  Windows' thread priority within the normal class is untried.
- **Windows x86_64: the stall near 36 ms** in a call's path through WinFsp to the daemon, every quiet run: find it
  with the daemon's own timing before any change.
- **Windows arm64: the 4–5 ms wait on every open and close of a written file**, all three runs, not on x86_64. The
  daemon's status named no WinFsp event, so no purge round ran, and `fsbench`'s open test (files never written) costs
  1.2 ms an open and close there. Not yet explained: find whose wait it is with the daemon's own timing first.
  **Not reproduced 2026-11-20 (w-bugs, goal-83 B5; main 137bf3633, diag-w-bugs-b5-4):** 200 opens and closes of a
  64 KiB file just written, timed in PowerShell on CI's runners, p50 (p90): arm64 slates 229 µs (267), WinFsp's own
  memfs 186 µs (211), NTFS 68 µs (83); x86_64 slates 93 µs (127), memfs 44 µs (50), NTFS 13 µs (16). The 4–5 ms is gone,
  most likely with the receiver's later changes (A-212, A-215, A-560); slates stays within 1.3× of memfs on arm64.
- **macOS: fewer calls per change**, the transport question owed since 2026-10-07.
- **Linux, quiet: the mutating calls' publication** (about 30 µs a call).
- **Bare metal:** every cell here is a CI VM; the bare-metal x86_64 reference stays the 2026-10-19 box run (a FUSE create
  16 µs against overlayfs's 6 µs).

### 2026-10-12: the DAX mapping gate is built in the VFS (§4.6, A-9, AC-4.12)

**Superseded 2026-11-01 (A-195):** the gate is removed with every window over the arena's blocks; both placers map
per-file backings (the 2026-11-01 entry). Kept as the record of what was built and the escapes it closed.

"Mapping isolation, pinning and teardown" — the invariants §4.6 requires before a VMM's DAX capability may be
advertised — are **built and proven by use**. An earlier experiment on this branch (`writable-dax`) demonstrated, with
eight red tests, that *no daemon-side check can make writable DAX safe* (a hardware DAX guest accesses the page through
its own page table and never calls the daemon), so the defense had to be at the memory level. It now is:

- **Pinning** (`crates/mem/src/arena.rs`): `ChunkArena::pin`/`unpin`/`is_pinned`, layered above the buddy (untouched).
  A `free` of a pinned block is deferred (bytes kept, unscrubbed) and the block is never handed to another allocation
  or trimmed, until the last unpin releases and scrubs it (A-99). 6 by-use tests, Miri-clean.
- **Registry + teardown** (`crates/vfs/src/dax.rs`, a `DaxRegistry` in `Store`): `dax_map_read`/`dax_map_write` pin and
  register a mapping; `dax_revoke`/`dax_revoke_inode`/`dax_revoke_writable_of_prefix`/`dax_revoke_volume`
  tear down (`dax_revoke_block` was here too and was **removed 2026-10-18** — see that day's entry). `write`/`truncate` revoke the inode's mappings (one write boundary); `snapshot` revokes
  writable mappings before sharing (read-only survive — the allowed immutable-shared case); `destroy` revokes the whole
  volume's. The hardware path (`dax_read_raw`/`dax_write_raw`) models the MMU — inert for a revoked mapping.
- **Evidence:** `crates/vfs/tests/dax.rs` 42/0 (every former escape now closed: exfiltration, cross-file and
  cross-volume injection, the concurrent pile, TOCTOU, block-move lost update, snapshot-share corruption,
  revoke-then-reuse, past-length tail scrub, reclamation; plus the multi-tenancy layers below); vfs + mem suites
  green; clippy `--all-targets -D warnings` clean.

- **Multi-tenancy (the §4.6 Rowhammer threat model, 2026-10-13).** The async-revocation/TLB race is closed by the
  two-phase revoke (`dax_revoke_pending` keeps the block pinned; `dax_release_after_unmap` unpins only after the VMM
  confirms the unmap + cross-core TLB flush); the map-storm/fault DoS is bounded three ways (registry cap, §4.9 credit
  window, cooperative serve loop). The Rowhammer layered defence is built in the VFS: **L0** writable DAX is a
  per-volume opt-in (`Volume::enable_writable_dax`; read-only default, 4b411da9; **its premise corrected 2026-10-31,
  A-193:** reading alone hammers, so the read-only default bounds a guest's stores into the arena, not hammering; see
  the 2026-10-31 entry below); **L2** the moving target
  (`Volume::dax_migrate` + `stripe_target`, bounded no-quarantine placement, measured 242 ns/migration, 68b4a9c5);
  **B2** the self-healing net for read-only content (`Store::dax_guard`/`dax_scrub`, BLAKE3 checksum + heal, 6922fcf2).
  **Owed:** **L1** physically-contiguous hugetlb zones + guard rows (the deployment layer that makes L2's shift move
  real physical rows) and the adaptive migration trigger from a privileged PEBS/IBS broker — both wired into the
  device loop with L0/L2/B2.

- **The daemon→device revoke channel, built end to end (2026-10-14).** The two-phase revoke's device half now rides
  the production serve loop. A VFS mutation of a mapped inode (`write`/`truncate` → `Store::dax_revoke_inode`) revokes
  phase-one (registry entry gone, block kept **pinned**) and **enqueues the inode** on the shard's `DaxRegistry`
  (`pending_revokes`); the device drains that queue every service pass (`AdmittedDevice::service` →
  `Bridge::take_pending_dax_revokes` → `Device::request_revoke_inode`), munmapping the guest's window and only then
  unpinning (`dax_release_after_unmap`) — so a reused block is never reachable through a stale TLB. It rides the real
  loop for free (`serve_loop` → `one_pass` → `service`; `crates/server/src/virtiofs.rs` serves through it unchanged),
  and the in-process seam the loop drives itself needs no separate wake. Non-vacuity counter
  `AdmissionCounters::dax_window_revokes`. Proven by use: `crates/vfs/tests/dax.rs` (enqueue on the mutation; the guard
  freed at phase one), `crates/bridge-virtiofs/tests/device.rs` (a write of a mapped file drained with a **real**
  window, the transient per-pass bridge modelling the shard), and `tests/admission.rs`
  (`a_service_pass_drains_a_pending_dax_revoke_and_tears_the_window_down`: the same through `service` over a real
  SETUPMAPPING cache window, the counter moving 0→1). A **correctness pass fixed a latent leak**: phase-one revoke
  (`dax_revoke_pending`) now drops a read-only mapping's integrity guard (B2) and frees its clean copy — it only
  unregistered before, so a guarded read-only mapping revoked two-phase (a `write`/`truncate` of a guarded inode, a
  device window teardown) leaked the guard's pinned clean copy until the volume dropped. The queue is bounded +
  deduped + non-vacuous by test (`the_pending_revoke_queue_is_bounded_and_deduped`, `pending_len`): a write storm on
  one mapped inode enqueues it once, distinct inodes once each, never past the registry cap (CLAUDE.md #8).
- **Profiling pass (M5 Max, release, `t_dax_device_map_path_latency_profile`, n=300):** the SETUPMAPPING map path is
  ~4.5 µs/map, first/last 0.94 — **flat, syscall-bound**: the O(live) overlap scan is negligible against the
  `MAP_FIXED` cost, so no map-side index is warranted. The teardown (`request_revoke_inode`) is ~477 ns base
  (munmap + unpin) with the O(live) window scan **visible** at ~1.8 ns/window (first/last 1.64 at n=300), so a *bulk*
  drain of P pending inodes is O(P × live) — fine at these sizes, dominant only at a large registry cap. An
  inode→window index (revoke → O(windows-of-inode)) is **deferred, not premature-built**: the path is empty in
  production until DAX is advertised, and a positional index through `swap_remove` is error-prone; the optimization
  hierarchy says measure a real advertised guest's drain pattern first.
- **Window authorized-bound hardening (2026-10-15, adversarial escape pass).** `serve_dax` bounded a SETUPMAPPING to
  the arena block's power-of-two length, not the file's pages, so a guest could map a whole page of buddy padding past
  its own file (a four-page block behind a two-page-plus-one file). No cross-tenant leak — the block is the guest's
  own and all three map paths zero the tail `[file_len, block_end)` at map time — but the shared surface was larger
  than the file warranted and rested on the scrub never regressing. Now the window is bounded to `file_len` rounded up
  to the window's own granule (`DaxCacheRegion::page` — the host page, or a VMM's negotiated FUSE_MAP_ALIGNMENT),
  capped at the block, so a page lying entirely past the file is refused EINVAL by bound, not only by the scrub. The
  bound is granule-aware: a naive `page_span` (DAX_PAGE = 4 KiB) bound would wrongly reject a legitimate host-page-
  aligned map where the host page (16 KiB here) exceeds DAX_PAGE. Proven red-first by
  `a_setupmapping_of_the_block_padding_past_the_file_is_refused` (`crates/bridge-virtiofs/tests/device.rs`); device 28
  / vfs dax 43 / admission 11 / serve 5 green, clippy `-D warnings` + `cargo xtask check` clean.
- **Local zero-copy read (A-135) — BUILT + proven end to end on x86_64 Linux (2026-10-15).** A same-kernel, same-uid
  (`SO_PEERCRED`) client reads a file with no copy: `MapRead` over the ring → the daemon mints a read mapping and
  sends the arena block's descriptor over the retained control socket by `SCM_RIGHTS` → the client `mmap`s it
  (`crates/ipc` `Control::send_mapping`/`Liveness::recv_mapping`; `crates/server/src/merge_service.rs`
  `map_read`/`try_local_map`; `crates/client/src/client.rs` `map_read`/`MappedRead`). A non-same-uid peer, a
  non-plain/non-head view, a path with no shared-object backing, or a volume whose owner shard is not the client's
  home shard falls back to the copy path (`read`), so the client always gets its bytes; the zero-copy upgrade is a
  non-vacuity counter (`dax.local_map`). Proven by use: `crates/client/tests/client.rs`
  `a_same_kernel_client_maps_a_file_with_no_copy` (one-shard daemon, 20 KiB arena-backed file, mapped zero-copy,
  bytes equal). `cfg(unix)`; a non-Unix `MapRead` reads by copy. The first real descriptor map surfaced and fixed a
  latent arena bug — `block_backing` returned a region-relative offset against the whole-object descriptor, which
  would have mis-mapped the guest DAX window too (`docs/bugs/2026-10-15-block-backing-returned-a-region-relative-offset.md`).
  **Owed:** the cross-shard owner→home descriptor hand-off (a cross-shard `MapRead` copies, not maps, for now); a
  prompt per-drop release (3b built the reap revoke — `crate::reap` revokes a client's maps when it is reaped, over a
  `ClientSlot::dax_maps` list, so a dropped/dead client's read maps no longer pin versions toward the registry cap; a
  release on the `MappedRead` drop would be prompter, and no dax-map count observable exists yet for a reap
  count-assertion test — both owed); the macOS control socket (refusing stubs, so it reads by copy).
- **Directory-window coherence — decided point-in-time (not an open design call).** A directory DAX window
  (`dax_map_dir`, the READDIR/READDIRPLUS snapshot) is a point-in-time view the guest re-maps to refresh, and that
  is correct, not an owed revoke: POSIX/NFS `readdir` guarantees no consistent snapshot across concurrent mutations
  (a listing is inherently racy — the same NFS readdir-cookie semantics slates already serves), and revoke-on-every-
  dir-mutation would be pathological in the create-storm (every CREATE would tear the parent's window). It does not
  leak (a re-map at the same slot frees the old throwaway block; a held stale window pins one cap-bounded block). So
  unlike a file *content* window — where a stale read after a write must re-fault, hence `dax_revoke_inode` on
  write/truncate — a directory window needs **no** coherence wiring. File bytes may not be stale; a dir listing may.
- **ADVERTISEMENT-GATING, found by measurement 2026-10-18: the message-based map hands the frontend a descriptor
  for the WHOLE arena object, not the authorized block.** `Store::dax_backing` → `ChunkArena::block_backing` returns
  `(region.backing_fd(), base + offset, len)` and its own comment says "`backing_fd` is the whole object";
  `BackendReqChannel::send_map` passes that fd over `SCM_RIGHTS`. `fd_offset`/`len` scope the *request*, never the
  *descriptor*. Measured on a two-tenant store: `object_size=1048576`, `authorized_len=16384` — the frontend is
  handed **64×** what it may map, with the other tenant's blocks inside it, and a real shard's arena is far larger.
  Unreachable today (`admission::unsupported` refuses `dax` unconditionally; the message form is reached only by the
  harness-only `attach_vhost_user_device_dax`), and the fd-sharing form does NOT have this property — there the
  backend maps and the VMM never gets a descriptor. But if advertised, tenant isolation across VMM processes would
  rest on each frontend honouring `fd_offset`/`len` rather than on what slates handed it, which is the wrong side
  of the trust boundary for a gate that exists because the guest is untrusted. **Ada's call between three options,
  before the gate flips:** a backing object per tenant (keeps zero-copy and confines by construction, but cuts
  against A-64's one-image layout), a per-mapping `memfd` copy (confined but it is the "view" arm already
  measured-and-rejected, and loses writable zero-copy), or advertising DAX over fd-sharing only (no code change,
  but it drops the crosvm/QEMU route chosen 2026-10-16 for multi-tenant hosts). No test pins the current
  behaviour — a test that enshrines a weakness is worse than the record of it; when the option is chosen the test
  to write asserts the descriptor's extent EQUALS the authorized window's. Record:
  `docs/bugs/2026-10-18-the-message-based-dax-map-hands-the-vmm-the-whole-arena.md`.
- **Cross-tenant isolation at the DEVICE seam is now proven (2026-10-18)**, where before only the VFS half was: two
  tenants in one store, each with its own device, cache region and context, both windows live at once showing only
  their own bytes; a context binding another tenant's volume is refused (`authorize_write`'s volume check — red-
  checked: disabling `authorize_read`'s alone does not turn it red, since a writable SETUPMAPPING authorizes as a
  write); a foreign inode number never yields the other tenant's bytes, scanned over the whole cache region. Also
  proven at the device seam: a truncate's leftover bytes are not reachable through the window a device grants,
  which is wider than the mediated path's `page_span` wherever the host page exceeds `DAX_PAGE` (16 KiB against
  4 KiB on Apple Silicon) — `page_span`'s doc claimed otherwise and is corrected.
- **The sibling teardown paths — investigated, each is a *different* case (an earlier note wrongly said all three
  should route through the pending-enqueue; that would break destroy). All are safe today — DAX is unadvertised, so
  no live window exists — and each is gated on the advertisement decision:**
  - **destroy** (`dax_revoke_volume`) **stays synchronous by design**: its own comment says it unpins so the volume's
    blocks are reclaimed; two-phase would keep them pinned (deferred frees outliving the volume), the opposite of
    what it must do. Its correctness rests on a *server-ordering invariant* — the device attachment is torn down
    first (`release_dax` munmaps every window), so by the time `dax_revoke_volume` runs there is no live window to
    munmap. Owed: assert that ordering at the server once DAX is advertised. Not a VFS change.
  - **snapshot/clone** (`dax_revoke_writable_of_prefix`) — the **writable-only recall mechanism is now BUILT and
    tested, end to end through the step-5 channel** (2026-10-14): `dax_revoke_writable_of_prefix` is two-phase
    (enqueues `writable_only=true`, block kept pinned); the bridge carries `(inode, writable_only)`; the device
    serve-loop drain dispatches `Device::request_revoke_writable_inode` (tears writable windows, keeps read-only) vs
    `request_revoke_inode` (all); and `DaxRegistry::has_writable_of_prefix` / `has_pending_of_prefix` let a caller see
    when the device has drained. Proven: `a_snapshot_revokes_the_volumes_writable_windows_two_phase_and_keeps_read_only`
    (vfs), `request_revoke_writable_inode_keeps_the_read_only_window` (device). **The verb TRIGGER is now BUILT**
    (`server(dax)`, 2026-10-14): `snapshot` (`crates/server/src/verbs.rs`), before it freezes, checks
    `has_writable_of_prefix`; if a writable window is live it hands it to the device (`dax_revoke_writable_of_prefix`)
    and refuses **retryable** (`Overloaded`, the shape `await_deferred_completion` uses) while `has_pending_of_prefix`
    holds, so it freezes only once the device has drained the recall — no live writable window can reach a shared
    block. A sync verb cannot block, so this refuse-retry (the write-delegation shape) is the correctness gate; it is
    a **no-op in production** (DAX unadvertised, `virtiofs.rs:233` asserts the device does not advertise it), so
    `snapshot` proceeds unchanged — recovery arbiter 39/0, server lib clippy clean, the check's components tested in
    `vfs/tests/dax.rs`. **The liveness kick is also built** (`serve::kick` + `serve_round`'s additive drain-on-kick
    branch + `virtiofs::kick_volume_devices`; the snapshot verb kicks the volume's device loops so an idle-guest
    device munmaps on the recall, not on its next doorbell kick; unit-tested, recovery 39/0). **(a) the re-arm livelock is CLOSED
    (2026-10-18).** A guest could re-map a writable window between the snapshot's retries, putting the snapshot back
    where it started, and a guest doing it deliberately could hold the snapshot off forever. The registry now
    carries a per-volume `recalling` set (`DaxRegistry::begin_recall`/`recalling`/`end_recall`), and
    `Volume::dax_map_write` refuses a volume in it `VfsError::RecallInFlight` (EBUSY) before any effect, so the
    retry converges. Read-only DAX is unaffected — the exclusion is of writable windows only.
    **Whoever retries owns the recall:** it is begun by the `snapshot` *verb*, not by
    `dax_revoke_writable_of_prefix`, and ended in one place by a wrapper around the verb on every answer but the
    retryable `Overloaded` — so a client that simply stops retrying cannot leave a volume unable to take a writable
    window. That ownership was not the first design: beginning it inside the revoke also caught `Volume::snapshot`,
    which has no "the snapshot is over" moment, and two existing tests
    (`a_writable_map_after_a_snapshot_copies_up_and_spares_the_snapshot`, the clone sibling) went red for exactly
    that reason — the tests found it, not review. A `destroy` ends the recall too, so a prefix's next holder
    inherits no ghost. Bounded and deduped by `cap` like every other structure here. Proven by use:
    `a_guest_cannot_re_arm_a_writable_window_while_the_snapshot_is_recalling_it` (both the recalled file and a
    neighbour of the same volume are refused; the same map succeeds before the recall and after it ends, and a read
    map is admitted throughout, so the refusal is the recall's) and
    `recalls_are_deduped_bounded_and_released_by_destroy`. vfs dax 51/51, virtiofs suites green, recovery oracle
    39/39, clippy `-D warnings` and `xtask check` clean. **(b) is now DECIDED, not owed — waiting is
    correct.** The companion hardening was written down as "a bounded recall: revoke the window if the device does
    not drain within a lease, as a delegation is revoked on lapse". Checked against what the two-phase revoke is
    for, that analogy does not hold and the hardening would be a bug. A lease on a *delegation* can be taken back
    because the holder is a cooperating client slates can refuse; a DAX window is a **page table entry in an
    unmodified guest kernel**, and only the VMM's `munmap` removes it. Phase one has already unregistered the
    mapping and kept the block pinned exactly so that "a block the daemon is about to move/reuse is never reachable
    through a stale TLB" (§4.6 step 5). Unpinning on a lapse would hand that block to another allocation while the
    guest's page table still points at it — the escape the two phases exist to prevent. And tearing the attachment
    down does not help either: closing the backend connection does not unmap the guest's window, so a hung VMM
    simply cannot be made to let go. **So the snapshot must wait, and refusing until it can freeze safely is the
    right terminal state, not a missing bound.** It is already bounded in practice by the client's own reply
    deadline, and since 2026-10-18 the recall is ended on that path by the verb's wrapper, so nothing leaks when a
    client gives up. What remains is a *diagnostic* nicety and is recorded as such: after a budget the refusal
    could become non-retryable and typed ("the device has not released its window") so a client learns the
    snapshot will not succeed instead of retrying blindly. That needs the clock plus per-volume recall-start state
    and buys no safety, so it is not built. A through-the-client e2e needs a live writable
    window, advertisement-gated like all DAX e2e.
  - **advance — revoke on the moving reader is BUILT (2026-10-15, a7f317af); takeover/landing need no revoke.** An
    earlier note here called advance-revoke "unneeded," reasoning that a read mapping pins its version so the guest
    "reads it validly and re-maps." **That reasoning was wrong and is corrected.** The DAX client is an unmodified
    guest kernel that speaks only FUSE and never sees slates' control-plane `advance`, so it would keep its old
    page-table windows and read the *old* snapshot's bytes for the changed files with no signal to re-map — exactly
    the "old names with new bytes" the body forbids (SLATES_DESIGN.md:1534) and the revoke the body requires "before …
    `advance` completes" (SLATES_DESIGN.md:2650). Lazy is not a cheaper equivalent; it is a stale-read bug for the only
    client DAX has. So `advance` now kicks the advancing attachment's own device (`virtiofs::kick_volume_devices` from
    `snapshot_view::advanced`), which re-validates its windows against the new view (`Device::revalidate_windows` →
    `Bridge::dax_window_current` → `Volume::dax_still_current`) and tears only the windows whose content block the new
    view no longer holds — the changed inodes — keeping every window onto unchanged, block-shared content; a device
    whose view did not move tears nothing (the volume-wide kick is self-scoping), and the cost is proportional to the
    real delta (`paths_changed_between`), on a rare control-plane re-pin, never a per-op path. Proven:
    `an_advance_revalidate_tears_the_stale_window_and_keeps_the_current_one` (`bridge-virtiofs/tests/device.rs`). The
    **sibling** paths genuinely need no revoke, and that part of the earlier analysis stands: a **write**-advance
    changes content through the write path, which already revokes (`dax_revoke_inode`, step-5); **migration** (L2
    `dax_migrate`) does its own two-phase revoke+remap; **takeover** starts the successor with **no** mappings (the
    dead owner's guests die with it — host-local registry); and **landing** reads content out to disk without moving
    the arena block. `dax_revoke_block` remains the defensive primitive for a block genuinely *moved/reclaimed* under a
    live window; a future path that moves a mapped block uses the writable recall pattern (enqueue +
    `request_revoke_writable_inode`/`request_revoke_inode` + kick). **Amended 2026-10-18: it was removed.** This
    entry's analysis of landing and takeover stands and was re-derived independently that day; what changed is
    the keep decision. A defensive primitive with no caller anywhere — not even a test — is the "just in case"
    second path CLAUDE.md #7 forbids, and the reclaim case it defended is already held by the pin (the arena
    defers a `free` of a pinned block and declines a `trim` of one). The recall pattern named here is still the
    right shape for a future mover, and it is fifteen lines when one exists.

**Owed before DAX is advertised (the next steps):**

1. **Wire the gate to the virtio-fs device seam** (`crates/server/src/virtiofs.rs`). **The teardown half is built
   (2026-10-14/15):** the device serves SETUPMAPPING/REMOVEMAPPING over a real cache window and revokes through
   `dax_revoke_*` on write/truncate (step-5), on `snapshot`/clone (the writable recall), on detach
   (`Device::release_dax`) and on `advance` (`Device::revalidate_windows`, a7f317af — see the advance bullet above).
   **The map half is now built and proven live (2026-10-16):** DAX admission (FUSE_INIT `FUSE_CAP_DAX`), `dax_map_*`
   through the device, and the message-based `VHOST_USER_BACKEND_SHMEM_MAP` binding run end to end — a real crosvm
   guest reads a file through the DAX window (`crates/client/examples/crosvm_dax_ab`, the recorded A/B), with an
   in-tree hermetic proof of the map-ack park (`a_message_based_setupmapping_parks_until_the_front_end_acks_then_answers_the_guest`).
   It stays **withheld in production** with step 4 (advertise) until step 2 (the tamper-proof/fleet registry) lands:
   the `FUSE_CAP_DAX` advertise is flipped only by the A/B harness, and a production DAX request is refused
   `AttachmentUnsupported`.

2. **Make the registry un-fabricable and tamper-proof, including across the fleet.** No agent may interfere with,
   fabricate or tamper with the registry. The design, given slates' distributed nature:
   - *Agent isolation (already holds).* The registry is daemon-local RAM. Agents reach the daemon only over the ring/
     wire (command verbs) or the guest virtqueue — never its address space (R1, R10). No verb supplies a `Mapping`;
     `dax_map_*` **mint** it, and only after device admission authenticates the consumer and reads its rights from the
     volume's access list (§4.6). An agent can request a map, never forge or edit an entry.
   - *Unforgeable handle.* A guest must reference a mapping by a daemon-minted opaque capability (a generational id),
     not a raw `Mapping`, so it can neither name a mapping it was not granted nor forge the block/length fields.
     **Satisfied, by a different mechanism than this line prescribes — checked against the code and its tests
     2026-10-20, and no longer a blocker.** The property has two halves and both hold.

     *A guest cannot name a mapping it was not granted.* `crates/bridge-virtiofs` contains no reference to
     `MappingId` at all; the device keys a window by `moffset`, the guest's own offset into the DAX cache region
     the device gave it. `DaxCacheRegion::fixed_addr` refuses anything else: a `moffset` or `len` that does not
     fit `usize`, a zero or non-page-aligned length, a `moffset + len` that overflows, and any `end` past
     `window.len()`. The window is per-device, so the furthest a guest can reach is its own region. Proven by
     `a_setupmapping_past_the_window_is_refused` and `two_tenants_dax_windows_each_show_only_their_own_bytes`.

     *A guest cannot forge the block or length.* `SetupMappingIn` has five fields — `fh`, `foffset`, `len`,
     `flags`, `moffset` — and **none of them is a block.** The guest names a file handle and an offset in the
     file; the daemon resolves that to a block through the bridge. The length is capped to the file's authorized
     pages rather than honoured
     (`a_setupmapping_reaching_past_the_file_is_capped_to_its_authorized_pages`), and
     `a_device_window_past_the_files_length_shows_zeroes_not_the_truncated_secret` holds the tail.

     *Adversarially.* `hostile_dax_requests_are_refused_and_establish_no_window` drives a truncated SETUPMAPPING
     body, `len = u64::MAX`, an unaligned window offset, a SETUPMAPPING of an inline (non-mappable) file, a
     truncated REMOVEMAPPING and a REMOVEMAPPING claiming `u32::MAX` entries — each a typed refusal or a no-op,
     no window established, the block a refused map briefly pinned released, no panic, and a valid map still
     works after. `device_chaos_step` puts the same seam under the random schedule.

     So the id never needed to cross to the guest for this property to hold, and the parenthetical that said
     "the device wiring adds the id" described a plan rather than the design that was built. The minted id is
     still real and still load-bearing *daemon-side*: `MappingId`'s inner is module-private so a `Mapping` can
     only come from the mint paths, every one carries an id (five `mint_id` call sites), and `is_live` is
     consulted on the production paths (`dax.rs:1086`, `:1282`, `:1329`).

     **What is left is a separate, non-blocking item:** `MappingId::as_u64` exists for a release-by-id path that
     does not exist — no `DaxRelease`/`MapRelease`/`dax_release` anywhere in `wire`, `server/verbs.rs` or
     `client`, and `dax_release_after_unmap` takes a daemon-held `&Mapping`. Whether a same-host client should be
     able to name a mapping and release it is a question about the guest interface, not about confinement, and it
     does not gate advertising. The accessor is kept with its doc corrected to say nothing calls it; it is unwired
     planned work, not the superseded code `dax_revoke_block` was when it was deleted (e74daf77).
   - *Integrity at pin.* `ChunkArena::pin` already refuses an extent that is not a live allocation (`ForeignExtent`),
     so even a daemon-internal slip cannot pin a forged or stale block.
   - *VMM-enforced teardown.* Revocation is not "ask the guest": the daemon tells the VMM/hypervisor to remove the DAX
     window from the guest's address space (the MMU then faults the guest). The VMM is the OS-shipped trusted broker
     (R10); the guest cannot refuse. The in-process and inherited-fd forms are mmaps the daemon owns outright.
   - *Fleet.* A DAX mapping is **host-local** — the guest is co-located with the owner shard that serves its content —
     so the registry is per-owner and never replicated; a mapping cannot exist on a node that does not serve the
     content, and there is no distributed registry to tamper with. Cross-host safety is a *version-lifetime*
     obligation: a mapping pins a version, and that pin must ride the existing fenced retention protocol (D-26,
     "Destroy/revoke releases credits only after … mappings"), so no other node's merge/`advance`/landing reclaims a
     version a remote mapping pins. On takeover the dead owner's guests die with it, so the successor starts with no
     mappings — nothing to inherit or forge.

     **Audited 2026-10-20; this is the one sub-item still open, and narrower than it reads.** What was checked:
     a `Mapping` carries `id`, `inode`, `block_file_start`, `block`, `file_len` and **no version** — it pins a
     *block* through `ChunkArena::pin`, not a version, so "a mapping pins a version" is not literally what the
     type does. `crates/server/src/content_retention.rs` contains no mention of DAX or of a mapping, so the
     retention path does not consult the registry. What does protect the guest is the revoke-on-`advance` path,
     and that **is** wired in production: `serve.rs:385` calls `revalidate_windows` on the drain kick, tearing
     any window the device no longer backs (its discarded result is deliberate and the comment above it says
     why — the lapse is folded into the pass below, not lost).

     So the question is one of *ordering*: whether the block can be reclaimed before the revoke completes.

     **Closed 2026-10-21, and it was not a coverage gap — it was two defects.** Following
     `revalidate_windows` down to the teardown it shares with every other revoke (`teardown_dax_window`)
     found the ordering broken in both of its arms:

     - *Local placer.* `let _ = cache.unmap(..)` followed by an unconditional
       `dax_release_after_unmap`. A refused unmap leaves the window mapped and the block went back to the
       arena anyway. `mmap(MAP_FIXED)` over a sub-range splits a VMA, so the unmap can fail with `ENOMEM`
       at `vm.max_map_count` — which a device with many live windows walks toward by doing exactly this.
       Fixed in `45937ac8`; red-checked (restoring the old code fails the test with `0 pinned`).
     - *Message placer (the out-of-process VMM, so crosvm and QEMU).* It unpinned on **any**
       `begin_unmap` refusal, under a comment saying a failure means the channel is gone. Only
       `Channel(..)` means that. `TooManyOutstanding` means the ring is at its bound with the channel
       alive and the front end still holding the window; `BadRange` means the unmap was never attempted.
       **An advance is how this is reached without a hostile guest** — `revalidate_windows` tears every
       stale window in one pass and each `begin_unmap` takes an outstanding slot, so a volume whose stale
       windows outnumber the bound overflows it partway through, and every window past that point was
       unpinned while still mapped. Fixed in `c4343670`.

     **Verified on every architecture slates ships**, 2026-10-21 — not inferred from one:

     | host | how | result |
     |---|---|---|
     | macOS arm64 | native | 73 passed (whole crate) |
     | Linux arm64 | `rust:1.98` container, native on Apple Silicon | 41 passed, 0 failed |
     | Linux x86_64 | same image, `--platform linux/amd64` | 41 passed, 0 failed |
     | Windows | n/a — virtio-fs and the DAX path are Unix; the lane is green on CI | — |

     **On chaos.** The teardown path is already under the random schedule: `device_chaos_step` has five
     operations and four of them (unmap, write, truncate, sweep) produce a teardown, with the pin ledger
     balanced across the run. The two *refusal* arms this change added are not reached by it, and
     deliberately are not chased there: each is a single branch inside one call (`if unmap.is_ok()`,
     `if matches!(refusal, Channel(_))`) with no interleaving component for a schedule to find, and each is
     held by a targeted test that was red-checked by restoring the old code. Chaos earns its cost on orderings;
     these are decisions.

     Five tests hold the property, all run on both Linux architectures:
     `a_revoke_whose_unmap_is_refused_keeps_the_block_pinned`,
     `a_message_based_teardown_holds_the_block_until_the_front_end_acks_the_unmap`,
     `a_teardown_refused_short_of_a_dead_channel_keeps_the_block_pinned`,
     `an_advance_that_tears_a_window_balances_its_pin` and
     `an_advance_revalidate_tears_the_stale_window_and_keeps_the_current_one`.

     **On the origin of the advance**, which this entry previously treated as the open part: it does not
     reach the teardown. `revalidate_windows` is handed the device's current view and compares its windows
     against it; nothing in that path knows or can know whether the advance it is reacting to began with a
     local write or a remote merge. That is R8's one code path, and it is why a fleet-originated test would
     exercise the same function a third time rather than a different one. Recorded as a deliberate
     non-test, not an omission.

3. **File-shape scope and the open-frontier rule (2026-10-16).** DAX maps a chunk only in its **open (plaintext)**
   representation; a **sealed** chunk (AES-GCM at-rest, A-92/A-99) reads over **FUSE_READ** — a guest's MMU would read
   ciphertext. **Built:** single-block *unsealed* files map their block directly, and **inline** files are
   materialized into a throwaway page block the mapping owns (`Volume::dax_map_read`,
   `an_inline_file_is_mapped_read_only_through_a_materialized_block`; the snapshot `dax_still_current` fix rides it).
   A multi-block file reads correctly over FUSE_READ; its open tail is not yet mapped.

   **Audited 2026-10-21: most of what the paragraph below calls owed is built and tested.** Taken in turn:

   - *The open-frontier gate* — built, and proven by
     `the_open_tail_maps_directly_and_the_sealed_head_is_reopened_in_place` (passes). The device backs each
     chunk rather than one span (`device.rs:1757`), the open tail zero-copy and a sealed chunk per its arm.
   - *pin-defers-seal* — built, and the code names the rule in those words at `volume.rs` in `reseal_inode`:
     "A mapped chunk is not cold at all: the window still reads it, and sealing under a live window would hand
     the guest ciphertext (the pin-defers-seal rule)", guarded by
     `store.content.arena().is_pinned(c.block)`. Proven by
     `the_idle_sweep_defers_sealing_a_mapped_block_until_it_is_unmapped` and
     `a_reopened_dax_chunk_is_resealed_once_its_window_is_revoked` (both pass).
   - *The device's sealed-refuse* — **there is no sealed-refuse, because the design does not refuse a sealed
     chunk; it reopens it.** `Volume::dax_map_read_at`'s sealed arm calls `Content::reopen_in_place`, with the
     reason in the code: "a guest MMU would read ciphertext, and a refused SETUPMAPPING SIGBUSes a
     `dax=always` mmap. Reopen it in place." So what this line asked for would be the wrong behaviour.
     **Which means "Gated follow-on (b)" below — `reopen`-on-map, recorded as "built only if a
     read-only-large-file zero-copy workload asks for it" — is already built**, and
     `the_open_tail_maps_directly_and_the_sealed_head_is_reopened_in_place` proves it (passes).

     That matters beyond bookkeeping: **a DAX read of a sealed chunk changes data at rest.** The chunk is
     decrypted into its own canonical block — it allocates, can fail `NoSpace`, dirties the recovery image and
     adds re-seal churn — and `pin-defers-seal` is the only thing keeping the sweep from encrypting it back
     under the live window. `dax_map_read_at`'s own doc claimed the opposite ("a sealed chunk … is refused"),
     so a reader reasoning about A-92 from that doc would have concluded a DAX read can never turn ciphertext
     into plaintext on the host. Corrected at the function in the same change.
   - *force-seal-revoke-on-growth* — **no separate mechanism exists and none is needed**, which is why
     searching for one finds nothing. A file grows by a write, and `Volume::write_with` revokes the inode's
     DAX mappings *before* the write (`volume.rs:2479`, "a second write boundary onto content a guest holds
     mapped: revoke its mappings first so the one boundary stays single"), as `truncate_with` does
     (`volume.rs:2709`). So a live window cannot be present when the single open slot changes hands; the
     blanket rule subsumes the named one. Recorded rather than built.

   This is the third ledger entry today found describing as owed something the code already does — after the
   2026-10-18 caller table and `dax_migrate`'s own doc. The pattern is worth naming: an entry written when a
   piece was planned, never revisited when it landed.

   **The paragraph as it was written (kept for the rejected alternatives it records):** the gate that maps the open chunk at a
   `SETUPMAPPING`'s offset and refuses a sealed one (the open tail of a growing/edited file is then zero-copy, the
   sealed body FUSE_READ); **pin-defers-seal** (the DAX pin extends to block the *encrypt* of a mapped chunk, not just
   its free/reuse, so a seal never swaps plaintext→ciphertext under a live window) and **force-seal-revoke-on-growth**
   (a mapped chunk yields the file's single open slot to a new tail through the two-phase revoke) — both in the
   seal/open paths, with the recovery oracle (`cargo test -p slates-server --test recovery`) the arbiter; and the
   device's sealed-refuse. Because a file has exactly one open chunk, the device needs **no** N-`SHMEM_MAP`-per-request
   and no N-ack park. **Rejected:** a decrypted-chunk cache (a divergent second copy owing coherence against every
   mutation — the staleness/timing/correctness slates avoids) and a volume-wide plaintext-at-rest opt-out (surrenders
   A-92/condition-9 for the whole volume); the open-frontier rule keeps one representation and leans entirely on the
   existing pin/revoke/single-writer. **Gated follow-on (b):** `reopen`-on-map flips a *cold* sealed chunk sealed→open
   on a read map (same pin/revoke, still one representation, no cache), giving a never-edited large file zero-copy too,
   at the cost of a read/map triggering a canonical state change (it allocates, decrypts, can fail `NoSpace`, dirties
   the recovery image, adds re-seal churn) — built only if a read-only-large-file zero-copy workload asks for it.

### 2026-10-13: write delegations were offered unilaterally, costing ~26% of the create-storm's RPCs (A-80 amended)

Profiling a 96k-file Linux-kernel clone on a slates NFSv4.2 mount (the Linux kernel client, in Docker;
`/proc/self/mountstats` per-op counters) found the create-storm issues ~708k RPCs (~7.4 per file), with the ops
near 1-per-file each: GETATTR 15%, OPEN 14%, WRITE 14%, LOOKUP 14%, SETATTR 13.5%, CLOSE 13.5%, **DELEGRETURN 13%**.
The DELEGRETURN ≈ one-per-file was the tell: `delegations_allowed` (compound.rs) offered a **write** delegation on
essentially every owned-file open with a live back channel *even when the client set no delegation-want bit* (the
Linux client sends `wishes=0x2`/`0x3`, want-mask 0 — confirmed by logging), and the write-once-close clone returned
each one unused. This is the same write delegation that conflicts with writable DAX (§4.6).

Fix (A-80 amended, measured): offer a **read** delegation by default and a **write** one only on an explicit
`OPEN4_SHARE_ACCESS_WANT_WRITE_DELEG`. A/B on the same binary (daemon toggle): keeping read-but-not-write delegations
cut the clone's RPCs ~26% (695,978 → 512,538; DELEGRETURN 91,034 → 4; GETATTR 101,368 → 5,424 — the kept read
delegation also spares the post-return attribute revalidation) and its wall-clock (9–25% across two single runs under
shared load — a controlled best-of-N is owed for a precise figure). It also removes the write-delegation ↔
writable-DAX conflict for every client that does not ask; the mechanism is unchanged for one that does
(`a_plain_open_is_not_pushed_a_write_delegation` + the four write-delegation tests, which now set the want). Native
tests green (v4 suites 63/0, nfs_mount delegation subset 10/0); clippy `--all-targets -D warnings` clean.

**Owed:** the next metadata levers toward 2×-vs-tmpfs — GETATTR (still ~1/file in the baseline op mix) and SETATTR
(~1/file, git's per-file mode/mtime) — profiled but not yet addressed; and the controlled best-of-N wall-clock for
the delegation change.

**Two routes to SETATTR closed by reading, 2026-10-21, before anyone spends a clone run on them:**

1. *"slates ignores the mode the client set at create, so the client must SETATTR after."* **False.** The v4
   `OPEN` decodes `createhow4`'s attributes (`open_createhow` → `decode_fattr_set`) and carries them through
   `create_or_open` into `create_new`, so an `UNCHECKED`/`GUARDED` create applies them. The per-file SETATTR is
   git setting mode and mtime *after* writing, which is the client's choice and not something the server
   forces.
2. *"Offer a write delegation again so the client can cache the attribute set."* It would work — RFC 8881
   §10.4 lets a write delegation cache attribute changes and flush at `DELEGRETURN` — **and it is the trade
   this section already measured and lost.** A write delegation saves roughly one SETATTR per file and costs
   roughly one DELEGRETURN per file; the A-80 amendment above removed write delegations and that alone cut
   DELEGRETURN 91,034 → 4 (13% of all RPCs). Re-offering them to chase SETATTR would hand most of that back.

   So the two levers pull against each other, and the measurement already chose.

3. **And the third reading is that there is no lever, because the op is protocol-mandated.** An `EXCLUSIVE`
   create stores the verifier *in the file's times* (RFC 8881 §18.16.3), so the client **must** follow it with
   a SETATTR to set the real attributes — `exclusive_open` in `v4/compound.rs` does exactly this and its own
   comment says why: "The times hold the verifier: naming them tells the client to set its own". Git creates
   with `O_CREAT|O_EXCL`, which the Linux client maps to `EXCLUSIVE4`.

   **The existing profile already corroborates it and nobody read it that way: OPEN 14% and SETATTR 13.5% are
   near-identical**, which is the signature of one mandated SETATTR per exclusive create, not of an
   independent op that happens to land near 1/file.

   **Measured 2026-10-21, and it holds.** A probe on `open_createhow`, run against the real Linux kernel
   NFSv4 client through `crates/server/tests/nfs_v4_kernel.rs` in a privileged container — no clone run, as
   predicted — counted the modes actually on the wire:

   ```
   10 × createmode4=0   UNCHECKED
    5 × createmode4=3   EXCLUSIVE4_1
   ```

   So the client does issue exclusive creates, and it uses `EXCLUSIVE4_1`, not `EXCLUSIVE4`. That refines the
   conclusion rather than overturning it. `EXCLUSIVE4_1` carries an attribute set beside its verifier and
   slates honours it — `open_createhow` decodes both and `exclusive_open` applies the attributes — so **mode
   is settable at create and costs nothing extra**. But the verifier still lives in the file's times
   (`suppattr_exclcreat` excludes them, and slates refuses an atime/mtime in the create attrs for exactly that
   reason), so a client that wants real times **must** SETATTR afterwards. There is no way to carry them in
   the create.

   **Conclusion: for an exclusive create the follow-up SETATTR is required by RFC 8881 §18.16.3, and no
   server-side change removes it.** The profile's OPEN 14% against SETATTR 13.5% is consistent with git's
   storm being overwhelmingly exclusive creates. The 2×-vs-tmpfs target has to come from the other ops, and
   the remaining per-file budget is LOOKUP, OPEN, WRITE and CLOSE.

   What is *not* established: the exclusive share of git's own create storm specifically. The 10:5 split above
   is this test's workload (create, write, mkdir, rename, symlink, link, truncate), not a checkout.

## DAX sealed-chunk backing decided by A/B; the re-seal hold is learned (§4.6, 2026-10-17)

Rule (a) of the open-frontier decision — map only a file's one open chunk, refuse a sealed one to FUSE_READ — was
taken to a live crosvm guest and failed. A guest's single `SETUPMAPPING` spans a whole DAX range, not one chunk, so
the device must back every chunk in the range (an N-map loop, and for the message-based placer an N-ack park); and a
refused sealed chunk SIGBUSes a `dax=always` mmap rather than falling back. Both candidate backings were then built
in full on separate branches and measured head to head (`BENCHMARKS.md` 2026-10-17): the decrypt-**view** throwaway
and **reopen**-in-place. Both carry a live guest's multi-block mmap byte-for-byte (`GUEST-MMAP-OK`).

Measured: the view needs one byte of RAM per byte simultaneously mapped (slope 1.0 across 256×), and a real guest
fills its DAX cache exactly (8 MiB cache → 8.000 MiB high-water; 4 MiB → 4.000 MiB), so its cost is the whole
advertised cache — 256 MiB as the harness shipped. Reopen needs none, pays one extra AES-GCM pass per chunk per cold
cycle (+0.08–0.18 s per GiB streamed), and is ~8× faster when the guest returns to a chunk still held plaintext.
**Reopen lands; the view is recorded measured-and-rejected.**

The re-seal hold is **learned**, because the measurement showed no fixed delay is right: the guest's revoke→remap
interval moved 8× (67 ms to 537 ms) for one workload merely by changing its DAX cache. The volume starts at zero and
grows the hold a sweep each time the gate catches a re-seal the guest immediately undid (`reseal_regret`, the
non-vacuity counter), resetting on quiescence; the sweep is the hold's clock. Its ceiling is derived from the idle
sweep's own aging — a mapped read must not be a weaker at-rest guarantee than an ordinary write — and policy may
lower it.

Green: vfs dax 48/0 (including the learned-hold and re-seal tests), vfs lib 43/0, bridge-virtiofs device 28/0, the
recovery oracle 39/0 serial, clippy `--all-targets -D warnings` clean.

The learned hold is now measured, not just unit-tested: on a quiet box (load 2.98) the re-read workload with sweeps
running between the reads — reopen's worst case, which it *lost* by 1.1–1.7× before the hold existed — becomes a 3.9×
win, because the sweeps no longer re-encrypt a chunk the workload is about to read again. The landed code also
carries the live guest's heavy workload (32 MiB working set through an 8 MiB cache, two full passes, hundreds of
reclaim/re-map cycles) byte-for-byte.

**Owed:** the live guest's revoke→remap figures (67 ms/537 ms) were taken under load 34 and before the hold existed,
so the churn the hold removes *in a real guest* is inferred from the in-process workload rather than re-measured
there; and DAX stays advertisement-gated.

## A FUSE invalidation written from the serving thread deadlocked the mount (§4.6, 2026-10-17)

Found by widening the regression sweep for the DAX work, then proved pre-existing. A Linux FUSE mount wedged
permanently — `crates/server/tests/fuse_mount.rs::a_scoped_fuse_mount_presents_one_directory_and_follows_it` hung
forever (13 minutes at 1 s of CPU; exit 124 under a 240 s timeout), taking its **shard** with it.

Root cause, confirmed by kernel stacks and a trace rather than inferred
(`docs/bugs/2026-10-17-fuse-notify-deadlocks-the-serving-thread.md`): `FuseChannel::write_invalidation` did a
blocking `write(2)` of `FUSE_NOTIFY_INVAL_ENTRY` from `deliver_owed`, which runs inside the same `serve_step` /
`dispatch_ready` that reads a request and produces its reply. The kernel's `fuse_reverse_inval_entry()` takes the
parent directory's inode lock, which a concurrent lookup holds for the whole request — so the one thread that would
answer the lookup and release the lock was the thread blocked waiting for it. `FUSE_EXPIRE_ONLY` does not avoid it
(the kernel locks the parent before reading the flags), and neither does any ordering inside our own loop (the
kernel holds the lock from the moment it issues the request).

Fixed: a round of invalidations is written on a thread of its own, owned and joined by the `ServeState` that
started it, mirroring the landing barrier's thread (A-132) which exists for the same reason. The API that wrote a
notification on the caller's thread is **gone** (replaced by `encode_invalidation`), so a new caller cannot
reintroduce the hazard. One round is out at a time — `Bridge::invalidations` consumes what it reports, so a second
is never gathered while one is in flight, which is also its bound — and the cursor is rewound if the kernel refuses
the write, so nothing is dropped. §4.6 Cache posture is amended in the same change: the claim that delivery precedes
each request is withdrawn (it was never achievable); the property that posture rests on, proven delivery, is kept.

Verified: 5 runs out of 5 green in ~0.22 s where it previously hung every time; a deterministic unit test
(`a_round_whose_write_blocks_does_not_hold_its_owner`) holds the invariant with no kernel; a watchdog now aborts the
suite with a named reason instead of hanging CI, since `cargo test --workspace` includes it. Regression on the box:
bridge-fuse all suites, `nfs_mount` 36/0, `daemon` 22/0, `virtiofs` 18/0, `attach_forms` 8/0, recovery oracle 41/0,
clippy `--all-targets -D warnings` clean.

**Owed:** on a refused delivery the cursor is rewound, but the base-plane entries `take_stale_base_entries` already
consumed are gone — the journal half replays, the base half does not (pre-existing, found while fixing this, not
widened into it). And the daemon's serve loop waits on device readability, so a finished round's outcome is seen at
its next turn; `ServeState::wakes_with` exists for a loop that carries a change signal.

### 2026-10-17: the A-61 resend test raced its own precondition (CI red, fixed)

`a_write_in_flight_at_the_daemons_kill_is_resent_and_every_acknowledged_write_survives` failed the ubuntu lane of
run 39090330413 with `3 cycles, 0 resent` while the product was correct throughout — nothing lost, no `fsync`
reporting a loss. The test needs the `SIGKILL` to land while the daemon holds a request it has read and not
answered, since only those are resent, and it had no way to make that true: the catch probability is the serve
loop's duty cycle, because `turn()` reads, serves and replies to one request and the kernel's processing list holds
at most one at a time, so extra writers lengthen the pending queue and cannot raise it. Measured, binaries
differing only in the page constant and run alternately (cachyos box, 32 cores, kernel 7.2.9, pinned to 4): cycles
caught 4 KiB 33/58 = 0.57, 16 KiB 12/14 = 0.86, 64 KiB 12/13 = 0.92, 256 KiB 37/37 = 1.00. Two beliefs in the test
were false — that several writers keep one request always in flight, and that waiting for a writer to be inside
`write(2)` is sufficient (on fedora `in_write` was 4 throughout and the kill still missed). Behind them sat the
kill itself: a `slates status` round trip plus `kill(1)`, 27.3-46.0 ms from the observed window to the signal,
against a window of microseconds.

Fixed by resolving the pid before the writers start and sending the signal with one syscall (7.2-15.9 µs, about
3400× tighter), and by writing one `init::MAX_WRITE` page instead of 4 KiB; `WRITES_BEFORE`/`WRITES_AFTER` become
one `WRITES_PER_PHASE` derived from a writer budget. No attempt count or timeout was raised.

Verified: cachyos, 30 interleaved runs per arm — 256 KiB caught 30/32 cycles (0.94), 0 failures; 4 KiB 30/48
(0.63). Fedora (kernel 6.19.10, pinned to 2 cores): current tree 10 runs of 10 green, 10/11 cycles (0.91); 4 KiB
with the fast kill 2/15 (0.13), so the fast kill alone is necessary and far from sufficient. `clippy --workspace
--all-targets -D warnings` and `fmt --check` exit 0; the cli suite 31/31. Record:
`docs/bugs/2026-10-17-the-in-flight-resend-test-raced-its-own-precondition.md`.

A second defect in the same test, found by running the committed tree: the writers' loop was unbounded. The
successor daemon answers as soon as it is serving, but the test learns of it only at the next 20 ms `await_daemon`
poll, and four writers fill that interval at full speed with pages no phase counts — enough to take `ENOSPC`
instead of the resend under test in 2 runs of 12 and 1 of 7. The volume is not at fault and an earlier draft that
said it overcharges was wrong: filling one file by `dd` until `ENOSPC` reached 67108864 B of a 64 MiB bound to the
byte at both 4 KiB and 256 KiB pages, a charge-to-length ratio of 1.000, with A-109's inode allowance over four
files four orders below the budget. A writer now counts only its before-plus-middle allowance and appends to a
throwaway file after that, reopened empty every phase's worth, so what a cycle adds to the volume is bounded by
construction (CLAUDE.md #8) and does not depend on how fast the host writes. Pausing at the allowance instead was
tried and rejected: it bounds the volume and breaks the test, since the kill waits for a request in flight and a
paused writer has none — no run completed at all. The two symptoms are coupled, which is why the budget alone
looked sufficient over 30 runs and then failed 2 of 12 on the same tree: a run that catches on its first cycle
never approaches the bound, so the overflow only shows on runs needing a second or third cycle.

Bounding the writers exposed what the page size had been masking: the catch is a draw, not a certainty, and three
attempts were never derived from it. A cycle catches with p = 0.709 measured over 100 runs of the shipped binary,
and the tail is geometric (the share of runs still going after k cycles fell 1 → 0.305 → 0.100 → 0.035 over a
200-run series, a ratio of 0.33-0.35 at each step), so `IN_FLIGHT_ATTEMPTS` is now ⌈ln(1e-5)/ln(0.35)⌉ = 11 and a
run misses every attempt below once in 100000. The derivation is inverted to match: `WRITES_PER_PHASE` is the
shape, `WRITER_BUDGET_BYTES` is what the writers can append if every cycle misses (99 MiB) and the held mount's
bound is twice that (198 MiB) — a quota, not an allocation, and attempts cost nothing unless a cycle misses (67 of
100 runs took one cycle). Four interleaved arms at allowance 1x/4x/16x/uncapped measured 0.833/0.909/0.833/0.870,
so the cap itself costs no catch rate. Verified: 360 runs, 0 failures, 0 `ENOSPC`; a run forced through all 11
cycles finishes in 2.1 s inside the anchor's restart policy; `clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings` and
`fmt --check` exit 0; the cli suite 31/31.

**Owed — CLOSED 2026-10-19.** The entry read: "`wanted()` in `crates/bridge-fuse/src/init.rs` never asks for
`FUSE_MAX_PAGES` and the INIT reply writes `max_pages = 0`, so the kernel keeps its own pages-per-request ceiling
and the advertised `max_write` of 256 KiB is not what one request carries — verified in our source by two
independent readings, but the kernel half is read from `fuse_perform_write`, not measured here, and no `strace` of
the daemon's reads was taken."

Both halves are now settled. **Measured** (the evidence the entry said was missing, taken as a count rather than
an strace): each FUSE request is one `read()` from `/dev/fuse`, so the daemon's `syscr` over a known write is
load-independent — writing 256 MiB, a 128 KiB buffer cost 4,101 reads (2,048 one-request calls, pinning the scale
at 2.0 reads per request), and before the fix a 256 KiB buffer cost the same ~4,100, i.e. two requests per call.
**Fixed**: `wanted()` asks for the flag and the reply carries `max_pages = MAX_WRITE / page_size` (run-time,
clamped to the kernel's `FUSE_MAX_MAX_PAGES`); after it, 256 KiB is 2,058 reads — one request — and 1 MiB is
2,051, four. Half the round trips for every write ≥ 256 KiB.

Two things the entry did not anticipate. The device's `writable_cap` was derived from the kernel *default* page
count, so negotiating a larger one would have let a 64 KiB-page guest ask past the cap the device enforces; it
now follows the negotiated count. And the **read** side does not move — 128 KiB per READ request at any buffer —
because the mount's readahead window is 128 kB (`/sys/class/bdi/<maj:min>/read_ahead_kb`, read directly), which
is root-owned and therefore a host knob, not something an unprivileged daemon can lift. Full record in
`BENCHMARKS.md`. **The x86_64 leg is no longer owed — taken 2026-10-19** on an idle 32-core Fedora host
(kernel 6.19, page 4,096, load1 1.6-2.2) as an interleaved A/B against the same tree with the one line
`| flags::MAX_PAGES` deleted, two rounds each. With the flag a 256 KiB and a 1 MiB write both resolve to 256 KiB
requests; without it, 128 KiB. The 128 KiB buffer is the built-in control -- under both caps, so both arms must
issue one request per write, and they agree within 2% there -- and at a 1 MiB buffer, where both arms make the
same 64 `write()` calls, the measured gap is 1,166 - 654 = 512 reads = exactly twice the 256 extra requests, with
an overhead term of 142 in *both* arms. Same conclusion as aarch64, on the other architecture and page size.

### 2026-10-18: a zero-copy read handed the peer the whole content arena, writable (A-135; escape closed)

**Found by attacking the local zero-copy read (A-135), closed in the same change.** It is the live sibling of the
message-based DAX finding above: the same accessor, the same mistake, but on a path that is **not**
advertisement-gated and **not** harness-only — every Linux `MapRead` served by the zero-copy arm did this.

- **What was handed over.** `try_local_map` sends the content block's backing descriptor over the control socket by
  `SCM_RIGHTS`. The reply's `region_off`/`file_len`/`block_len` scope the *request*; a descriptor carries its whole
  object, read **and** write. `ChunkArena::block_backing` says so in its own comment — "`backing_fd` is the whole
  object" — and the object is the anchor's content RAM for the host.
- **Measured e2e** (x86_64 Linux, kernel 7.2.9-2-cachyos, a one-shard daemon, two volumes of one account; the peer
  maps *its own* 20 KiB file): `object_bytes=189833572352 authorized_bytes=20480` — **176.8 GiB for a 20 KiB read,
  9,269,217×** — `neighbour_marker_occurrences=1280` (the other volume's *whole* 20 KiB file readable), and
  `writable_map=granted`. A second run finished the escape: find the neighbour's bytes in the handed object,
  overwrite them, read that volume through the ordinary verb — `"OWNED-BY-A-PEER!SL-NEIGHBOUR-SEC"`. **A read verb
  gave cross-volume read and cross-volume write with no lease, no attachment and no verb.**
- **The false premise.** The gate was `same_uid`, documented as "its own trust domain". A §4.13 consumer is an
  untrusted process of exactly this uid holding exactly this channel, and `MapRead` is dispatched with a `Principal`
  like any other read — so a consumer confined to one volume reached all of them. §4.6's body carried the same
  wrong sentence and is corrected in this change.
- **A read-only duplicate is not a fix, and that is measured** (`/tmp/fdprobe.c`, same host): a same-uid peer
  re-opens a read-only memfd duplicate `O_RDWR` through `/proc/self/fd` and maps it writable. What does hold is
  `MFD_ALLOW_SEALING` + `F_SEAL_FUTURE_WRITE|SHRINK|GROW` applied **after** the owner takes its own writable map:
  the owner keeps writing through that map while the peer is refused every writable map, every `pwrite`, every
  `ftruncate` — including when it holds the writable descriptor itself.
- **The fix is at the boundary, not at the caller.** `Control::send_mapping` → `confined_for_a_peer` is the one
  place a descriptor leaves this process for a peer, so no caller can skip it and the rule cannot drift: `fstat`
  must show the object *is* the window (`region_off == 0`, `object_len == block_len`) and `F_GET_SEALS` must show a
  write seal with `SHRINK` and `GROW`, else the typed `IpcError::UnconfinedDescriptor { object_bytes,
  authorized_bytes, writable }`. `try_local_map` already treats a failed send as `LocalMap::Fallback`, so the client
  is served by copy and always gets its bytes; the minted mapping's pin is released on that arm as before.
- **What it costs.** No backing satisfies the rule today — a shard's content arena is one object holding every
  volume (A-64) — so on Linux a `MapRead` now reads by copy and A-135's zero-copy arm is not taken. That is the
  honest price of closing a live escape, and the alternative was preserving the behaviour that caused it.
- **Owed — one decision, now shared by both findings.** Restoring zero-copy needs a backing whose **object is the
  unit of authorization**: (1) a sealed backing object per tenant (keeps zero-copy, confines by construction, cuts
  against A-64's one-image layout), (2) a per-mapping sealed object holding only the block (confined, one copy at
  map time — for DAX this is the measured-and-rejected "view" arm, but A-135's baseline is a copy *per read*, so
  copy-once-map-many is a *different* measurement and has not been taken), or (3) keep the copy path. Option 1 is
  the only one that serves both callers. **A sibling the fix does not cover:** `Store::dax_backing` still hands the
  same unconfined descriptor to the vhost-user message placer, which does not route through `send_mapping`; it stays
  advertisement-gated and recorded. **The real hazard is `block_backing`'s contract** — a descriptor for an object
  its own comment calls "the whole object", with nothing in its signature saying that handing it over authorizes
  everything in it. Both escapes came from that; if option 1 is taken it should have no unconfined sibling.
- **Tests.** `crates/ipc` `a_descriptor_that_would_authorize_more_than_the_hand_off_is_never_sent` (three shapes a
  real arena produces, each refused, and nothing waiting on the peer's side afterwards);
  `crates/client/tests/client.rs` `a_zero_copy_reads_descriptor_authorizes_its_window_and_nothing_more`, written as
  the invariant so it keeps its meaning when a confined backing lands — zero-copy ⇒ the descriptor shows none of the
  neighbour's marker and refuses a writable map; copy ⇒ **no** memory-object descriptor was installed in the peer at
  all. Non-vacuity: the marker must first be found in this process's memory objects (10,240 occurrences).
  `a_same_kernel_client_maps_a_file_with_no_copy` reports its path instead of asserting it, since asserting it would
  pin today's state in place. Record:
  `docs/bugs/2026-10-18-a-read-handed-the-peer-the-whole-content-arena.md`.

### 2026-10-18: GAP-A9-9 measured — on macOS a same-uid stranger opens any client's ring, by name

> **2026-11-06: the ring half fixed by A-233** (the entry at the top of this file); the segment, the bootstrap object
> and Windows stay open there.

The ledger has carried "same-uid isolation (GAP-A9-9) owed" since §4.7 was written. This is the first
**measurement** of what that costs, and it is worse on macOS than the wording suggests.

Linux hands a client its ring as a **descriptor** over an abstract-namespace socket, so the memfd has no
name anywhere and only a process the daemon passed it to can reach it. macOS has no abstract namespace,
so the rendezvous is a **named** object and everything it leads to is opened by name —
`/slates-rv-<instance>-<uid>`, `/slates-cr-<instance>-<client_id>-<uid>`,
`/slates-seg-<instance>-<uid>` — every part of which is public (the instance is how clients find the
daemon, the uid is the caller's own, a client id counts up from 1). `shm_open` mode `0600` leaves the
uid as the only barrier, and the uid is exactly the boundary that must hold: a §4.13 consumer is an
untrusted process of the daemon's own uid, as `crates/ipc/src/delivery.rs` says when it picks an
inherited descriptor as "the one channel other same-uid processes provably cannot read".

Measured (macOS arm64; a stranger that never connected and holds no capability):

```
victim is client 1; it wrote its secret through its ring
stranger opened /slates-cr-mr78796-1-501 read-write: 278528 bytes, no capability at all
the victim's secret appears 2719 times in the ring a stranger just mapped
the stranger also wrote into it (header byte flipped and restored)
stranger opened /slates-seg-mr-79327-501 read-write: 148892368896 bytes
stranger opened /slates-rv-mb72074-501 read-write with no capability at all
```

Ring disclosure, ring **injection**, and read-write access to the daemon's 138.7 GiB segment, without
being a client.

**Windows: the same, from source and labelled as such** (not measured — no Windows host here). The section is
created with a **NULL** `lpFileMappingAttributes`, so it takes the creating token's default DACL, which grants
the creating *user*; its name is `Local\<name>` over the same derived names; and slates opens by name with
`OpenFileMappingW(FILE_MAP_ALL_ACCESS, …)`, the very call a stranger would make. Narrower than macOS only in
that `Local\` is per-session rather than per-uid, which does not help against a §4.13 consumer the harness
spawns into the same session. **The fix is already in the tree, used elsewhere:** `crates/ipc/src/delivery.rs`
hands the consumer capability to exactly one child with `PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_HANDLE_LIST`; handle duplication
is Windows' capability-passing primitive, the counterpart of `SCM_RIGHTS` and of the Mach fileport below.

**A measured negative, so the Linux doorbell theft does not carry over:** a stranger can write the
macOS doorbell word, but restoring it after every ring does not slow the victim — `Bell::ring` follows
its `fetch_add` with an explicit `wake_one` on the address, and the waiter is woken by that, not by the
value. Three arms interleaved with a CPU-matched control: idle 402 µs p50, control 400 µs, suppressing
396 µs over 211,635,442 stores. No effect.

**Two scan traps worth keeping:** macOS shm objects answer neither `SEEK_DATA` nor `pread` (`false` and
`0` bytes), so the first version of the probe reported a clean object that was wide open — any scan of a
macOS shared object must `mmap` it. And the segment's 256 MiB prefix held none of the victim's content,
which is a bounded negative and not an absence; the object is 138.7 GiB and scanning it all would commit
it.

**Why no patch here:** a random name per object and an `shm_unlink` after hand-over both fail, because
the region's name is published in the bootstrap object's claim slot and a stranger polling that object
managed 211 million reads in one run. A Unix domain socket would end the class as it does on Linux but
needs a path, which R1 forbids "if any alternative exists". **An alternative does exist and it is the
macOS-native one:** a Mach port *is* a capability, the bootstrap namespace is per-user rather than a
filesystem, and `fileport_makeport`/`fileport_makefd` pass a descriptor over a Mach message — the
`SCM_RIGHTS` hand-off with no path and no name to guess, so it answers R1 rather than trading against
it. **Ada's call.** Record:
`docs/bugs/2026-10-18-macos-shares-by-name-so-a-stranger-opens-any-clients-ring.md`.

### 2026-10-18: the shard doorbell is shared, and a peer steals its wakes (GAP-A9-9, Linux half)

The connect hand-off gives every client a duplicate of the **shard's** kick eventfd, and an eventfd
duplicate can be read as well as written. A read drains the counter, so one client consumes the wake
another just posted. Requests are still served — this is latency, not loss.

Four arms interleaved round-robin against a real one-shard daemon (x86_64 Linux):

| arm | the hostile peer | p50 |
|---|---|---|
| A | nothing | 1,802 µs |
| B | spin-read **a private eventfd** (the CPU-matched control) | 1,812 µs |
| C | spin-read **the shard doorbell** | 7,805 µs |
| D | **`poll`, then one read** of the shard doorbell | **69,970 µs** |

B is indistinguishable from idle, so the cost is not the core the attack burns. **D settles the
mechanism:** it is the cheapest attack — a few touches a second against C's millions — and the most
damaging, 38× idle. Contention would rank them the other way round; what D maximises is the fraction of
wakes taken, so it is theft. One wake stolen per attacked round, every round.
