    - `MapRead` does not refuse a file an in-process guest maps writable (the DAX registry's `has_writable_of`), which
      `MapWrite` refuses: that guest's stores bypass the write boundary, so a read-only copy made meanwhile would go
      stale. `Volume::dax_map_write` refuses the other order already. **Unreachable in a daemon, checked 2026-10-29:**
      a writable window over a file's own block needs the volume's writable-DAX opt-in, and nothing in the daemon calls
      `Volume::enable_writable_dax` (only vfs and bridge tests do), so `has_writable_of` is false there; a daemon's guest
      windows map per-file backings that write-through keeps equal (A-168). If a daemon opt-in is ever added, `MapRead`
      must refuse as `MapWrite` does, in `Fill::begin` where both resolve their inode.
    - The fill's deferral answered its never-expected route refusal with the copy still held: the fill's drop runs
      inside the state's borrow there and cannot reach the store. The shared deferral lets the copy go on both of its
      refusals now.

      is its id's residue, and a copy is handed only to a client of the volume's shard. Its container connected after
      three status calls and landed on the volume's shard; the writable test's, after four, was refused
      `MapUnavailable`. Both run a one-shard daemon now, as the client suite's do.

        `ENOTSUP`, `fcntl` record locks `EBADF`), and the socket route's `InUse` decides by a socket file, which is
        authorized for the DAX route alone;
      - a bootstrap name is the first registrant's and is free when its holder's port dies: a second process refused
        (1100), a second registration of the same process refused (1101), 200 of 200 re-registrations accepted at once
        after a holder dropped its right (worst 0.105 ms), 20 of 20 after a holder killed with `SIGKILL` was reaped;
      - at the top of the chain (a namespace that is its own parent) one name serves every session of the user: from
        this GUI session the chain was three deep and every level accepted a registration, and a name registered in the
        parent was refused to a second process both there and in its own namespace;
      - the machine-wide alternative, a SysV semaphore held with `SEM_UNDO`, fits the limits here (`kern.sysv.semmni`
        87,381, `semume` 10 per process) but names a set by a 32-bit key other software draws from (5 sets under this
        user already), and a crash leaves its instance's set behind.
      Proven: `a_second_owner_of_a_live_instances_rendezvous_is_refused` now runs on macOS, and
      `a_second_process_is_refused_a_live_instances_rendezvous` (new) checks the refusal across processes on every
      platform; the rendezvous suite 14 of 14 on this Mac and fedora, `slates-ipc` linted on all three. Red-checked on
      this Mac with a token that never meets a holder: both fail. Bug record:
      `docs/bugs/2026-10-26-a-second-owner-took-a-live-macos-instances-rendezvous-over.md`. Owed: the token's reach
      measured beyond one GUI session, an ssh login's parent namespace and a launchd job's (CI's macOS runner runs
      both tests);
    - on every platform, a client's direct map outlives its daemon: after a `kill -9` and restart the map keeps the file
      as it was when the daemon died and follows it no more, with no signal to the client (its object lives on in the
      client's process). A replayed map reply now fails rather than adopting such a copy (A-175's record rule; Linux's
      and macOS's hand-offs fail as well), but a map made before the death goes stale silently. The same holds while the
      daemon lives when a `MappedRead` outlives its `Client`: the client is reaped and its copies let go, and the map
      keeps the bytes as they were. Owed: a decision on how a client learns its map ended. Facts for it: the client's own
      liveness question is one syscall (`ExitWatch::exited`: `kevent`, `poll` on a pidfd, or `WaitForSingleObject` with
      no wait; Linux's control-socket peek), its cost not yet measured here (estimated, not measured, at about a
      microsecond), against a steady mapped read of 0.4 to 1.1 µs at 4 KiB and a copy read of 4.8 µs (the box) to 33 µs
      (this Mac); and a read is exact if the question follows the load, since no newer write is accepted until a new
      daemon has started.

- **The Python async SDK's loop-hold test failed now and then on CI's macOS runner (found 2026-10-25, fixed
  2026-10-26).** Runs 40227172048 and 40239373189: the event loop, idle in its own selector, woken about 0.28 s late,
  judged against a noise figure that measured another primitive's timer delay. The cause, the measurements and the
  fix are in §8a-sdk-loop's last paragraph and
  `docs/bugs/2026-10-26-the-async-sdk-tests-noise-was-another-waits-timer-delay.md`. Measured on the runner since: in
  the fix's own CI run (40251576842) the macOS SDK job printed `time.sleep 76.5 ms, the selector 3.2 ms`, the delay
  this Mac reads, and the fixed test passed with a worst charge of 0.010 s against the control loop's 0.011 s
  (ubuntu: `time.sleep 0.1 ms, the selector 0.1 ms`; 0.002 s against 0.000 s).
- **On macOS, shipped code's std timed waits run up to eight times longer than asked under a launchd job's timer
  policy (open, measured 2026-10-26).** From a process launchd started (this Mac, load 19 to 41), Rust's
  `thread::park_timeout` came back late by 6.0 ms at 1 ms asked, 76 ms at 10 ms, 148 ms at 100 ms and 148 ms at 1 s
  (medians; `thread::sleep` and `Condvar::wait_timeout` alike at 10 ms), while a kevent timeout came back within 0.25
  to 2.01 ms at every interval. A daemon run as a launchd agent, CI's macOS runner and kiln's agents all start that
  way. The runtime's own timers wait through kevent and are not affected. The std waits in shipped code are:
  - the client's reconnect and transient-refusal backoff (`crates/client/src/client.rs`, `park_timeout`). Each pause
    may run eight times its derived length, so a reconnect notices a restarted daemon later;
  - the anchor's graceful-stop steps and its pause when it has no descriptor to poll (`crates/api/src/role/anchor.rs`,
    `park_timeout`), and the daemon's heartbeat park (`crates/server/src/daemon.rs`). The anchor's usual wait is not
    stretched: it polls the daemon's exit watch and its hold channel with `poll(2)`, which XNU builds on kqueue, and
    a 10 ms `poll` came back 1.98 ms late at the median (a `select` beside it, 78.6 ms), so a death is still seen at
    once;
  - `recv_timeout` in `crates/rt/src/task.rs`, `crates/rt/src/registry.rs` and `crates/server/src/observe.rs`.
  Not yet measured: what it costs end to end, such as a restart's time to the first answered call with and without
  the policy. A candidate symptom: locally, with the test's slowdown factor at 1, phase (1) of the async SDK test came
  back `Stalled { after_ns: 1000000000 }` in 2 of 10 runs of the old test file and in none of 10 of the new one, too
  few to show a difference. Next: measure a restart's phases under the policy, then decide per site between a kevent
  timed wait and a documented tolerance.
- **A DAX copy slice past the bridge's 256 KiB read cap dropped a guest's stores (A-163, fixed 2026-10-25).** CI's
  ubuntu lane on `d71ce235` (run 40211222944) failed two Shards tests: a store through a guest's DAX map past the first
  256 KiB of a copy slice never reached the volume at `FSYNC`, which answered 0. Root cause, reproduced on fedora by
  forcing a 4 MiB slice: the ingest's compare and the refill read a slice in one bridge call, which the volume bridge
  cuts at `MAX_READ`, and took the cut for the file's end (the refill padded it with zeros into the guest's map). Only
  a machine whose derived slice exceeds 256 KiB shows it; fedora, adacachy (load 242–249) and this Mac never did.
  - **Fixed:** `read_whole` (`crates/bridge-core/src/dax_backing.rs`) reads a slice call after call; the Shards tests
    run every targeted case and every generated history with the machine's slice and with a whole range a slice, and
    the refill test compares the whole range (`docs/bugs/2026-10-25-a-dax-slice-past-the-read-cap-dropped-a-guests-stores.md`).
  - **Verified:** this Mac, Shards 25 of 25; fedora, the three tests green, and all three red with `read_whole` cut to
    one call.
  - **Siblings found by the sweep:** WinFsp's host answered a Windows read with one bridge read, so a read past
    256 KiB returned short mid-file, which a program takes for the file's end and Windows zero-fills on a paging read.
    **Fixed 2026-11-18 (g079, goal 83):** the host answers a read through `read_whole`, in as many bridge reads as the
    cap takes, stopping short only at the file's end. The failing test is
    `a_read_longer_than_the_bridges_cap_returns_every_byte_asked_for` (`crates/cli/tests/winfsp.rs`: one unbuffered
    1 MiB read from a longer file's start; it reads 256 KiB without the fix). It is a live-drive test on CI's Windows
    lanes, filed for main's run (`run-requests.md`); `cargo xwin check` is clean. Record:
    `docs/bugs/2026-11-18-a-winfsp-read-past-the-bridges-cap-came-back-short.md`. FSKit's shim does the same and is
    not shipped: slates never mounts through FSKit.

- **The direct map on macOS (A-173, G-direct step 4, 2026-10-25): built, and proven on this Mac by a real client.**
  - **What:** a `MapRead` on macOS is answered `MapOffered`. The file's copy is a shared-memory object whose name went
    as soon as its two descriptors were open; the read-only one is offered on the daemon's socket route (A-161, now
    version 2: the hello names the offer's kind, a stream end or a map's copy) behind a fresh single-use secret the
    reply carries, and the client claims and maps it. macOS has no seals, so the descriptor's access mode is the
    capability, judged before the offer (`confined_read_only`: read alone, exactly the authorized length).
  - **Proven** on this Mac (arm64, Darwin 25.4.0): the client binary 21 of 21 and `reap_map.rs` 1 of 1 over a real
    daemon (zero copy asserted at 20 KiB, 4 MiB and every size from empty to 1 MiB; every change within the map seen with
    no request; the release, the share, a destroy, an unlink and a `SIGKILL`ed mapper's reap as on Linux); the handed
    descriptor's shared writable map refused `EPERM`, a write `EBADF`, its read-only map turned writable `EACCES`, a
    resize either way `EINVAL`, a private writable map `EINVAL`, a reopen read-write through `/dev/fd` `EBADF`; the
    Shards suite 25 of 25 over route version 2; ipc, server unit; workspace clippy clean on macOS and on fedora, where
    the client binary, `reap_map` and the server's unit tests pass unchanged.
  - **Red-checked** in a scratch copy, each arm rebuilt: the read-write descriptor handed in the read-only one's place
    was refused unconfined at the hand-off (the neighbour's map came by copy); with the judge bypassed too, the test
    failed at the access mode; with that assertion lifted too, at the shared writable map, which was granted (as was
    the turned map; the write answered `ESPIPE` and the resize `EINVAL`, so the write is held to `EBADF`, the access
    mode's own refusal, and the resize to XNU's rule for every descriptor).
  - **Fixed on the way, failing test first:** a copy released before its offer was claimed left the offer claimable,
    a live object outside the client's share (`docs/bugs/2026-10-25-a-released-maps-offer-stayed-claimable.md`); every
    copy let go now withdraws its offer (`direct_map::let_go`).
  - **Open:**
    - a test of the reap's withdrawal of its own: it shares the release's code, and a test would race the offer's own
      expiry (both two liveness budgets), so it is owed rather than written flaky;
    - **sibling found by the sweep:** a Shards stream offer outlived an attachment that ended before its claim, a dead
      end held until it expired. **Fixed the same day**, failing test first: an ended attachment withdraws its offer
      (`docs/bugs/2026-10-25-an-ended-attachments-stream-offer-stayed-claimable.md`);
    - this Mac's map arm of the break-even bench (step 3), now that the map is direct here: **measured the same day**
      (BENCHMARKS, the entry's Mac table);
    - a hand-off that fails at the client after the copy was made (a claim refused on macOS — `Busy`, an expired offer,
      a confirmation that does not open — or, on Linux since A-171, a delivery that never arrives) returned the error
      and left the copy held on the client's slot, unreachable by `release_map` (which takes the map), until the
      client was reaped. **Fixed the same day, A-174:** the client gives the copy back by its id before the failure
      returns; proven on this Mac and on fedora by a client process capped at its descriptors
      (`crates/client/tests/reap_map.rs`), red-checked.

- **Copy-once-map-many against copy-per-read, measured (G-direct step 3, 2026-10-25).** BENCHMARKS, "Copy-once-map-many
  against copy-per-read". On the box (load 65–80, capped) and on fedora (load 13), two runs each, best of 15: a steady
  mapped read costs 3.7 % to 10.3 % of a copy read at 4 KiB, 1 MiB and 64 MiB alike; a map repays its setup after one
  read from 1 MiB up (its whole setup, the fill included, already costs less than one copy read: 64 MiB in 39–97 ms
  against 94–191 ms) and after 3 to 5 reads of a 4 KiB file. The two runs agree within their spread on each machine.
  This Mac's map arm read by copy until step 4, so it was first recorded as the copy read's baseline only. **Since step 4
  (A-173), measured on this Mac too** (load 15.5–19.6, two runs): a steady mapped read costs 1.1 % to 2.1 % of a copy
  read; the route's claim makes a 4 KiB map's setup 83–94 µs, repaid after 3 reads; from 1 MiB the whole setup costs
  less than one copy read (64 MiB: 49–74 ms against 314–329 ms).
  - **Fixed on the way, CI's ubuntu lane (run 40209801720 on 604e0875):** the share test asked for a third map right
    after a second client connected and expected the share halved; on CI the shard had not yet taken the second client
    in (a client reaches its shard as a task after its connect returns), so the share was still two. The test now has
    the second client make a request first, whose answer shows the shard serves it.

- **The direct map's lifetime and bounds (A-172, G-direct step 2, 2026-10-25): built, and proven on Linux by real
  clients.**
  - **What:** `ReleaseMap` (and `Client::release_map`) gives a copy back; a reap gives back every copy a dead client
    held; a destroy or a file's last unlink detaches its copies from the write-through index, and they stay held and
    counted until released or reaped (the client's map keeps pages the daemon wrote, so forgetting them would let a
    client pin uncounted daemon memory: A-171 had done exactly that). A shard holds at most `direct_maps_per_shard`
    copies (half the process's descriptor and mapping limits over what a copy holds, over the shards) and its fill
    budget's bytes; a client's share is that over the clients served now, and a map past it is refused
    `MapShareExhausted` with nothing made.
  - **Proven** on fedora (x86_64 Linux): the client binary 20 of 20, `reap_map.rs` 1 of 1 (a re-invoked test binary holding
    a map, `SIGKILL`ed, its copy reaped; its own binary, since `reap.rs` counts process-wide reaps), the vfs backings tests 11 of 11, the server's unit tests of the share
    and the derivation 3 of 3; workspace clippy clean.
  - **Red-checked** in a scratch copy, each mutant rebuilt: no removal on release, no removal on reap, no share check,
    no detach, and a detach that releases (A-171's old rule) each failed their test; the restored tree passed 6 of 6.
  - **Rejected on the way:** a share per client seat (the budget over `clients_per_shard`) gave every client about four
    ring regions, 1,081,474 bytes on fedora, too small for a 4 MiB map on any machine, and a count of 0 or 26.
  - **Fixed on the way, failing test first:** a read of a direct map at or past its end answered `OutOfRange` instead of
    0 (`docs/bugs/2026-10-25-a-direct-maps-read-past-its-end-was-refused.md`).
  - **Fixed on the way, CI's ThreadSanitizer lane (run 40204561799 on 8a86d124):** the hostile-descriptor test's
    non-vacuity check counted the neighbour's marker in the content arena, which the idle sweep seals at rest (A-99); under
    the lane's slowdown the sweep came first and the check found none. The test now maps the neighbour's file too, whose
    copy is never sealed, so the marker is certain; no race was reported.
  - **Owed:** a release on `MappedRead`'s own drop (a drop cannot reach its client: today a dropped map's copy waits for
    an explicit release or the reap); and raising the daemon's own descriptor limit from its soft to its hard value at
    start, which would raise every shard's count without a change here (systemd gives services a soft limit of 1,024
    by default; fedora's session had 524,288).

- **The same-kernel direct map hands a live, sealed copy of one file (A-171, G-direct step 1, 2026-10-25): built,
  and proven on Linux by a real client.**
  - **What:** a `MapRead` is answered with a copy of the file that is the unit of authorization: a sealable memfd of
    the file's page span, the daemon's own writable map taken first, then sealed `F_SEAL_FUTURE_WRITE | F_SEAL_SHRINK
    | F_SEAL_GROW | F_SEAL_SEAL`. It is filled a slice at a time in a task of the owner shard (`crates/server/src/
    direct_map.rs`) and kept equal to the file by the write boundary (`ShardsBackings::insert_peer`), so the client's
    read-only map is a live view within its length. The client reads it through atomics (`slates_mem::PeerView`);
    `MappedRead::bytes()` is gone for `read_at`, `to_vec` and `descriptor`. Decided: a live view over A-135's pinned
    version (the amendment says why).
  - **Proven** on fedora (x86_64 Linux), 5 of 5, `crates/client/tests/client.rs`:
    - zero copy asserted for 20 KiB and 4 MiB files and at every size from empty to 1 MiB, every byte equal;
    - the handed descriptor, used as a hostile peer would: shared writable map, `write`, shrink, growth and hole punch
      refused `EPERM`; a read-only map turned writable refused `EACCES`; its reopen read-write through
      `/proc/self/fd` granted, and that reopen's writable map and `write` refused `EPERM`;
    - another volume's marker (present in the arena, non-vacuity) in none of the copy's bytes, and no other object
      arrived beside the copy (judged by inode: the daemon runs in the test, so its own descriptor of the copy is new
      too);
    - from a second client, a write at 1 MiB, a cut to 1.5 MiB, a growth to 3 MiB and one past the map to 5 MiB, each in
      the map with no request of the mapping client;
    - `slates-mem`'s `peer_object.rs`: 6 of 6 on Linux, 5 of 5 on macOS.
  - **Red-checked** on fedora in a scratch copy with its own target dir, each mutant rebuilt (the harness lists the
    crates it recompiled): without the seals and the confinement check, the shared writable map was granted; without the
    seals alone, the hand-off was refused unconfined and the read came by copy; without the write-through, the write at
    1 MiB never reached the map; with the old arena hand-off restored, it was refused unconfined. The restored tree
    passed 5 of 5.
  - **Regressions run:** vfs 43 binaries (397 tests), bridge-core 109, the client binary 13 and the server's virtio-fs
    9 and Shards 25 suites on macOS; bridge-virtiofs 102, bridge-core 109, the server's virtio-fs 22, mem 132 and the
    client binary 15 on fedora; recovery 41 of 41 (see the sibling below for its first run); workspace clippy and the
    doc gate on fedora.
  - **Owed:**
    - macOS (its descriptor over A-161's socket route) and Windows (handle duplication): G-direct steps 4 and 5; **macOS
      done the same day, A-173** (the entry above);
    - the release, reap and cap behaviour as its own step (G-direct step 2): **done the same day, A-172** (the entry
      above this one);
    - the measurement of copy-once-map-many against copy-per-read, and of the cut's zeroing by stores (G-direct
      step 3);
    - the cross-shard hand-off: a client served by another shard reads by copy;
    - overlays: an untouched file follows the disk, which no write boundary sees, so an overlay reads by copy;
    - a `MapRead` retried across a daemon restart meets its recorded `Mapped` reply with no descriptor behind it, and its
      client's `recv_delivery` waits out the reply deadline. Pre-existing (the reply was recorded before A-171 too);
      not reproduced.
  - **Siblings found, not changed:**
    - `image.rs` `defer`: a refused spawn drops the job inside the shard state's borrow, where its `Drop` cannot reach
      the state (the nested `with_state` answers `None`), so what the job admitted may not be released. The direct map
      releases its copy explicitly on that path. To check by test.
    - `recovery.rs` `memory_others_take_from_a_roomy_host_is_held_only_where_it_eats_into_the_daemons_room` failed once
      in the whole suite on this Mac at load 8–9 ("the daemon took its first sample": the sampler's first reading did
      not come within `within_sampler_wait`), then passed 3 of 3 alone and 41 of 41 in the suite again. A wait that

      pages; diagnostics run 40821794698, 3 runs of 3): a page dirtied through the map (`Z` at byte 0) and not synced
      while another path replaces the file with 16,384 `C`. After a `stat` the map still showed `ZAAAAAAA`, and after
      the map's `msync` the file held `Z` and 16,383 stale `A`: the client wrote its whole page back, and every byte of
      the other path's write was lost. NFSv3 has no recall to make the client flush first. NFSv4.1 would not help
      through Apple's client either: in its source (apple-oss-distributions/NFS, NFS-343.100.5) a `CB_RECALL` only queues

      locks and sends `DELEGRETURN` with no flush of dirty data, where RFC 8881 §10.4.1 asks the client to write
      modified data back first. Nor can the server tell a client's store from the stale bytes of the page it writes
      back, and choosing bytes between the two would be an inferred merge (banned item 11). So on macOS a program that
      maps a file writable and needs another path's concurrent writes kept takes the socket route's writable map

      changes and every other change to the volume) and refuses, `NFS3ERR_IO`, one that would put stale bytes back over
      a newer change. The mask (applying the write-back except its stale bytes) was not an arm: it is the inferred merge
      banned item 11 forbids, and Ada's answer did not authorize it.

- **A READ reply past 64 KiB closed the RPC-with-TLS export (found and fixed 2026-10-25, `3e05c70d`).** rustls caps
  its buffer of sealed records at 64 KiB, and the session's send wrote a reply with `write_all`, so any READ reply past
  it ended the connection, and the kubelet's `hard` mount retried it for good: through a kubelet-mounted export a file
  past about 64 KiB could not be read at all. The node's `mountstats` read 2,953 READs with 2,952 errors, and the
  daemon's `nfs.tls.session` stood at 2,520 and climbing. Found by G-mount step 5's map leg, whose pod never finished
  its first touch of a 64 KiB map; the lane's earlier legs had never sent a large READ. Record:
  `docs/bugs/2026-10-25-a-read-reply-past-64-kib-closed-the-tls-export.md`; test `crates/server/tests/nfs_tls.rs`
  `a_reply_larger_than_the_tls_send_buffer_is_sealed_whole`.
- **A daemon refused every client it cannot see by pid, by undefined behaviour (found and fixed 2026-10-27).** Linux
  reports a socket peer's pid as the reader's pid namespace sees it, and 0 for a process outside it: a client in a
  container of a pod beside the daemon's, with no process namespace shared, which is a pod's default. rustix 1.1's
  `socket_peercred` reads the pid into a non-zero `Pid`, and the invalid value read back as an error through the pid's
  niche, the uid's low bits taken for an errno: "SO_PEERCRED refused (code Some(4))" for uid 65532. The claim was closed
  unanswered. Found by the KIND direct leg's first run. Fixed by `crates/ipc/src/peer.rs`, which reads `SO_PEERCRED` as
  plain integers, at both of its sites (the rendezvous, and the vhost-user seam's check of its front end). Test
  `crates/ipc/tests/rendezvous.rs` `a_client_whose_process_the_daemon_cannot_see_is_served` (a listener in a user and pid
  namespace of its own): red at HEAD on adacachy (`refused SO_PEERCRED refused (code Some(-1000))`), green with the fix,
  the suite 16 of 16. Record: `docs/bugs/2026-10-27-a-peer-whose-process-the-daemon-cannot-see-was-refused-by-undefined-behaviour.md`.
  **Open, reported:** a claim the rendezvous refuses for another uid, or for a peer it cannot read, is closed without
  telling the client why. The client reads "the daemon closed the rendezvous before answering the claim"; only the
  capacity refusal is typed on the wire.
- **The Windows binary needs the Visual C++ runtime (closed 2026-11-04 by c0c8d28c, A-210; seen 2026-10-27).** Built as
  the workspace builds it, with the C runtime linked dynamically (`x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`'s default; neither
  `.cargo/config.toml` nor `release.yml` sets `+crt-static` for Windows), `slates.exe` needs `vcruntime140.dll`, which
  Windows does not ship and Nano Server and Server Core images lack: in a process-isolated `nanoserver:ltsc2025` container
  it exits `0xC0000135`, `STATUS_DLL_NOT_FOUND`, before any code runs (CI's `windows-2025`, run 40580524733). Built with
  `-C target-feature=+crt-static` it runs there whole, the daemon included (run 40582122662). **Addressed 2026-11-04
  (A-210):** `release.yml` builds both Windows binaries with `+crt-static`, and the x86_64 one must answer `slates
  version` in a process-isolated `nanoserver:ltsc2025` container before it may ship. The CI run is recorded in A-210.
- **A CLI attachment ends about a second after the `slates attach` that made it (open, seen 2026-10-27; fixed
  2026-11-06 by A-230, the entry above).** The reaper
  removes a dead client's attachments at the liveness cadence (`crates/server/src/reap.rs`, every 1 s), and each `slates`
  run is a client of its own. So `slates attach`, then `slates write`, then `slates detach`, each a process, races the
  sweep. The KIND legs' helper (`write_through_slates` in `xtask/src/kind_export.rs`) does exactly that. On this Mac at
  load 18 its detach answered `NotFound` (the direct leg's red-check run, 2026-10-27), after the write had landed. The
  direct leg now writes from one client (`crates/cli/examples/pod_direct_probe.rs`, its `write` mode); the export leg's
  helper still races. A user's `slates attach` at the command line meets the same window. Owed, Ada's call: a CLI
  attachment that outlives its process until `slates detach` (as the export's own attachment does), or a `slates write`
  that attaches for itself.
- **The KIND export leg's cluster deletion fails (open, pre-existing, seen 2026-10-26).** `kind delete cluster --name
  slates-export` exits 1 ("did not receive an exit event") in CI runs 40243755704 and 40253147189, after the leg
  passes: the worker's `hard` NFS mount of the export outlives the export's pod, so the node's container does not
  stop. On adacachy it was freed by writing 1 to `/sys/fs/nfs/<device>/shutdown` inside the node's network namespace,
  entered through Docker's `SandboxKey`. Owed: end the consumers and the mount (the pods, then the PersistentVolume)
  before the cluster is deleted, and fail the leg when the deletion fails.
- **A file mapped through the WinFsp mount hides another path's change from every reader of it (A-177, 2026-10-26):
  closed 2026-10-30 by A-190.** After each notification round Windows took, the mount's thread opens each changed file
  Windows holds open through the drive, unbuffered, and writes the changed range from zeros: WinFsp's non-cached write
  flushes the file's dirty pages and purges the range with `CcCoherencyFlushAndPurgeCache` (`src/sys/write.c`), which
  invalidates user mapped views, and the host answers the write without applying it (an open this process made
  unbuffered, named by `FspFileSystemOperationProcessIdF`; recognition fails closed, and with no such export no purge is
  made, counted `winfsp.purges_unavailable`). CI's runners, diagnostics run 41133474977: on x86_64 and arm64 the view
  followed an SDK rewrite within one 20 ms poll, a read through another handle in 169.5 and 169.6 µs, a fresh open
  after the view in 493.5 and 492.6 µs (3.03 s before), the daemon counting 1 purge and 1 write answered without being
  applied; red-checked with no purge planned, the view and a handle's read stale for 10 s (job 124330034929). Still
  open, stated in A-190: a cut under a live view leaves the view's pages past the new end (Windows refuses to cut a
  mapped file, and another path's cut cannot be shown to it); a program's store and another path's write to the same
  page race, the purge's flush writing the program's page first; and a process serving a WinFsp mount must not write
  its own mount unbuffered, since such writes are taken as purges and dropped. The record of the open entry, kept: While any process maps a file through a WinFsp mount, WinFsp's purge of its pages is refused (`CcPurgeCacheSection`
  "will not purge mapped files"), so the notification the mount sends reaches no reader. CI's Windows runner (Windows
  Server 2025, WinFsp 2.1.25156): a read through a second handle, opened while the view stood, stayed stale for 10 s
  (runs 40249524066, 40250856246, 40252840969); once the view and every handle were closed, a fresh open read the change after
  3.03 s (run 40252840969), and after 10 s or more while open contexts were freed twice (runs 40249524066 and 40250856246, before the
  fix in `docs/bugs/2026-10-26-a-winfsp-file-opened-twice-freed-its-first-context-twice.md`). Nothing tells Windows
  again after the views go, so what ends the staleness is Windows releasing the file's section (a hypothesis: not
  instrumented). The candidates, none built: a WinFsp change to `CcCoherencyFlushAndPurgeCache`, which Microsoft says
  invalidates user-mapped views (upstream, not slates'); a notification sent again for a changed file at its last
  close; opening a mapped file uncached, which WinFsp's user-mode API does not expose (`DisableCache` is a field of the
  kernel's reply, `fsctl.h`, set by no callback). The test prints both reads and asserts only the view
  (`a_mapped_view_through_a_winfsp_mount_after_another_paths_change`).
- **The FUSE chaos test refused a write-back once on CI's Linux lane (2026-10-26, run 40252840969): open, not reproduced.**
  `generated_map_stores_direct_reads_and_other_writes_never_revert_another_paths_write`
  (`crates/bridge-fuse/tests/coherence_mount.rs`) panicked at line 1027 unwrapping `EIO` on a third seed after two passed
  (55 and 346 bytes kept back, one write-back refused unknown each). The same code passed on the change's first run
  (40249524066) and 10 of 10 on fedora (2026-10-26). A write-back over an unknown byte is refused `EIO` by design (A-144);
  the test's seeds expect that refusal only where they make it. Not attributed: no log of the run's rounds.
- **A-190's mapped view stayed stale once in main's Windows job (2026-10-31): closed 2026-11-01 (Step 8 of the VFS and
  DAX plan). The cause was a purge Windows did not take; each purge is now read back and made again until it takes.**
  - **What was seen.** In run 41148561681 (slates adeb5fa5, `windows-latest`, image windows-2025-vs2026
    20261021.278.1, WinFsp 2.1.25156) the view and a read through a handle opened after it held the old bytes for 10 s
    each, as before A-190, on a runner the daemon's profile measured loaded. The same test passed in 25 unloaded
    diagnostics iterations (runs 41151000035 and 41166727208).
  - **Reproduced.** The view test ran alone beside two CPU spinners a core and two I/O loops, logging each round's
    purge plan and outcome and each read the host served: 9 of 200 iterations stale on the x86_64 runner, 0 of 200 on
    arm64 (runs 41326838360 and 41327264613).
  - **The cause.** Of the three candidates the third held, a purge made that did not take. Each stale iteration planned
    its purge, made it, had its write dropped and refused nothing, and no read of the file reached the host after it.
    Each of the 95 passing iterations of the second run saw one. `CcCoherencyFlushAndPurgeCache` reports a page it could
    not invalidate as `STATUS_CACHE_PAGE_LOCKED`, a success status, which WinFsp turns into `STATUS_SUCCESS`. What held
    the page is not visible from user mode: nothing the host saw (the purge's open delay, its write time, the last read
    before it) told the stale iterations apart.
  - **The fix.** Each purged piece is now read back through Windows' cache and around it. A purge whose two reads
    differ is counted untaken and made again on its own, after a wait that doubles from a tick. It is given up, counted
    kept, if Windows still keeps the page once the volume's 300 s request timeout has passed (at most 14 attempts;
    A-190, amended).
  - **Measured after** (diagnostics run 41336524903 unless named):
    - x86_64, the reproducing load: 0 of 200 views stale; 10 purges untaken were taken at their first or second retry,
      and none was given up.
    - arm64: 0 of 100 at that load. Beside 40% of memory held, where the code before the fix kept 1 of 100 views stale
      (run 41346373137), the fix kept 0 of 100 (run 41346376630).
  - Bug record: `docs/bugs/2026-11-01-a-winfsp-purge-windows-did-not-take-left-a-mapped-view-stale.md`.
- **The anchored export test binds its export's TCP port unreserved (2026-10-30): open, seen once.**
  `an_anchored_node_serves_its_export_over_rpc_with_tls_across_a_daemon_restart` (`crates/cli/tests/cli.rs`) failed in
  the Linux CLI suite on fedora-2 at load 22–31 (75 of 76 passed) with `AddrInUse` at its own
  `TcpListener::bind(("127.0.0.1", port))`, before any daemon ran, and passed 3 of 3 alone. Its port block holds only
  UDP sockets (`HeldBlock`, the 2026-09-28 fix for a released port taken before the daemon bound it), while
  `start_anchor` binds TCP on the block's base port, which nothing reserved, so any other process can hold it. Owed: the
  block holds the export's TCP listener too, and `start_anchor` hands that one over.
- **Firecracker maps a volume's image with DAX through virtio-pmem (A-165, 2026-10-24): proven by real runs.**
  The image A-160 builds, read through a slates mount, is the pmem device's backing file. The guest loads the nine
  modules its distribution kernel builds virtio-pmem and nd_pmem as, then mounts the device as ext4 with `dax=always`.
  Nothing in the daemon changed.
  - **Proven on the box** (`crates/cli/tests/guest_image.rs`, gated; Linux 7.2.9, Firecracker v1.17.0, capped runs at
    load 38–84):
    - the pmem test, 5 of 5 whole-binary rounds on the committed code: the guest's unsynced store is in the host's file,
      the host's write reaches the guest's map in 8–13 µs, the guest's sync reaches slates, and the merge is exact;
    - the takeover test, 10 of 10: a daemon killed under the live map loses nothing, and the host's write reaches the
      map 83–3,351 µs after the takeover;
    - the crash test, 5 of 5: a killed Firecracker's unsynced store reaches the volume, and the merge refuses the image
      `NotClean` until `e2fsck -fy` has checked it.
  - Six red-checks, each failing at its own check (A-165).
  - **What a user meets after a guest's crash:** the merge refuses the image `NotClean`, and goes on refusing it after
    a later guest's clean unmount (ext4 keeps an unchecked file system unchecked). `e2fsck -fy` on the image through its
    mount makes it clean, and adds a `lost+found` (root's, mode 0700) that the merge takes as a new directory. Recorded,
    not changed: e2fsck puts any orphans it recovers there, so the merge must not drop it. `docs/cli.md` says so.
  - **Owed:** the arm64 guest's pmem DAX (Firecracker's doc covers aarch64, with `CONFIG_ARM64_PMEM`): G-arm64-guest.
- **Proven 2026-10-25 (G-vhost step 4): the VM and the daemon killed under a guest's live map.**
  `crates/cli/tests/guest_vhost.rs`, two tests on the box beside step 3's:
  - **The VM killed** (`a_vm_killed_with_unsynced_stores_leaves_them_in_the_session_through_its_devices_end`): the guest
    stores over three spans without syncing, and once past the file's end. crosvm and its device processes take
    `SIGKILL`, and a mount write races the device's end over part of one span. Once the device has ended, the session
    holds each store within the file (the stream's end ingested them), the mount's later write where it wrote, and
    nothing of the store past the end. A second guest's map holds the same. **Red-check:** with no ingest at the
    stream's end the test fails at that check (byte 4196 holds the seed where the dead guest stored 2).
  - **The daemon killed** (`a_daemon_killed_under_a_guests_live_map_ends_its_device_and_loses_nothing_the_guest_synced`):
    after synced stores, a mount write and an SDK write, and one store left unsynced, the daemon takes `SIGKILL`. The VM
    ends by itself: crosvm takes a vhost-user back end's hangup for a crashed device ("vhost-user worker thread exited
    with an error: ... Backend device disconnected early", "device crashed", "exiting with success", exit status 0;
    `VmEventType::DeviceCrashed` in `devices/src/virtio/vhost_user_frontend/mod.rs` at 1c8d17a85). The successor holds
    every synced byte and acknowledged write and not the unsynced store, which died with the daemon. Recovery removed
    the device's record (`slates detach` of its attachment answers `NotFound`). The session's FUSE mount is taken over
    (A-61), and a fresh VM through the successor sees a write made after the takeover.
  - **Runs:** on the fixed code, the daemon kill 9 of 9 (5 alone, 4 in the whole binary) and the VM kill 4 of 4, capped
    as in step 3; `guest_dax.rs` 3 of 3 beside them. **Found:** the A-170 bug below, in 2 rounds of 3 before the fix.
  - **Owed, a later goal:** a VM that outlives its device's daemon. The anchor would have to hold the device's socket
    end and its state (vrings, memory table, back-end channel, windows) across the restart, as A-61 holds a FUSE device.
    This vhost-user route logs each guest write in the shard's write log before its used element since A-410
    (2026-11-18; before, it answered a write with neither a log record nor a publication, safe only because the VM died
    with the daemon), so that precondition is met. The Shards stream route already lets a VM outlive its daemon, and it
    logs: see the route table in GAPS 2026-11-18, "a WinFsp write answered before its publication was lost".
- **Fixed 2026-10-25 (A-170), found by step 4: a clone's copy-up sealed its origin's open extent behind the origin's
  image, so a crash lost the shard.** `docs/bugs/2026-10-25-a-clones-copy-up-sealed-its-origins-open-extent-behind-its-image.md`.
  - **Symptom:** the daemon-kill test failed 2 rounds of 3, then 3 of 4, always the fastest rounds. The successor logged
    "partition 1: the recovery images' blocks were not claimed, no volume is rebuilt: EIO" and refused the origin, the
    boot volume and the session.
  - **Cause, named by instrumenting the claim:** two images named one open block, `(64, 0)`, with births 0 and 1. The
    session's copy-up had sealed the origin's shared open extent in place, and the origin, still clean, kept
    publishing the extent the seal freed; the session's next extent took the block.
  - **Exposure:** any clone whose origin's snapshot held a file's last window open, changed by the clone, then a crash
    before the origin published for a reason of its own. No VM or DAX is needed.
  - **Fix:** a clone copies an open extent its origin owns (`ChunkStore::copy_open`); only a volume's own is sealed in
    place.
  - **Failing first:** two vfs tests (claim refused, `RecoveryIncomplete`) and a daemon restart test (the origin's file
    read back as zeros), each red-checked with the in-place seal restored; the vfs (43 binaries) and recovery (41)
    suites pass.
  - **Price:** at most a chunk copied per such file, charged to the clone (`retained_bytes.rs` restates the rule).
  - **Siblings:** the copy-up's seal refusal left a retention charge uncredited. The fix's one method for the seal and
    the copy credits it now, untested, and a test injecting the refusal is owed. The cold reseal
    (`Volume::reseal_inode`) changes shared chunk records with no ownership check and no dirty mark: reported, not
    changed, owed a recovery test first (the bug record has both).
- **Fixed 2026-10-25, found sweeping A-170's siblings: a seal the chunk slab refused left the file on a freed block.**
  `docs/bugs/2026-10-25-a-seal-the-chunk-slab-refused-left-the-file-on-a-freed-block.md`.
  - **Cause:** under a cipher (A-99), sealing an open extent whose block the committed image names copies the bytes to a
    new block. `seal_where_safe` freed the old block, deferred to the next commit, before the replacing chunk was
    recorded. A refused record (the chunk slab full) then leaked the copy and put the file's open extent back on a block
    already let go; after the next commit another file's write took it.
  - **Fix:** the old block is freed only once the replacing chunk is recorded, and a refused record gives back the
    seal's tags and the copy. The cold reseal (`ChunkStore::reseal`), whose failed seal left a record on the freed old
    block, now frees a copy it cannot use.
  - **Failing first:** `a_seal_the_chunk_slab_refuses_leaves_an_imaged_open_extent_whole` (a one-record slab). It found
    32,768 bytes leaked and the file reading another's bytes after the next commit, and passes after.
  - **Exposure:** a sealing daemon at its chunk slab's bound (the idle sweep and a write's window seal reach it). The
    reseal twin was latent: the daemon runs `seal_pending`, not `seal_idle`, so it never reseals.
  - **Owed:** a test of the reseal's failure after a copy.

  (`SOCKET_PLACEHOLDER`, used only by the Unix arm of `exec_vmm`); the constant is now named by its path there. The

- **Proven 2026-10-25 (G-vhost step 3): a real crosvm guest maps a session's file through slates' own device with
  DAX.** `crates/cli/tests/guest_vhost.rs`, gated like `guest_dax.rs` (the box: KVM, crosvm 1c8d17a85, host and guest
  Linux 7.2.9-2-cachyos). `slates vhost-user SESSION --dax-window 8MiB -- crosvm run --vhost-user
  type=fs,socket={socket} ...`; the guest's probe mounts the tag `dax=always`. The session is a clone of a snapshot of
  an origin: a guest's writes land in it directly, so no merge follows (the image route merges; this one need not).
  Each check holds the guest's map, read as memory alone, and the session, read through slates, to a model, byte for
  byte:
  - another path's change shows in the map the moment its writer is answered, with no request of the guest's: a
    `slates mount` write, the SDK's whole-file write, a growth past the end the guest knows, zeros over a cut (where
    the mount route's guest hangs: "a stated limit of DAX under KVM", above), and a growth past the last page once the
    guest maps again;
  - the guest's stores reach the session at its `msync` and at its close without one; a store past the file's end
    never does, and a later extension over it zeroes it in the session and in the guest's own map (POSIX.1-2024
    `mmap`: "the system shall never write out any modified portions of the last page of an object which are beyond
    its end");
  - the origin keeps its own bytes, and its later write never reaches the session's map (A-166, by use);
  - three generated histories of 80 steps mix it all (73 stores, 11 past the end; 52 mount writes opening 14 holes; 16
    SDK writes; 12 size changes; 30 new maps; 44 checks).

  **Green 3 of 3** (`cargo test -p slates-cli --test guest_vhost` in a `systemd --user` unit: `MemoryMax=20G`,
  `CPUWeight=1`, `Nice=19`, the nvme IO caps; 1.63–4.79 s a run at load 24–140; one round before them, on the draft
  that neither printed the counters nor drained the probe's console, passed too). **Red-checked** from a scratch copy
  with its own target, each mutation failing at its own check: no write-through (the map as the mount's write is
  answered holds the seed); no ingest (the session by the sync's answer lacks the guest's store); no window (the
  guest's `dax=always` mount is refused). **Non-vacuity:** the device now adds its backed DAX counts to the owner's
  status as it runs (`virtiofs.dax_*`, A-168); the histories counted one map sent, one upgrade answered with no message,
  123 requests held for ingests, 51 to 58 runs ingested across the rounds, and the backing let go at the end. The stand-in route test holds
  the counts' exact values; without the report it fails at the first.
- **Fixed 2026-10-25: the guest probe cut its last reply short.** Found by the no-window red-check: the probe's fatal
  reply arrived as `"mount virtiofs tag slates at /mn"`. The probe powered the VM off once the tty held its bytes, not
  once the serial port had sent them. It now drains the console first (`tcdrain`); the same red-check then showed the
  whole reply, `... at /mnt: Invalid argument (os error 22)`, and `guest_dax.rs` (3 of 3) and `guest_image.rs` (4 of 4)
  pass with it. `docs/bugs/2026-10-25-the-guest-probes-last-reply-was-cut-short.md`.
- **Built 2026-10-25 (A-169): an out-of-process VMM attaches slates' own virtio-fs device by the attach verb.**
  `AttachRequest::VhostUserFs` hands the client the device's socket end over its control socket; `slates vhost-user ID
  -- VMM ... {socket} ...` runs the VMM with it as `/proc/self/fd/N`. Linux only; elsewhere refused `BindingNotBuilt`.
  Proven by use with a stand-in front end on both shards, its refusals typed with nothing left behind, the whole DAX
  route through the daemon's real serve loop (map, another path's write in the window, the writable upgrade, the
  guest's store at FSYNC), and the CLI with a real anchor; and through a real crosvm guest, the VM and the daemon
  killed under its live map included (G-vhost steps 3 and 4, the entries above).
- **Fixed in the device 2026-10-25 (A-168), and proven through a real crosvm guest the same day (G-vhost step 3,
  above): slates' own DAX window showed stale bytes, then zeros, after another path's write.**
  `docs/bugs/2026-10-24-slates-own-dax-window-shows-stale-bytes-then-zeros-after-another-paths-write.md`.
  - Found by a real crosvm run (2026-10-24): `A` for 40 s after an SDK write of `B`, then, once a guest request drove a
    pass, SHMEM_UNMAP left crosvm's zero pages and the map and `pread` read 0.
  - The message placer's window now maps the file's backing (A-163's object), which the write boundary keeps equal to
    the file, so nothing revokes it and no change reaches it as a message. Re-pointing the window was rejected: the
    vhost-user specification forbids a map over a live one.
  - Proven by eleven hermetic tests against a stand-in front end, on Linux x86_64. The pre-fix code fails the same
    checks (stale bytes, then the window torn), and eight mutations each fail their own test (A-168).
  - **Owed, decided in A-168:** the fd-sharing placer keeps pinned blocks for now (no in-process VMM is wired; the L1/L2
    DAX defenses are built on them), but by the same sources its revoke leaves a guest at a `PROT_NONE` hole it will
    not re-ask for. Before an in-process VMM ships, it takes the backed route or is retired.
- **Observed 2026-10-25, not changed: the FUSE edge answers an exhausted arena `EIO`.** `bridge::errno` maps
  `VfsError::Memory(MemError::ArenaExhausted)` to its catch-all `EIO`, on every path: a FUSE write, and now a DAX
  write-back's FSYNC (`a_refused_write_back_fails_the_fsync_that_asked_for_it` asserts whatever the edge names it). The
  arena calls the refusal retryable after growth, so `ENOSPC` or `EAGAIN` would tell a writer more. A mapping decision
  across every transport, left for its own change.
- **Fixed 2026-10-25 (A-166): a change of a clone reached a guest's DAX map of its origin.**
  `docs/bugs/2026-10-25-a-clones-change-reaches-its-origins-dax-backing.md`. The store kept DAX backings by inode number
  alone, and a clone (a snapshot a device presents is one) shares its origin's numbers, so either volume's write reached
  the other's guest's map. Exposure was the Shards route (A-163) on a volume with a clone in the same shard. Backings are
  now keyed by the volume's own prefix and the number together; `a_change_of_a_clone_never_reaches_a_backing_of_its_
  origin` failed before the fix and passes after, and the 25 Shards tests pass unchanged.
- **Fixed 2026-10-25 (A-167): a range a guest maps past a file's end missed later writes into it.**
  `docs/bugs/2026-10-25-a-range-mapped-past-the-files-end-missed-later-writes.md`. The fill clipped an asked range to the
  file's size, so a guest whose size was stale (another path cut the file) mapped a range write-through never reached,
  and read zeros there after a later extension. `covered` now covers every range an ask touches;
  `a_range_asked_past_the_files_end_takes_a_later_write_into_it` failed before and passes after.
- **Fixed 2026-11-18 (A-419, goal 83 B7, g079): a fill refused part-way unmarked its range but left the pages it
  stored in the object, and a later fill of the range skipped what the volume then held as holes or zeros, so those
  pages reached a guest's map.** A fill refused or given up part-way now leaves its range uncleared: no write reaches
  it, it stays counted against the fill budget, and its next fill clears it before storing anything
  (`docs/bugs/2026-11-18-a-dax-fill-refused-part-way-left-its-bytes-for-a-later-fill-to-show.md`). Tests, with an
  injected refusal (`crates/bridge-core/src/dax_backing.rs`): `a_fill_refused_part_way_leaves_nothing_a_later_fill_shows`,
  `a_fill_abandoned_part_way_leaves_nothing_a_later_fill_shows` and
  `a_part_way_fill_stays_counted_until_its_range_is_filled_again`; red without the fix 3 of 3 (the first slice still
  read `A` after the file was zeroed; one range counted where two held bytes), green with it, on the Mac Studio.
  - **Fixed 2026-11-18 (A-526, goal 85, g079): a successor's adopted DAX object (A-365) could hold a fill's bytes in a
    range its range table does not name** (a range the dead daemon was filling, or one that failed there), which the
    successor's next fill skipped as before A-419. A backing taken back from a dead daemon now clears each range not
    filled before its first fill (`ShardsBacking::owes_clear`); held by
    `a_range_a_dead_daemons_fill_left_part_way_reads_the_volume_once_filled_again` (bridge-core's unit tests), red
    without the fix on the Mac Studio. Record:
    `docs/bugs/2026-11-18-a-range-a-dead-daemons-dax-fill-left-part-way-showed-its-bytes-to-the-successors-guest.md`.
    **Left:** those bytes are counted by nothing until the range is filled or the backing goes (at most the ranges the
    dead daemon's fills had begun and not finished).
  - **Fixed 2026-11-18 (A-530, goal 85, g079): on Windows a range was committed before its charge was asked, so a
    `Budget` refusal left a committed range uncounted that Windows never gives back.** A range's fill now begins with its
    charge (`dax_backing::begin_range`): refused, nothing is readied or cleared; a readying or clear the OS refuses after
    it gives the charge back and refuses `Object`. The ordering is held on every host by
    `a_range_is_charged_before_anything_is_made_for_it` (bridge-core's unit tests), red with the old order on the Mac
    Studio. Record: `docs/bugs/2026-11-18-a-windows-dax-range-was-committed-before-its-budget-charge-was-asked.md`.
    **Owed (main's):** the Windows run of the lib tests and a Windows Shards DAX map past the budget. **Run 2026-11-20
    (w-bugs, goal 87):** `a_range_is_charged_before_anything_is_made_for_it` and
    `a_range_a_dead_daemons_fill_left_part_way_reads_the_volume_once_filled_again` pass on Windows x86_64 (jupiter, main

- **Open, reported by A-166's sibling sweep (each from reading; each to be proven by a test before a change):**
  - **Fixed 2026-11-18 (g251):** write-log replay (`verbs::replay_one`) routed a logged FUSE write by its inode number's
    prefix, which for a clone's inherited file is its origin's: a replayed write landed in the origin and the clone lost
    it (proven by `a_replayed_write_to_a_clones_inherited_file_lands_in_the_clone`, red with the prefix routing put
    back). Every write-log record now names the volume it was written through and is replayed there, the `FORGET`s too;
    the log's header carries a layout word, and a log of the layout before that holds records is reported as lost writes,

  - the in-process DAX gate's recall (`has_writable_of_prefix`, `writable_of_prefix`, `recalling(no.prefix())`) counts

  - `DaxRegistry::has_writable_of` keys by number alone: the backed session's `EBUSY` over-refuses across volumes;
  - `volume_config` wraps `next_prefix` at 65,535 with no check against live volumes' prefixes.
- **Fixed 2026-11-08 (slabs), found by the new tests: a read-only attachment was not a read-only file system to its
  client.** On every FUSE transport an open for writing was granted and each write refused `EPERM`; NFS answered `PERM`.
  Now an attachment that may read but not write, and a snapshot's view, answer `EROFS` (at the open for a write-mode
  open, and at every mutating verb): `NFS3ERR_ROFS`/`NFS4ERR_ROFS` over NFS, `STATUS_MEDIA_WRITE_PROTECTED` from WinFsp,
  one mapping in the bridge's `authorize_write` (§4.6 "A read-only attachment is a read-only file system"). An
  attachment with no rights stays `EPERM`. Windows' disposition delete asks `CanDelete` first (`authorize_change`): a
  read-only drive's four changes are each refused `ERROR_WRITE_PROTECT` on both Windows runners (diag-slabs-37, run
  42483804345: the WinFsp unit tests 80, the CLI suite 17); `DeleteFile` succeeded with that check taken out
  (diag-slabs-38, run 42483804058). On Linux at c275acbb the bridges, the server suite and the CLI flow passed
  (diag-slabs-39, run 42486855316). Nobody has run the conformance suites on this branch: conformance expects no change
  to its records, from reading the harness (no suite mounts read-only, and pjdfstest's `EROFS` cases are FreeBSD-only),
  and its expected-failure lists have no `EROFS` entries.
  Record: `docs/bugs/2026-11-08-a-read-only-attachment-was-not-a-read-only-file-system.md`.
  - **The open over a kernel NFS mount: fixed 2026-11-08 (slabs; found by conformance's read-only pjdfstest run, CI run
    42498995934).** Through a read attachment the kernel's v3 and v4 clients granted `open(O_WRONLY)` and `open(O_RDWR)`
    of an existing file, and v4 answered `open(O_RDONLY|O_TRUNC)` `EACCES`: ACCESS granted the write bits from the mode
    alone, the kernel decides a v3 open from it, and v4's OPEN asked the same ACCESS. Now ACCESS grants no write bit
    where the bridge refuses a change, a v4 OPEN for writing asks `CHANGE_ALLOWED` first and answers `NFS4ERR_ROFS`, and
    a change under a state id is refused ROFS before its state id is judged. Through the kernel
    (`crates/server/tests/nfs_read_only_kernel.rs`): on main, v3 `[granted, granted, EROFS]` and v4 `[granted, granted,
    EACCES]` (diag-slabs-42, run 42517407649); with the fix, v4 `EROFS` for each and v3 `EACCES` for each open
    (diag-slabs-43, run 42517769901, with workspace clippy, the NFS bridge and the server's kernel NFS suites green). v3's
    `EACCES` at open is its limit, not a miss (A-269). The bridge's read-only export test is red with the ACCESS mask
    taken out (granted 29 for 1). Conformance's probe counts the v3 opens as that limit (its 0fad3bb2). Its run on this
    fix (diag-conformance-32, run 42523564648): v3 10 of 14 `EROFS` and the three opens at the limit, v4 13 of 14; the

  so a 4 KiB-page guest of a 16 KiB-page Mac is told 16 pages: 64 KiB a request where a write may be 256 KiB. The
  kernel mount needs the host's count (its channel buffer is fixed); a VM route could name 64. Not measured yet; owed
  with part 2's real boot, where the request rate is measured.

    a mount's kernel held would stay referenced until the next restart's recovery settles it. The test: unmount a FUSE
    mount that holds a removed file and read the volume's referenced bytes, as `a_closed_stream_gives_back_what_its_
